items.title: Trump's silly Reflecting Pool story masks something serious
items.summary: Donald Trump spent a lot of time this spring talking about renovations he wanted to make at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool . Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Donald Trump's renovations for the Reflecting Pool haven't worked out. Trump could blame himself — he's the one who ordered it. Instead, he offered stories about vandals. We're used to Trump falsehoods. When they are turned into federal charges — like this one did — it should freak us out. On July 2, federal prosecutors charged David Hearn, a 67-year-old former Olympian, with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC. Hearn had made a " a violent effort " to damage the pool, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro said. A month later, Pirro's office told the court she wanted to drop the case. It turns out, Pirro said in a court filing late Friday, that the pool's well-documented problems probably weren't a result of vandalism. Instead, they were likely because of "hasty and botched work" performed by a contractor. A standard news management rule of thumb is that you put out embarrassing news right before the weekend, when it's least likely to get noticed. And most of the coverage of the Hearn case has indeed focused on the embarrassment it is generating for the Trump White House. Primarily because up until now, Pirro has been a loyal Trump supporter. But if we treat this story like a standard-issue optics narrative for the Trump White House, we're doing it wrong. Because this is something much more important: It's the Trump White House using federal prosecutors as a tool to punish perceived enemies. In a normal administration, this would be a giant story. The fact that we're treating this like business-as-usual should be a giant story, too. The story of the Reflecting Pool, and Trump's obsession with it, has been well told. The shortest version is that last spring, the Trump administration ordered a poorly conceived renovation using contractors without experience doing that kind of work. So instead of a clear pool with an "American flag blue" bottom, the pool became an algae-infested bog. But Trump wouldn't acknowledge that his plan hadn't worked. Instead, he insisted that rogues had attacked the pool with a box-cutter and somehow gouged a " 300-foot slit " in the pool's lining. That made the pool a "Trump says thing that's obviously not true" story — the kind that initially seemed unique back in 2017, when he insisted that his lightly attended inauguration was actually the world's biggest . Now that kind of tall and easily disprovable tale just elicits shrugs. Last month, Pirro turned Trump's fibs into something much more serious by using them as the basis for a felony charge (her office later charged three other Americans with misdemeanors for similar theoretical offenses). In Pirro's motion to dismiss the charge against Hearn, she argues that she was misled by Trump's Department of the Interior, which oversees the pool. The DOI initially provided "less than fulsome information" about the case, Pirro said. So her office didn't really understand what had happened until late July — weeks after a grand jury had indicted Hearn. That's silly. Throughout the spring, story after story from mainstream news outlets reported that Trump's attempt to transform the pool was misguided , poorly executed, and had made things worse . Just as important: Trump's claims about vandalism weren't remotely plausible . So, again: It's one thing not to correct Donald Trump when he says things that aren't true (Trump continues to insist that VANDALS are the cause of the pool's problems, as he argued on Truth Social this weekend; when I asked his press office for comment Monday, they referred me back to his post. He told reporters Monday that Pirro "made a mistake.") It's another thing to tell stories about the president that don't seem to be true . But turning a Trump falsehood into a federal criminal charge is something very different. It's also not the first time we've seen federal prosecutors turn themselves into Trump-branded prosecutors. The New York Times, for example, has documented hundreds of flimsy charges the administration has filed against immigrants and protesters during its ICE crackdowns in the last year. Almost half of those have fizzled, the Times reports: "Juries acquitted defendants, judges threw out charges, or prosecutors withdrew them." The Times itself has been the subject of a Trump legal campaign — last month Trump's Department of Justice filed subpoenas against Times reporters who'd written about security issues with Trump's new Air Force One, then dropped them after getting scolded by a federal judge . In the Hearn case, it's tempting to brush this aside: After all, Pirro dropped the charges. The system worked, right? But Hearn, whose case attracted support from prominent allies , should never have had to face a felony charge — and to take on the legal, reputational, and financial obligations fighting that charge entails — in the first place. So the fact that the federal government has seemingly conceded that it brought a bogus case shouldn't give anyone comfort. It should make you wonder how many dubious charges Donald Trump's prosecutors have filed so far — and how many more we'll see while he's in office. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: How to Secure AI Agents, MCP Servers, and LLM Apps in Production
items.summary: Agents, MCP integrations, and LLM-powered applications are entering codebases faster than most security programs can track them. Mend.io’s new practitioner guide , ‘ Securing AI agents, MCP servers & LLM apps: A practical framework ’ , targets that gap. It is organized around three moves: see what matters , fix what matters faster , protect AI in production and ships seven reusable artifacts. Why traditional AppSec breaks AppSec was built on one assumption: applications do what their code says. Agentic AI breaks it. Agent behavior emerges from a model, a system prompt, retrieved context, user input, and the tools it may call. Two identical deployments can behave differently. The failure modes are new too. Prompt injection arrives through data, not code. An over-permissioned agent can take harmful actions without any vulnerability being exploited. A deprecated model keeps serving predictions after its maintainer stops patching it. A poisoned tool description on an MCP server can redirect an agent’s behavior without touching the application. None appear in a CVE feed. The mandate is two-sided: shift left, and protect right. Artifact 1.1: the five-layer attack surface map Interaction : user inputs, retrieved documents, inter-agent messages → prompt injection, context poisoning, data exfiltration Agent : system prompts, configs, memory, autonomy settings → over-permissioned tools, unsafe defaults, goal hijacking Integration : MCP servers, tool definitions, plugins, APIs → poisoned tool descriptions, unscoped credentials, shadow servers Model : foundation and fine-tuned models, embeddings → EOL models, supply chain risk, unsafe generations Code : AI-generated code, AI frameworks, SDKs → vulnerable code, framework CVEs, malicious packages See: agent and MCP discovery Agents rarely arrive through procurement. Three categories to hunt: shadow agents , unregistered MCP servers , and embedded AI frameworks . Every MCP server needs an owner, an access scope, and a review. There are five discovery methods. First, scan repositories for agentic signatures. Second, watch network egress for calls to model API endpoints. Third, audit service accounts and API keys. Fourth, make declaration cheap via lightweight registration. Finally, automate continuously, since point-in-time discovery goes stale fast. Artifact 2.1 extends the AI-BOM with nine fields per agent or MCP server: identity, model dependency, autonomy level, tool permissions, credential scope, data reach, MCP endpoints, prompt location, last review. Artifact 2.2 is a 12-point misconfiguration checklist : credentials scoped to specific resources, not broad service-level access; no shared credentials between agents; high-impact tools requiring human approval; system prompts in version control, not editable in production; MCP servers authenticating clients; tool descriptions reviewed for injection-bearing content before adoption (tool poisoning); model versions pinned with EOL monitoring and an owner. Fix: prioritization and triage AI expanded the finding surface, not just the attack surface. The pipeline is enrich → prioritize → triage. Prioritization signals, in order of value: reachability, exploitability context, business context, agentic amplification, fix availability. Artifact 3.1 draws the automation line: Decision Disposition Reachability/dataflow, well-understood classes Automate FP/TP assessment with evidence trails Automate, with sampling Tier-3/high-risk applications AI-assist, human decides Novel classes, AI behaviors, no evidence Human only Accepting risk or deferring a fix Human only, documented Two rules govern it . Every automated closure carries evidence; if the system cannot show why something is a false positive, it goes to a human. Error rates get sampled review, with thresholds triggering retraining. Protect: runtime security Runtime protection involves guardrails, prompt hardening, policy enforcement, and monitoring. Operating as a loop with AI red teaming, red team discoveries improve guardrails, while guardrail logs guide subsequent red teaming. Guardrails deploy in two ways: via an in-app Python SDK (supporting Online or isolated Offline modes) or as a standalone API Server (Docker) requiring no code changes or Python dependencies. The minimal viable setup includes inbound guardrails catching prompt injections, out-of-policy requests, and jailbreaks, alongside outbound guardrails catching credentials, PII, proprietary code, unsafe content, and policy violations. System prompt hardening follows five patterns: assuming disclosure, separating instructions from data, constraining the blast radius, versioning/reviewing, and adversarial testing. Setting strict permissions is more effective than prompt instructions—preventing tool access removes the need to instruct against dangerous actions. Artifact 4.1 contains seven validation checks. The maturity roadmap Four stages: Emerging, Developing, Controlling, Leading. It is aligned to NIST AI RMF , OWASP AIMA , ISO/IEC 42001 , and the EU AI Act . Artifact 5.1 is a 15-question self-assessment: 0–5 Emerging, 6–10 Developing, 11–13 Controlling, 14–15 Leading. Key takeaways Agent behavior emerges from model, prompt, context, input, and tools — not code alone. Five risk layers: interaction, agent, integration, model, code. Hunt shadow agents, unregistered MCP servers, embedded AI frameworks. Automate evidence-backed triage; keep risk acceptance and novel findings human-only. Guardrails ship as an embedded Python SDK or a standalone Docker API Server. Check out the full guide here . Thanks to the Mend.io team for the thought leadership / resources for this article. items.title: Research roundup: 6 cool science stories we almost missed
items.summary:
It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. July’s list includes outfitting cyborg cockroaches with a tiny diving suit for navigating flooded terrain; confirmation that a Medici duke died of malaria, not poisoning; the best evidence to date that Betelgeuse is orbited by a companion star; and evidence that some ancient Egyptian princesses were skilled archers. Sacrificial Incan boy died of blunt force trauma Credit:
          Administrative Archive, Regional Museum of Iquique–CORMUDESI It's known that the Incas practiced a human sacrifice ritual known as Capachoca, in which children were offered to the mountains and believed to become divine themselves, serving as intermediaries with the gods. This often involved pilgrimages to the remote sacrificial sites, with colonial accounts describing strangulation, asphyxiation, and blunt force trauma as the most common methods of sacrifice. Archaeologists have reanalyzed the remains of one such victim and concluded the boy died from blunt force trauma, rather than freezing to death as previously believed. They described their findings in a paper published in the journal Science Advances. Read full article Comments

It's known that the Incas practiced a human sacrifice ritual known as Capachoca, in which children were offered to the mountains and believed to become divine themselves, serving as intermediaries with the gods. This often involved pilgrimages to the remote sacrificial sites, with colonial accounts describing strangulation, asphyxiation, and blunt force trauma as the most common methods of sacrifice. Archaeologists have reanalyzed the remains of one such victim and concluded the boy died from blunt force trauma, rather than freezing to death as previously believed. They described their findings in a paper published in the journal Science Advances.

items.title: I tried a photobooth in NYC that matches you with a mystery soulmate — but there's a big catch
items.summary: Business Insider reporter Sydney Bradley tried out a "missed connections" photobooth in NYC. Sydney Bradley/BI A dating startup and popular social media page teamed up for a photobooth pop-up in New York City. The "Missed Connections Booth" opened in July and pairs people with a compatible match. BI's Sydney Bradley tried the booth out herself — and there's a catch. Between a flash flood warning and running late for dinner plans in Manhattan, I figured I'd have just enough time to snap a photo in a photobooth. The photos weren't for my own vanity, though. It was in the pursuit of … love! Dubbed the "Missed Connections Booth," the photobooth is a collaboration between Matchbox (a dating startup) , Meet Cutes NYC (a popular social media account), and Faceplace (a photobooth vendor). Here's how it works: Fill out a 26-question survey, pay $10, take some photos of yourself, and a compatible match will print alongside your strip of selfies. "The whole thing is very rom-com coded," Liam McGregor, Matchbox's cofounder , told me. Since opening in mid-July, foot traffic has been steady, with 3,500 people getting matches, McGregor said, and some days have had lines wrapped around the corner. He added that the age demo stopping by typically falls between 18 and 35. The "Missed Connections Booth" is located outside the Santo Taco Union Square location. Sydney Bradley/BI There's one glaring obstacle, however. The only information about your match you get is their photos and a first name — no last name, no age, and no contact information. The onus is on you to find that special someone (if you're smitten with that semi-anonymous somebody). "Despite the odds, if you could find your missed connection, wouldn't that be an exciting story?" McGregor said. While waiting my turn, I chatted with some of the people also in line on a rainy evening. Caroline, a 32-year-old who said she's "one of the last single ones" in her friend group (some of whom encouraged her to go try out the booth). Her match wasn't her type, "but I'm sure he's lovely," she said. A 22-year-old woman who lives in New Jersey and commutes to the city. She said she's not using any dating apps and would prefer to meet someone through friends. A 26-year-old woman who was mostly there for the photobooth, not the matchmaking. I asked if she believed in soulmates: "To an extent, yeah. But if it's meant to be … they'll find me." Bradley, a 35-year-old man, said he's "not hopeful about it, but it seems cool," he said. "And if it does, then that's a good story." Before taking photos, people fill out a 26-question survey. Screenshot/Matchbox After waiting about 30 minutes, I received my match within seconds of taking my photos (which, by the way, allows only one retake). I wasn't head-over-heels for the mystery match — Ben — I got, but then again, all I have to go off of are four black-and-white photos. Setting people up isn't the photobooth's goal, anyway. "I don't think that this is a replacement for dating apps," McGregor said. "If you want to find someone to go on a date with this Friday, I would not recommend going to the photobooth. But it has this whimsy and this magical feeling of there's someone out there for me ." Perhaps the illusion of a potential match is enough to keep thousands of New Yorkers optimistic about dating. The booth has already become a viral social media phenomenon on TikTok and Instagram Reels — from people documenting their experience, shooting their shot at finding their match, or, in McGregor's words, doing it "for the plot." Though the photo booth is a stunt, the energy it taps into has been running through the dating app world. To combat swipe fatigue, the old guard of dating apps and newcomers alike are fighting to prove that they can offer new ways to find love, from real-life events to AI matchmakers . Craving IRL connection and romance There was a throughline in my conversations outside the Missed Connections Booth: People would like to meet romantic partners in person or through existing social circles. McGregor himself met his fiancée through mutual friends, he said. McGregor, now 28, cofounded Marriage Pact (and its subsidiary matchmaking technology, Matchbox) in 2017 while a student at Stanford University. Marriage Pact helps students on college campuses find partners using a questionnaire, and Matchbox uses a similar survey and algorithm to pair up compatible people at IRL events. In 2022, Marriage Pact raised a $5 million seed investment round led by Bain Capital Ventures. The line for the booth wrapped around the taco restaurant — even on a rainy day. Sydney Bradley/BI Singles are "craving just a bit more connection" than the typical dating app swiping experience , McGregor said. Dating app giants like Tinder and Bumble are catching on, too, with initiatives focused on IRL dating events to woo younger daters. Venture-backed startups, meanwhile, have entered the fold with new offerings, such as IRL social app 222 , which told Business Insider in February that it has raised $13.7 million to date. "Dating in New York is so hard, you might as well try whatever," said Caroline, the single 32-year-old, who has tried apps like 222. As for the Missed Connections Booth's future, the pop-up will continue in New York through August. McGregor told me there are ideas of expanding the experience to other cities, too. I recommended a booth in an airport. Even more fodder for a rom-com fashion meet-cute. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Alexander Rakhlin named director of  the MIT Statistics and Data Science Center
items.summary: Alexander “Sasha” Rakhlin PhD ’06, the Distinguished Professor in Data, Systems, and Society at the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS); and a professor of brain and cognitive sciences at MIT, has been named the next director of the MIT Statistics and Data Science Center (SDSC). Rakhlin succeeds Ankur Moitra, the Norbert Wiener Professor of Mathematics, associate director of the IDSS, and a faculty member in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) who has been SDSC director since 2021. Philippe Rigollet, the Cecil and Ida Green Distinguished Professor of Mathematics and a core faculty member in IDSS, also served as interim director in 2024-25. “Sasha is one of the sharpest theoretical minds working in statistics and machine learning today, and also one of the most devoted mentors I know,” says Fotini Christia, the Ford International Professor of the Social Sciences and director of IDSS, which houses SDSC. “He has helped train an entire generation of interdisciplinary scholars through the Interdisciplinary Doctoral Program in Statistics (IDPS), while his own research keeps pushing the boundaries. The SDSC could not ask for a more fitting leader.” Rakhlin is the inaugural holder of the Distinguished Professorship in Data, Systems, and Society, an endowed chair created in 2025 by the generosity and vision of IDSS professor Richard “Dick” Larson, an “MIT lifer” and pioneer in operations research, queueing theory, and system optimization. “I am honored to take on this role,” says Rakhlin. “The strength of the Statistics and Data Science Center has always been its people — students, postdocs, and faculty from across MIT who bring sharply different perspectives to the most interesting problems of the day in statistics, machine learning, and AI. My goal is to support that community as it takes on the constantly evolving questions reshaping the field.” Rakhlin has been connected to the Statistics and Data Science Center as a visiting professor since 2016, before formally joining MIT in 2018 in the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences and IDSS. As the initial chair of the Interdisciplinary PhD in Statistics program at the SDSC, Rakhlin has seen the successful defense of over 75 IDPS PhD students across a variety of departments at MIT, including IDSS’ own Social and Engineering Systems program. “I have been fascinated by machine learning since my PhD work more than 20 years ago, drawn by its beautiful connections to statistics, probability, algorithms, optimization, and game theory,” says Rakhlin. “At the Statistics and Data Science Center, I work alongside colleagues who share this fascination and pursue these connections in many directions. The recent revolution in AI is extending this web into the sciences; it promises to accelerate discovery, and it raises new questions for statistics. Answering them demands a rigorous science of the tools themselves. As AI enters medicine, energy, and public life, its safety and security are, at their core, statistical and mathematical questions: quantifying uncertainty, providing guarantees, understanding failure, and resisting manipulation.” As Rakhlin puts it, the SDSC is built for this moment. “Statistics is a shared language across MIT,” he adds. “Through the Interdisciplinary Doctoral Program in Statistics, the center connects students and faculty from economics and political science to physics and engineering. Collaborations in areas from biology to nuclear fusion have shown how statistical thinking accelerates science itself.” As director, one of his goals is to deepen these interdisciplinary connections. He hopes to help make SDSC the Institute’s home for the rigorous foundations of data science and AI, and a bridge to the scientific and societal questions where those foundations are most needed. Rakhlin received his bachelor’s degrees in mathematics and computer science from Cornell University, and doctoral degree from MIT. He was a postdoc at the University of California at Berkeley in EECS before joining the University of Pennsylvania, where he was an associate professor in the Department of Statistics and co-director of the Penn Research in Machine Learning center.

items.title: A preventive neurologist shares 2 overlooked dementia risk factors
items.summary: A preventive neurologist said hearing loss is associated with a higher risk of dementia. Siarhei Khaletski/Getty Images A preventive neurologist said vision and hearing loss are risk factors for cognitive decline. Some researchers theorize that sensory loss reduces brain activity and stimulation. Wearing sunglasses or earplugs at concerts can go a long way in curbing vision and hearing loss. If you're trying to reduce your personal risk of developing dementia or Alzheimer's, the answer might be right in front of your eyes — or within earshot. Dr. Kellyann Niotis, a preventive neurologist and assistant professor of neurology at Weill Cornell Medicine, said vision and hearing loss are two risk factors for cognitive decline. "They're two big ones that people don't often think about as related to their brain," Niotis said at a June salon dinner with Julianne Moore to promote Brain Health Matters, a public health campaign from Lilly to encourage brain health awareness. "So if you are not up to date on your annual screenings, please, please, please do that." Niotis, who focuses on diseases like Alzheimer's, told Business Insider that she hopes more people will take risk factors like sensory loss more seriously as they age. A 2024 Lancet study found that nearly half of all dementia cases worldwide could potentially be prevented by mitigating risk factors , including vision and hearing loss. Niotis shared why our eyes and ears are so linked to brain health — and what to watch out for. Why sensory loss may be connected to cognitive decline Some researchers believe sensory loss can lead to more social isolation, increasing the risk of cognitive decline. Milamai/Getty Images Niotis said researchers are still trying to figure out exactly why hearing and vision loss are tied to neurodegenerative diseases like dementia. As of now, there are some hypotheses. One is related to brain stimulation. A big part of brain health preservation is challenging your brain , be it through puzzles, learning a new language, or playing an instrument, Niotis said. Sensory loss can make it harder to activate certain parts of the brain. "There's a thought that as someone loses their sight, they aren't being provided with that sensory stimulation that that region of the brain needs," Niotis said. Another theory is more straightforward: losing your sight or hearing has downstream effects on other brain-healthy habits . "If you can't see well, are you less socially engaged? Are you more socially isolated? Are you less willing to engage in activities, like exercise, that otherwise are keeping your brain active?" Niotis said. Watch out for halos or other people complaining about your hearing Cataracts might increase your risk of cognitive decline. Toa55/Getty Images When it comes to sensory loss, there are a few red flags to watch out for. For vision loss, conditions like cataracts are common in older adults and reduce visual sharpness. Even so, "if that's significantly impacting your ability to see, it could be putting your brain at risk," Niotis said, whether the loss of vision weakens signals in the brain or changes how you socialize. You should consider getting an eye examination if you experience signs of glaucoma (a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve), changes in how you perceive colors, seeing a lot of halos (such as when you're driving), and words "jumping" around the page, she said. These are not, on their own, direct symptoms of dementia or cognitive decline, and do not necessarily influence dementia risk. However, untreated, they could become risk factors down the line, Niotis said. Hearing loss is a little more subtle: "It's often recognized by people around you," Niotis said, so if you're suddenly fielding complaints from friends and family, it might be a sign to get your hearing checked — and not delay it. "Most people I find are not able to appreciate that loss the same way they are able to appreciate vision loss," she said, making it easier to dismiss. A few simple lifestyle tweaks can reduce your risk Wearing UV-protective sunglasses blocks harmful UV rays that can lead to vision loss in the future. Goodboy Picture Company/Getty Images Thankfully, there are some ways to preserve your hearing and vision. One of the biggest preventable causes of hearing loss "is completely in our control," Niotis said. "It's exposure to loud noises." She said taking precautions such as wearing earplugs at concerts or proper hearing protection when working loud machinery is very important. When it comes to vision loss, Niotis said wearing sunglasses and reducing direct sun exposure to the eyes can protect the eyes from ultraviolet radiation, which contributes to cataracts and some other UV-related eye damage. And while there's no research that links permanent vision loss to screen time, Niotis said it can still be a good idea to take screen breaks. items.summary_html:
A preventive neurologist said hearing loss is associated with a higher risk of dementia.

Siarhei Khaletski/Getty Images

  • A preventive neurologist said vision and hearing loss are risk factors for cognitive decline.
  • Some researchers theorize that sensory loss reduces brain activity and stimulation.
  • Wearing sunglasses or earplugs at concerts can go a long way in curbing vision and hearing loss.

If you're trying to reduce your personal risk of developing dementia or Alzheimer's, the answer might be right in front of your eyes — or within earshot.

Dr. Kellyann Niotis, a preventive neurologist and assistant professor of neurology at Weill Cornell Medicine, said vision and hearing loss are two risk factors for cognitive decline.

"They're two big ones that people don't often think about as related to their brain," Niotis said at a June salon dinner with Julianne Moore to promote Brain Health Matters, a public health campaign from Lilly to encourage brain health awareness. "So if you are not up to date on your annual screenings, please, please, please do that."

Niotis, who focuses on diseases like Alzheimer's, told Business Insider that she hopes more people will take risk factors like sensory loss more seriously as they age. A 2024 Lancet study found that nearly half of all dementia cases worldwide could potentially be prevented by mitigating risk factors, including vision and hearing loss.

Niotis shared why our eyes and ears are so linked to brain health — and what to watch out for.

Why sensory loss may be connected to cognitive declineSome researchers believe sensory loss can lead to more social isolation, increasing the risk of cognitive decline.

Milamai/Getty Images

Niotis said researchers are still trying to figure out exactly why hearing and vision loss are tied to neurodegenerative diseases like dementia. As of now, there are some hypotheses.

One is related to brain stimulation. A big part of brain health preservation is challenging your brain, be it through puzzles, learning a new language, or playing an instrument, Niotis said.

Sensory loss can make it harder to activate certain parts of the brain. "There's a thought that as someone loses their sight, they aren't being provided with that sensory stimulation that that region of the brain needs," Niotis said.

Another theory is more straightforward: losing your sight or hearing has downstream effects on other brain-healthy habits. "If you can't see well, are you less socially engaged? Are you more socially isolated? Are you less willing to engage in activities, like exercise, that otherwise are keeping your brain active?" Niotis said.

Watch out for halos or other people complaining about your hearingCataracts might increase your risk of cognitive decline.

Toa55/Getty Images

When it comes to sensory loss, there are a few red flags to watch out for.

For vision loss, conditions like cataracts are common in older adults and reduce visual sharpness. Even so, "if that's significantly impacting your ability to see, it could be putting your brain at risk," Niotis said, whether the loss of vision weakens signals in the brain or changes how you socialize.

You should consider getting an eye examination if you experience signs of glaucoma (a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve), changes in how you perceive colors, seeing a lot of halos (such as when you're driving), and words "jumping" around the page, she said. These are not, on their own, direct symptoms of dementia or cognitive decline, and do not necessarily influence dementia risk. However, untreated, they could become risk factors down the line, Niotis said.

Hearing loss is a little more subtle: "It's often recognized by people around you," Niotis said, so if you're suddenly fielding complaints from friends and family, it might be a sign to get your hearing checked — and not delay it. "Most people I find are not able to appreciate that loss the same way they are able to appreciate vision loss," she said, making it easier to dismiss.

A few simple lifestyle tweaks can reduce your riskWearing UV-protective sunglasses blocks harmful UV rays that can lead to vision loss in the future.

Goodboy Picture Company/Getty Images

Thankfully, there are some ways to preserve your hearing and vision.

One of the biggest preventable causes of hearing loss "is completely in our control," Niotis said. "It's exposure to loud noises." She said taking precautions such as wearing earplugs at concerts or proper hearing protection when working loud machinery is very important.

When it comes to vision loss, Niotis said wearing sunglasses and reducing direct sun exposure to the eyes can protect the eyes from ultraviolet radiation, which contributes to cataracts and some other UV-related eye damage.

And while there's no research that links permanent vision loss to screen time, Niotis said it can still be a good idea to take screen breaks. "If you're someone who's staring at a phone or screen all of the time, you're training your eyes to do one particular task, which is to converge and look in front of you," she said, potentially leading to temporary eye strain or eventual nearsightedness.

For that, she recommends taking a break and going for a walk — an already brain-healthy habit.

items.title: Alibaba’s AI coded for 16 days straight and every commit is on GitHub
items.summary: Alibaba has launched Qwen3.8-Max , a multimodal model with 2.4 trillion parameters and built for complicated tasks that may take several days to complete. Now available through QwenCloud and Alibaba Cloud Model Studio, it’s priced at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens. Qwen3.8-Max builds on the Qwen3.5 architecture and uses a sparse mixture-of-experts design with hybrid attention. Although the model contains 2.4 trillion parameters in total, it activates approximately 95 billion for each token. The mixture-of-experts architecture draws on the parts of the model needed for each task — instead of running all 2.4 trillion parameters every time. According to the company, the model weights will be published on Hugging Face and ModelScope next week, making it the first Qwen-Max model released with downloadable weights. The model’s mixture-of-experts architecture draws on the parts of the model needed for each task, which still leaves developers with an enormous model to host. How the harness works Even with only 95 billion parameters active at once, the full weights must be stored and distributed across multiple high-memory GPU nodes. In practice, that puts self-hosting beyond the reach of most developers and makes Qwen3.8-Max a more realistic option for large organizations and inference providers with the infrastructure to run it. quot Qwen3.8-Max is a realistic option for large organizations and inference providers with the infrastructure to run it. This brings Alibaba close to Moonshot AI’s new Kimi K3, which has 2.8 trillion parameters . Alibaba holds a 36% stake in Moonshot AI , so these are not fully independent rivals. Kimi K3 topped Arena’s frontend coding leaderboard within hours of its debut, and demand overwhelmed Moonshot’s GPU capacity so fast that the company had to pause new subscriptions. Kimi K3’s open-weight release ran into exactly this problem: Demand blew past GPU capacity within 48 hours, and the model’s 2.8T parameters made self-hosting impractical for all but the largest shops. Qwen3.8-Max now enters the same race. Other long-running demos According to Alibaba’s tests, Qwen3.8-Max spent 16 days building a command-line app , took five days to reproduce a research paper’s results , and improved a chip design after about 500 iterations . Alibaba has not released enough information for outside researchers to verify these results. Alibaba’s most ambitious software demo had Qwen3.8-Max spend 16 days building “oh-my-cli” on its own. During that time, it made 265 commits and opened 127 pull requests as it worked through 151 GitHub issues . The repository and its audit trail are public under qwen-code-dev-bot/oh-my-cli , so developers do not have to rely solely on Alibaba’s account of what happened. The difference between the model and its harness is key for long-running jobs. The difference between the model and its harness is key for long-running jobs. The model decides what to do next, but the system around it handles everything else. These parts can decide if an agent runs for 16 days or fails after just 16 minutes. That infrastructure layer is what Anthropic acquired the CI/CD startup Mendral to build out , and it’s the same lesson GoDaddy learned when it opened its registrar to AI agents ; the guardrails had to come first. Alibaba says it trained Qwen3.8-Max on complicated projects that an agent might actually encounter. The model performed similarly when tested with QwenWork, Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw and Hermes. The company has published guides showing developers how to connect it to those tools. Developers should soon be able to put that claim to the test. Model Studio works with the OpenAI and Anthropic API formats, so teams can bring Qwen3.8-Max into coding tools they already use without rebuilding their setup from scratch. Context window limits In one experiment, the model was given the paper “Unified Data Selection for LLM Reasoning” without any code. Alibaba says the agent wrote about 7,600 lines of code, started 33 GPU training jobs, and reproduced the paper’s six main results. It also tested 18 more ideas and improved the reported AIME24 result by 2.7 points. In another test, Qwen3.8-Max optimized a cryptographic circuit over about 500 iterations. Alibaba says the model cut the design from 8,298 logic gates to 678 . After running it through OpenROAD, an open-source chip design tool, the physical area dropped by 81%. This was not a one-shot coding test. The agent had to inspect each result and use it to decide what to try next. But even a million-token context window can only take an agent so far. Developers will want to see whether Qwen3.8-Max can remember earlier decisions and instructions as a project grows. Sending nearly one million tokens at every step would cause other problems — and as the economics of agentic AI have shown , cheaper per-token pricing does not automatically translate to cheaper projects when autonomous agents are consuming tokens at rates that dwarf human-supervised sessions. But even a million-token context window can only take an agent so far. Developers will want to see whether Qwen3.8-Max can remember earlier decisions and instructions as a project grows. Benchmarks need outside verification Alibaba’s internal benchmarks show Qwen3.8-Max performing close to models from Anthropic and OpenAI. According to Alibaba, it scored 86.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, compared to 88.8 for OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol (max). Independent runs of the same benchmark produce somewhat different scores for both models, so these figures may shift once outside labs repeat the tests. It also placed fifth in Text Arena and second in Vision Arena . In Alibaba’s own comparison table covering 31 tests , the model leads in six; Claude Fable 5 or GPT-5.6 Sol comes out ahead in most of the rest. These results make Qwen3.8-Max a strong contender, but they do not yet prove the model can maintain production software on its own for weeks. Once Alibaba releases the weights, developers can find out how well Qwen3.8-Max works outside the company’s own setup. If its performance drops when it is moved to different infrastructure or connected to other coding tools, that will tell us far more than its place on a leaderboard. items.title: Lego deploys Hubble Space Telescope as detailed desktop model
items.summary: For 35 years, the Hubble Space Telescope has looked out into the Universe. Now, Lego is inviting builders to look inward with its latest model of the orbiting observatory. The new Lego Icons Hubble Space Telescope (set no. 11382) was released on August 1 for $140 at the toy company's stores and its online shop. The 1,252-piece kit builds a 15-inch-long (38-cm) desktop model that is about twice as large as the previously released Lego Hubble models. The Icons Hubble is the first to be sized in comparison to a Lego minifigure, such that the included astronaut provides a sense of scale for the telescope. Read full article Comments

items.title: The US Air Force's plan to upgrade its 70-year-old B-52 bombers is billions over budget, watchdog finds
items.summary: The US has about 76 B-52s in its fleet. US Air Force photo by Airman Ben Selchow The US Air Force's B-52 bomber upgrades are delayed and over budget by billions of dollars. The B-52 Stratofortress has been flying since 1950, and the Air Force hopes to keep it around into the 2050s. The modernization plans include new commercial engines and radars. Cost and scheduling challenges have pushed the US Air Force's B-52 Stratofortress modernization program billions over budget, according to a new report. The aging B-52 has long been a workhorse of the Air Force, which is replacing the bomber's decades-old engines to keep the aircraft flying into the 2050s. But the upgrades have run into delays and rising costs. Last week, the Government Accountability Office, a government watchdog agency, released a report on the current status of the B-52 modernization and sustainment efforts. Of the 13 upgrades that the bombers are getting, 10 are experiencing cost, schedule, or performance challenges. The most expensive B-52 upgrade, the Commercial Engine Replacement Program, has seen a roughly $3 billion increase in cost since 2023, with the initial operational date pushed back more than 15 months. The GAO report said that the program "will likely continue to face significant challenges as the Air Force plans to begin production with little to no developmental flight testing." The other components being upgraded include new radars, communications systems, training devices, and advanced target pod displays. The B-52s are also being modified to carry the AGM-181 Long-Range Standoff weapon, a new nuclear-armed cruise missile under development. Completing B-52 upgrades at the same raises risks of future hardware work, the GAO found. US Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Helen Ly According to the GAO, there are challenges in the Air Force's approach, which involves working on many of these upgrades at the same time. "Work on one program may involve moving hardware on the aircraft that relates to work to be completed by other modernization programs," the report said. Previous GAO reports have highlighted challenges in the modernization program. In its most recent report, the GAO made six recommendations for the Air Force, including delaying the engine production decision until the program office analyzes recent cost growth and schedule delays to understand risks and benefits. Despite reported issues with the modernization program, officials have touted the significance of the B-52 modernization program. Last year, Vice. Admiral. Richard Correll, then the Trump administration's nomination to head US Strategic Command, told Congress the upgrades were "essential" to ensuring the bombers can fulfill their intended role in strategic deterrence. The engine replacements, which will put Rolls-Royce engines inside the B-52s, would, alongside the radar technologies, essentially make the B-52 bomber "a new airplane." Earlier this year, the B-52 demonstrated its continued ability to support combat operations by flying overland bombing missions over Iran. "Over the past 30 days, we've struck more than 11,000 targets," Air Force Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said in March, one month into the Iran war. "Given the increase in air superiority, we've successfully started to conduct the first overland B-52 missions, which allow us to continue to get on top of the enemy." Conversations surrounding the modernization of the B-52s come as defense experts and lawmakers sound the alarm about broader problems facing America's fleet of air assets, which is shrinking and aging at an accelerating pace. items.title: If the Labs Wobble, the Clouds Feel It First
items.summary: I have written separately about the shaky economics behind the data center boom and the growing pressure on the frontier labs . This post connects the two. Microsoft reported $24.1 billion of revenue from its OpenAI relationship, an amount equivalent to almost one-quarter of Azure’s scale, although the figure includes revenue-sharing payments as well as cloud consumption. The best estimates put OpenAI and Anthropic at another 11% to 14% of AWS. More important, Microsoft’s commercial backlog grew 84%, but only 25% without OpenAI. That does not prove an AI bubble, but it does show how concentrated the next stage of cloud growth has become. A large part of the infrastructure boom is being built today against future spending commitments from a handful of private companies whose revenues, margins, and funding needs remain difficult to assess. AI can keep improving while the assets financed around it still produce disappointing returns . That concentration would worry me less if OpenAI and Anthropic had obvious, durable pricing power. I do not think they do. Open models keep narrowing the gap, customers are routing more work to cheaper systems , and enterprises can increasingly turn their own data and workflows into specialized models they control . Microsoft reported $24.1 billion of revenue from its OpenAI relationship, an amount equivalent to almost one-quarter of Azure’s scale, although the figure includes revenue-sharing payments as well as cloud consumption. A large part of the infrastructure boom is being built today against future spending commitments from a handful of private companies whose revenues, margins, and funding needs remain difficult to assess. items.title: An AI-supervised remote exam went so badly that 58,000 students must retake it
items.summary: Earlier this summer, nearly 160,000 applicants took the entrance exam for UNAM, Mexico's largest university. For the first time, they did it completely remotely, using a "lockdown" browser and AI-powered webcam proctoring software, over several weeks from late May through early June. It was a disaster. When exam results came in, they bore little resemblance to past results, especially at the top. Between 2021 and 2025, 3.5 percent of test takers scored 100 or more on the 120-question UNAM test. This year, 16.3 percent did so. Read full article Comments

items.title: Top Consulting Group PwC Caught Using AI on “Thought Leadership” Report About AI, Resulting in Corporate Document Filled With Bizarre Hallucinations
items.summary: PwC, one of the “Big Four” consulting firms, has been caught red-handed publishing “thought leadership” reports about AI riddled with lazy and easily-spotted hallucinations. As the Financial Times reports , four reports published between 2024 and 2026, were meant to solicit consulting work for partners in the Middle East. But as investigators from AI detector firm GPTZero found , the reports were an utter mess, chock full of “hallucinated (vibe) citations, fabricated claims, and incomprehensible drafting and formatting decisions.” The offending reports contained “claims that are unrelated to or contradicted by the cited source.” For instance, a 2025 report included an entire section about a framework known as “Citizen Pulse,” which it alleged was being deployed by governments around the world. However, GPTZero found that the framework didn’t actually exist and was entirely hallucinated by an AI, including supporting citations. The findings highlight just how pervasive AI hallucinations have become, from lawyers being reprimanded by judges after being caught including fake legal citations in court documents to entire academic fields being inundated with dubious AI-generated papers. Even prestigious consulting firms are providing their clients with shoddy and entirely unverified slop, raising plenty of uncomfortable questions about the quality of their professional services. Just last month, another Big Four firm, KPMG, was caught including copious amounts of AI hallucinations in a report about how to integrate AI agents “across investment advisory, risk management and compliance monitoring.” The latest case is particularly egregious considering several of PwC’s slop-heavy reports were explicitly about “agentic” AI bots, including a guide for governments on how to improve public services for autonomous vehicles. The extent of the slop is baffling. One of the PwC reports included a footnote referencing a teenage blogger on Medium with 280 followers being cited as a source for a JPMorgan agentic AI initiative. GPTZero researcher Paul Esau found that a different PwC report had cited the same (correct) claim that human error is responsible for 90 percent of traffic accidents three times in just two pages, while using three different sources, something that “no human” would do, as he told the FT . In response, PwC downplayed the findings and failed to take accountability. In a statement to the newspaper, PwC Middle East claimed that it “takes the accuracy of our published research seriously and is updating a limited number of supporting citations” in the reports. “Consistent with our approach to responsible AI, we have quality control processes for research and content development we expect all our people to adhere to.” More on hallucinations: Consulting Firm’s Report on How Awesome AI Is Found to Contain Idiotic AI Hallucinations The post Top Consulting Group PwC Caught Using AI on “Thought Leadership” Report About AI, Resulting in Corporate Document Filled With Bizarre Hallucinations appeared first on Futurism .

items.title: Flock cameras are everywhere. Here's how they track cars.
items.summary: Flock cameras read the license plates of passing cars and then collect and store the data for future investigations. Mint Images RF/Getty Images Flock cameras read license plates and then collect and store the data for investigations. Flock cameras can misread plates, leading to wrongful arrests. Critics also raise privacy concerns. Police say Flock can help them track vehicles and solve crimes. Flock cameras are in thousands of communities across the country and often hide in plain sight. A Flock camera is an automated license plate reader, or ALPR, made by the public-safety technology company Flock Safety. The cameras are commonly installed along roads, at intersections, near neighborhood entrances, and around businesses or other private properties. When a vehicle passes, the camera captures an image and uses machine learning to turn its license plate, color, make, model, and other details into searchable information. That makes them useful for those deploying them, like the police. Law enforcement agencies say Flock's technology can help them track down vehicles and locate crime suspects. In some cases, officers can search for a specific car across tens of thousands of cameras nationwide. The technology has also sparked a growing backlash . Dozens of communities have cancelled, paused, or suspended contracts , citing privacy concerns, potential misuse of the cameras, and data sharing with federal immigration officials. Flock says its license plate readers do not use facial recognition and that customers — meaning the ones putting up the cameras, not the ones being monitored — can control access to and sharing of the data collected. "They are built to focus on the vehicle involved in an incident and the details that can help distinguish it from other vehicles on the road," Flock says. The company says that vehicle records are automatically deleted after 30 days by default, although customers may configure different retention periods when contracts and local laws permit. Who makes Flock cameras? The Sacramento suburb of Roseville, California, has been using Flock Safety's AI-powered cameras since 2021. Andri Tambunan for BI Flock cameras are manufactured by Flock Safety, an Atlanta-based company that develops surveillance and public-safety technology. Its CEO, Garrett Langley, founded the company in 2017. In a recent blog post published in May, he wrote: Nine years ago, I lived in a neighborhood in Atlanta where crime was ticking up. People were breaking into cars and pulling firearms out of glove boxes. Nobody seemed able to do anything about it. A police major told me something I've never forgotten: more than 70 percent of crime involves a vehicle, and most of those crimes go unsolved because police rarely have the license plate. So I did what engineers do. I built a system to find the plate. A few months later, it worked, and that was the beginning of Flock. Its customers now include police departments, local governments, businesses, schools, homeowner associations, property operators, and other private organizations. Flock says that it has deployed some 120,000 cameras across 49 states. In a recent X post , Langley said that during a single day, those cameras alerted authorities to more than 4,000 sex offenders, some 2,100 stolen cars, over 1,600 wanted people, about 160 missing people, and one Amber Alert. Flock operates as a subscription business, charging annual service fees for each camera. Flock was recently valued at $8.4 billion . The company also sells conventional video cameras, audio-detection technology, investigative software, and drones. Why is there controversy around Flock cameras? Some people are concerned about Flock cameras because the devices can collect information about ordinary drivers who are not suspected of crimes. Business Insider previously reported that in at least a dozen instances across the country, misreads, or a lack of verification by officers, resulted in innocent people being stopped at gunpoint or detained in jail, among other outcomes. In Toledo, Ohio, driver Brandon Upchurch was mauled by a police dog after a Flock camera misread the "7" on his license plate as a "2." In Roseville, California, Flock incorrectly read the plate in 71% of 1,427 stolen-vehicle and felony alerts issued during 2023 and 2024, a Business Insider investigation found. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit that advocates for civil liberties in the digital world, says Flock cameras constitute mass surveillance because they photograph every passing vehicle rather than only those connected to suspected crimes — like a speed camera might. Critics say a broad network of cameras can reveal intimate patterns showing when a vehicle visited particular homes, businesses, medical facilities, religious institutions, or political events. "It has been misused by police to spy on their ex-partners and could be used to target people engaged in First Amendment activities or seeking medical care," the EFF wrote in a blog post. The EFF obtained records showing that Texas deputies queried Flock's network during an investigation involving a woman suspected of self-managing an abortion. The EFF and the ACLU have also reported that local police departments shared or searched Flock data for immigration-enforcement purposes. Flock says that data sharing can expand the system's reach by allowing agencies to search records collected outside their jurisdictions. Are there Flock cameras near me? Flock does not publish a complete public map showing every camera in its network. The company says its cameras are used by law enforcement agencies, businesses, homeowner associations, and other private organizations in the United States. One way to find nearby cameras is to use DeFlock, an open-source, community-run project that maps automated license plate readers. Local government records can also clarify the location of cameras purchased or operated by public agencies. The ACLU says that residents can search city council agendas, police department policies, contracts, purchasing records, and meeting minutes for terms such as "Flock Safety" or "automated license plate reader." What does a Flock camera look like? Flock cameras can be powered by solar panels. Photo by Shellie Murdaugh/Bluffton Today/Reuters Flock cameras can be powered by solar panels. A typical Flock license plate reader looks like a small rectangular box mounted near the top of a narrow roadside pole. Several installations are also equipped with a small solar panel mounted on the pole, allowing the camera to operate without a conventional connection to the electrical grid. The camera is usually angled toward one or more traffic lanes to photograph the front or rear of passing vehicles. Flock says its cameras can be found along road shoulders, in medians, near neighborhood entrances, and around parking lots. Are Flock cameras constitutional? The Fourth Amendment prohibits unreasonable government searches and seizures. The law generally treats license plates and vehicles driven on public roads as information in the public domain. "ALPR cameras sit at fixed and obvious locations and register still images of vehicles at that location and time. They do not follow a vehicle from origin to destination, cover only a small fraction of a city's roads, and provide samples, not a seamless diary of one's movements," Flock said in a white paper published in November 2025. It added that "the constitutional concern arises when technology stitches together a comprehensive portrait of someone's movements over time that can reveal intimate and sensitive details. Fixed, point-in-time roadway observations occupy the other side of that line." Privacy and civil-liberties groups disagree. The ACLU and EFF say that networked cameras can collectively create a detailed and searchable record of where people travel, even if each camera captures only one location at a time. Correction: An earlier version of this story misstated the date of the data referenced in a post by Flock CEO Garrett Langley. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Tom Holland and Zendaya's PR strategy is leaving millions on the table. Pros say that's a good thing.
items.summary: Tom Holland and Zendaya promoting "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" in Germany. Tristar Media/WireImage Tom Holland and Zendaya recently married after years of keeping their relationship low-key. Outside of promo tours for "Spider-Man," the couple rarely appears in public together. PR pros say discretion benefits the couple's image, even if it's not the most lucrative strategy. If you look closely at a patch of skin on Zendaya's ribcage, you'll spy a tiny, discreet "T" tattooed in black ink . Her longtime partner, Tom Holland , has a similarly easy-to-miss "Z" tattoo tucked beneath his left arm. The permanent tributes to each other's initials go unseen at most events and red carpets, peeking out only in select moments — an almost too-perfect metaphor for Zendaya and Holland's public-facing relationship. Although Zendaya and Holland went Instagram-official in 2021, the exact timeline of their relationship is unknown. While many fans speculate the "Spider-Man" costars actually began dating years earlier, the couple's prudent navigation of fame and their respective careers means there's been precious little material to go on. Outside their promotional duties as Peter Parker and his love interest, MJ, in the MCU film franchise — their latest movie, " Spider-Man: Brand New Day ," earned the biggest domestic box office debut in history — the actors rarely broadcast their relationship, on social media or otherwise. They have never walked a non-Marvel-related red carpet together, and fans can count on one hand how often they've kissed in sight of photographers. Even when news broke last year that Zendaya and Holland were engaged , there was no official announcement from the couple, let alone a collection of Instagram-friendly floral proposal photos. Zendaya simply began wearing a diamond on her left-hand ring finger. The media rollout for their marriage was equally nonexistent, with Zendaya's stylist, Law Roach, spilling the beans . Holland then confirmed the news to Esquire , gingerly and succinctly. When and where did they tie the knot? Who was invited? What did Zendaya wear? With this anti-PR power couple, we may never know (though AI-generated photos of the wedding went viral). Zendaya at the Los Angeles premiere of "Spider-Man: Brand New Day." Amy Sussman/Getty Images And yet, the lack of intimate details doesn't cause fans to doubt that Zendaya and Holland are in love, or to cry "PR relationship." In fact, the effect has been quite the opposite. With only subtle signs of their affection for each other displayed in public, their relationship feels effortless. "It's the way they hold hands. It's the way they look at each other," Mike Fahey, the founder and CEO of the PR agency Fahey Communications, told Business Insider, adding, "None of that is rehearsed." "The fans, the people at home, that's what they relate to — that type of love," he continued. Indeed, the positive reaction to Zendaya and Holland's top-secret wedding shows how careful breadcrumbing has endeared fans to the couple's love story, even as they keep the meat and potatoes protected. "It wasn't a spectacle at Madison Square Garden ," Fahey said of the couple's nuptials. "It's like their love is their love and they show it outwardly in very subtle but beautiful ways." Of course, a certain level of secrecy can actually incite even more demand for attention. But with Zendaya and Holland, it's not that fans have nothing to fawn over — it's that the couple is giving just enough to signal there is a deeper, genuine relationship happening between them in private. They exchange adoring glances, but they don't pack on the PDA. They speak highly of each other in interviews, though often as a "best friend," not a husband or wife. They don't dismiss the topic of their relationship outright when asked about it, but they don't invite additional questions. Fahey called it "a masterclass in only giving people as much as they need." "Little gestures go so far, and I think that's what social media has picked up on. You can really see their bond," Fahey said. "We're looking at a couple here that has insane upward momentum and could really do whatever they want from here." The permanent tributes to each other's initials go unseen at most events and red carpets, peeking out only in select moments — an almost too-perfect metaphor for Zendaya and Holland's public-facing relationship.

Although Zendaya and Holland went Instagram-official in 2021, the exact timeline of their relationship is unknown. While many fans speculate the "Spider-Man" costars actually began dating years earlier, the couple's prudent navigation of fame and their respective careers means there's been precious little material to go on.

Outside their promotional duties as Peter Parker and his love interest, MJ, in the MCU film franchise — their latest movie, "Spider-Man: Brand New Day," earned the biggest domestic box office debut in history — the actors rarely broadcast their relationship, on social media or otherwise. They have never walked a non-Marvel-related red carpet together, and fans can count on one hand how often they've kissed in sight of photographers.

Even when news broke last year that Zendaya and Holland were engaged, there was no official announcement from the couple, let alone a collection of Instagram-friendly floral proposal photos. items.title: TimeSeries Tiered Storage Journey: Kafka/Flink Streams to Native Cassandra Cold Reads
items.summary: By Oleksii Tkachuk , Rajiv Shringi , Chris Lohfink , Abe Ratnofsky , Kartik Sathyanarayanan Introduction In an earlier post , we introduced the TimeSeries Abstraction, our high-throughput, low-latency platform designed to store and query temporal event data at scale. It has since become the operational backbone for Netflix’s largest datasets, which now span multiple petabytes. However, managing such large datasets in hot storage, tuned for low-millisecond latency access , is not cheap. At Netflix, cost-efficiency is a continuous discipline rather than a temporary initiative. This post shares two solutions that significantly reduce storage costs by continuously moving older, less frequently accessed data into cheaper object storage: Solution 1 : Uses Apache Kafka and Flink to stream data directly to S3 Solution 2 : Leverages Cassandra backups in S3 and pluggable Memtables to read data directly from S3 We’ll start with the Kafka/Flink-based design, then describe how we evolved to a native Cassandra-based cold tier. Challenges As Netflix’s TimeSeries datasets have expanded, we’ve encountered several compounding challenges: Growing retention demands : Users often push for increasing data retention to serve a broader range of use cases, which in turn increases the storage costs. Escalating costs : Maintaining massive, dense clusters for infrequently accessed historical data is prohibitively expensive. Sparse historical access: Most queries target recent events, but older data must remain readily available for occasional audits and investigations. Operational strain : High storage density on hot nodes complicates scaling, deployment, and cluster stability. Latency requirements : Even historical data sometimes requires sub-second query performance for internal tooling and analysis. This creates a clear opportunity: keep the most recent data on fast storage and migrate older, rarely read data to cheaper storage while preserving a consistent API . Done well, this can meet user and operational needs while greatly reducing our infrastructure spend. TimeSeries Abstraction Before we dive into the cold storage solutions, here is a quick recap of how TimeSeries partitions its dataset into multiple tables, each covering a window of time we call Time Slices . Time Slices and Immutable Windows This enables several key optimizations, most notably allowing a table to become immutable once it crosses the write boundary, which lets us safely apply further optimizations. For more details, refer to our previous post . This slice information is critical and is maintained in a dedicated metadata table: Time Slice Metadata Storage Creating new Time Slices and maintaining their metadata is a primary responsibility of the TimeSeries control plane. The TimeSeries data plane uses this information to correctly route the read and write traffic to the provisioned tables. TimeSeries Data and Control Plane With that background, let’s look at the different solutions we built for data tiering. Solution 1: Streaming with Apache Kafka and Flink Our first solution followed a familiar streaming pattern using Apache Kafka and Flink, where we streamed data to S3 in realtime while simultaneously persisting it to Cassandra. Streaming with Apache Kafka and Flink Getting Data Into S3 Efficiently To optimize data streaming to S3, the system hash-partitions Time Series IDs into buckets. This partitions the stream and lets dedicated Flink tasks handle each bucket, ultimately batching and reducing the write throughput to S3. Flink workers batch events into Parquet files grouped by event time within the hour. These files are great for high-throughput streaming writes, but not for low-latency reads. Enter the Compaction job. Compaction Job to Optimize Reads The compaction job runs daily and merges small Parquet files into a single, optimized daily Parquet file per namespace. The job further optimizes the Parquet files in the following ways: Small Row Groups : Creates small (4–8 MB) row groups to minimize lookup cost. We can then use the Parquet Java library to perform range reads of row groups from S3. This is intentionally well below Parquet’s recommended row group floor — smaller groups were better because our reads are dominated by point/range lookups rather than full scans. Event Sorting : Sorts events within a row group by time, eliminating brute-force scans when querying for a time range. Bloom Filters : Caches Bloom filters and file metadata in EVCache , allowing the TimeSeries query planner to efficiently skip unnecessary reads from S3. Compacted and Sorted Parquet File Layout Once the compaction job completes, all compacted files per partition are recorded in the TimeSeries control plane, and the hot storage slices can now be truncated! On some of our largest datasets, this job typically takes about 12 hours, prioritizing lower compute costs over execution speed. Compaction Burndown Per Day Streaming Cold Tier Read Once compacted files are optimized in cold storage, they are ready to be read. The TimeSeries data plane fans out a given query across both the hot and cold tiers and merges their result. The users still use the same query interface: TimeSeries Tiered Storage Read Path The Cold Tier Data Plane uses compaction metadata for aggressive planning and pruning, which dramatically reduces the S3 query fan-out. As a result, retrieving a full day of data requires at most three sequential S3 reads, even in the uncommon case where an ID spans two row groups. This yields a p50 latency of ~150 ms and a p99 latency of ~500 ms per read. Cold Tier Read Latency in Seconds At the time of writing, the streaming cold tier implementation was processing up to 1,250 reads per second from cold storage globally: Cold Tier Read Requests Per Second Why not stop here? The streaming cold tier has delivered real savings, shrinking both Cassandra’s EBS footprint and the Cassandra backup footprint in S3. But the streaming infrastructure itself is expensive and adds moving pieces that widen the team’s on-call scope: Additional Infrastructure and Operational Cost We wanted to improve this further and asked ourselves: Can we avoid streaming data into the object store and the associated data transfer costs? Can we reduce the compute and operational overhead of new components? That led to a more radical question: Can we read directly from existing Cassandra backups in S3? Solution 2: Cassandra Cold Storage for Immutable Data At Netflix, we back up Cassandra data into S3 at regular intervals for disaster recovery. The idea for tiering is simple: Read directly from these S3 backups instead of paying a separate data transfer cost to S3. Once TimeSeries marks a hot Time Slice as ready for cold storage, we can customize Cassandra to read directly from its backups, allowing us to delete the on-disk data copy. This would also incur minimal changes to the TimeSeries read path! New TimeSeries Read Path To make this viable in production, we had to answer a series of “How…?” questions. How Can We Read the Backups Efficiently? We introduced a new compaction strategy in Cassandra, which we call ReadOnlyCompactionStrategy (ROCS). Here is how it works: Once a time slice crosses the user-configured cold-tier boundary , TimeSeries stops accepting writes for that time slice making it immutable. This immutability unlocks significant optimization opportunities: SSTable overlap: Standard strategies (LCS, TWCS) often produce SSTables that overlap in the token space, and so a single partition key may exist across multiple files. Read fan‑out: Because a read must touch every SSTable covering the key’s token range, this overlap turns a single point-read into multiple lookups, increasing latency across all tiers. ROCS re-compacts all SSTables once, aligning them precisely with token ranges: ROCS SSTable Boundaries ROCS applies more broadly to all TimeSeries use cases, driving tail latency down on all storage tiers by reducing the SSTable fan-out during read operations: Tail Latency Improvement in Reads after ROCS Once the immutable Time Slices have been optimized, it is time to trigger backups. How Would We Leverage Backups? Cassandra backs up every node in the cluster, organizing each backup on S3 as a declarative manifest, along with the SSTables backing the keyspace’s tables: {bucket}/ └── {prefix}/                             ← cluster identity (env_backup/hash_app) └── {token}/                          ← node identity (ring token) ├── META_V2/                      ← manifests, one per snapshot │   ├── {snapshotInstantMs}.json │   ├── {snapshotInstantMs}.json │   └── ... └── SST_V2/                       ← actual SSTable files └── {backupTimestamp}/        ← snapshot timestamp └── {keyspace}/ └── {table-with-uuid}/ └── {compression}/ └── {encryption}/ ├── {component-file} └── ... The backup manifest orchestrates the backup, listing the paths to all its SSTables: manifest.json ├── info │   ├── appName              "cass-cluster" │   ├── region               "us-east-1" │   ├── snapshotInstantMs    1748908800000 │   ├── backupPathPrefix     "prod_backup/1234_cass/token" └── data[] └── [0] ├── keyspaceName     "ks" ├── columnfamily     "tbl-a1b2..." └── sstables[] └── [0] └── components[] ├── na-1-big-Data.db ├── na-1-big-Index.db ├── na-1-big-Filter.db ├── na-1-big-Statistics.db ├── na-1-big-Summary.db ├── na-1-big-CompressionInfo.db Alongside the large Data.db file, backups include a compact set of index, metadata, and integrity files. This structure allows us to quickly locate, validate, and restore specific partitions or data ranges without scanning the entire dataset . Furthermore, since the manifest catalogs every S3 path, we can download most of these components directly to the Cassandra node (excluding the Data.db file) where they occupy negligible space. These local components enable efficient query planning before any data is read from S3 . How Would Cassandra Read From Backups? Cassandra reads typically pull data from two sources: the Memtable , which holds recent unflushed writes, and flushed SSTables on durable storage. As of Cassandra 4.1, we can leverage pluggable Memtables to redirect reads from “cold” tables directly to the backup storage in S3. -- create table for a given Time Slice CREATE TABLE data_20260616_00_04 ( ... ..., PRIMARY KEY ((time_series_id, time_bucket, event_bucket), event_time, event_id, key) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (event_time DESC, event_id DESC, key DESC) ... AND compaction = ... AND compression = ... AND memtable = 'backupmemtable:timestamp=1781953200000' ← Custom memtable ... The timestamp marks the point at which the backup is guaranteed to cover the full table, and the table is guaranteed to be immutable. Opening a backup Memtable kicks off a state-machine initialization that pulls the index data from S3 onto the node once: State Machine for Cassandra Backup Memtable Initialization This process ensures all SSTable components are downloaded reliably through several resilience mechanisms: Retries and backoff: All S3 operations and file-system cache writes use retries with exponential backoff. Resource isolation: Initialization runs on a dedicated thread pool, isolated from normal Cassandra operations. Partial download protection: If a downloaded component’s size doesn’t match the manifest, it is deleted and re-downloaded. DDL change protection: A .timestamp file marks completed initialization and ties it to the backup timestamp. If the table’s backup timestamp changes, this file is removed and initialization restarts for the new timestamp. Read protection: Memtable initialization is asynchronous; reads to an initializing memtable block for at most half the read RPC timeout. Once initialization has pulled every SSTable component (except Data.db) from S3 onto the local disk, the Memtable is ready to serve reads. Here is what the read process looks like: Reading from Cassandra Backup Memtables To minimize latency, the system parallelizes S3 reads across requests, SSTables, and individual chunks. A shared cache deduplicates fetches and prefetches data, so chunks are ready before they are needed. We further optimize cluster and table settings to reduce the number of S3 calls: Larger compression chunks: Reduce S3 calls per partition by reading fewer, larger chunks (accepting some over-fetch on small reads). Read repair disabled: Avoid expensive, unnecessary repair traffic against immutable, pre‑repaired backup data. Speculative retries disabled: Prevent S3’s higher latency from triggering redundant, overlapping reads. How Would We Know When It Is Safe To Read From Backups? However, before the Memtable can point to a backup, we must confirm two things across the whole ring, and we use Cassandra Virtual Tables to do that. First, that ROCS re-compaction succeeded: cqlsh> SELECT * FROM netflix_views.cluster_view WHERE keyspace_name = 'system_views' AND table_name = 'sstable_tasks'; keyspace_name | table_name    | host     | value --------------+---------------+----------+------------------------------------------------ system_views  | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.1 | [{"table_name":"<.>","kind":"compaction", ...}] system_views  | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.2 | [] <---- no active compactions system_views  | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.3 | [] And second, that backups were fully captured (denoted by uploaded=True ): cqlsh> SELECT * FROM netflix_views.complete_backups WHERE keyspace_name = 'my_ks' AND table_name = 'my_table'; keyspace_name | table_name | timestamp     | num_tokens | num_uploaded | uploaded --------------+------------+---------------+------------+--------------+---------- my_ks         | my_table   | 1765211400000 |          3 |            3 |     True my_ks         | my_table   | 1765213200000 |          3 |            2 |    False How Would We Automate This Entire Flow? The TimeSeries control plane automates the entire transition as slices cross the immutable boundary: Automating Time Slice Lifecycle Transitions Each slice can be in any lifecycle stage at any time without impacting system availability, and the system remains resilient to delayed backups or lagging compactions. How Would Cassandra Handle The Additional Load? Serving data from S3 is much more CPU-intensive than reading from local storage. A sudden spike in read requests can overwhelm the Cassandra cluster and affect the hot path, t urning a cost-saving feature into a reliability risk. To avoid this, cold reads can optionally run on a separate Cassandra cluster that points its backup Memtables at the hot cluster’s backups: Isolated Cold Tier Cassandra Topology The cold Cassandra cluster must match the original cluster in topology but need not match it in hardware! We can run the cold cluster on much smaller, cheaper, storage-light instances. Real World Performance Cassandra Cold Tier was rolled out to the most storage‑intensive TimeSeries Abstraction clusters. It currently stores over 15 PB of compressed data in Cassandra cold storage and has allowed us to cut attached storage significantly on all affected clusters: Storage Reduction During Rollout: from 80% disk usage to 7% At the same time, it serves thousands of reads per second from cold tier storage in any given region: Cold Tier Read Requests Per Second Cassandra Cold Tier improves p90 latency by ~30% over the previous cold storage implementation, thanks to more efficient S3 access patterns and smaller read sizes, while keeping p99 latency under ~500 ms. Cassandra already handles bursts of cold reads gracefully via its chunk cache, so this design preserves that same resilience for the S3-backed cold tier: Cold Tier Read Latency: blue — p90 latency, brown — p99 latency; latency measured in seconds) Acknowledgements : Special thanks to our stunning colleagues who contributed to the TimeSeries Abstraction’s success and collaborated with us on the cold storage solutions: Kaidan Fullerton , Matt Lehman , Sumanth Pasupuleti , Carlos Matias Herrero , Nick Pavlakis , Bryan Keller , Francesco Di Chiara
