items.title: My husband dreamed of city living — I didn't. To compromise, we tried living in a high-rise condo downtown for one year.
items.summary: We rented a high-rise condo for a year to try downtown living. We loved it so much that we're buying the place and leaving the suburbs. Stacy Brooks My husband dreamed of city living, so I agreed to leave the suburbs for a year and give it a try. I thought I'd hate living in a high-rise condo, but the convenience and community won me over. Now, we're working on buying the condo and selling our place in the suburbs. I thought I would hate living in a high-rise apartment . I grew up in the woods of northern Minnesota, watching deer and the occasional bear wander through the backyard. I've spent my adult life in suburban townhomes near large park reserves, a compromise between rural landscapes and the job opportunities of the Minneapolis metro area. However, my husband of 15-plus years has long fantasized about urban living and skyline views. Whenever we drove by downtown apartment buildings, he gazed wistfully at the units on the upper floors. When we were planning a trip to Tokyo , he pored through online reviews to find a room with the best panoramic skyline view. At home, he watched YouTube videos of cityscapes and scrolled through real estate listings for urban condos. A successful marriage is all about compromise, so by the time we hit our late 30s, I offered to give urban living a try for one year, on a part-time basis. Since we don't have kids, it was feasible to split our time between our suburban townhome in the northwest metro and a 19th-floor condo we rented in downtown Minneapolis. As we lugged our furniture up the freight elevator on move-in day, my husband was thrilled about this exciting adventure. I was skeptical. For the first time in my life, I was surrounded by asphalt and multi-story buildings. Instead of a shady patio and a lawn, we had a small balcony perched above a busy street. The traffic noise was constant, punctuated by sirens from emergency vehicles going to and from the nearby fire station and hospital. Our downtown life is more pedestrian-focused The view from our living room doesn't get old. Stacy Brooks But as we settled in, I started to see the perks of urban high-rise life . When my husband and I travel, we gravitate to walkable city centers and compact towns, using walking as our primary mode of transit. Now I can take that same approach to my daily life. Three different grocery stores are within a 10-minute walk, and on Saturday mornings, the year-round farmers market is a five-minute walk away. Evenings out became centered on walking rather than driving, with the orchestra hall, ballpark, and multiple theaters within a mile of our condo. Minneapolis has a diverse dining scene, and now much of it is within walking distance, from an Eastern European deli and Latina-owned coffee shop to an Indigenous restaurant and chic Italian spot. Living in a high-rise apartment building makes it easier to socialize I love looking out of our windows at the world below. Stacy Brooks We also lucked out with the social scene in our particular building. In the suburbs, we never really connected with our neighbors. Social events were geared to families, and as a childless couple, we didn't have much in common with our neighbors. However, the majority of units in our building are one- or two-bedrooms, and most inhabitants are empty nesters or fellow childfree couples . Not having kids is less of a barrier to socializing, and there's an impressive lineup of events, from book groups to an annual building-wide holiday party. During the Super Bowl and World Cup, people gathered in the common room to watch the games on the big screen. Last spring, I rocked a thrifted dress at the building's first "prom for grownups." We've made friends with a few other couples in the building, and it's convenient to get together when we can walk to a restaurant a couple of blocks away. Beyond our building, I like feeling like a part of a vibrant urban area. In the suburbs, I mostly saw cars driving back and forth. When I'm downtown, I can step outside and see people of all different backgrounds sharing the same public spaces. I appreciate the views from our condo of the Mississippi River and the Minneapolis skyline , but my favorite part is watching the people down below, playing lawn chess, walking their dogs, or lining up at the neighborhood ice cream truck. We're ready to make downtown life permanent One year of living downtown wasn't enough for the two of us. Stacy Brooks A few months into our lease, my husband and I realized that one year wouldn't be enough. We both wanted to live downtown on a long-term basis. When we reached out to our landlord, we discovered that she was planning to sell the unit as soon as our lease was up. So, we put in an offer and are now negotiating the final purchase agreement. Once we've closed on the condo, we're planning to list our townhome and live downtown full-time. Although I'll miss my long runs in the park reserve, I'm ready for the next chapter. It's time to swap suburbia for the convenience and connection of urban life. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Free tiers are Hollywood’s next big idea in the streaming wars
items.summary: Disney and Paramount Skydance have brainstormed introducing free tiers for their paid streaming services. Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters has said his company will "continue to consider" a free tier. Anadolu Agency/Getty Images; Bloomberg/Getty Images; Michael Yanow/NurPhoto via Getty Images Free tiers could help paid streamers fight the rise of services like YouTube and Tubi. Disney and Paramount are exploring free tiers, Business Insider has reported. However, Netflix's co-CEO suggested that making some content free can be risky. To free, or not to free? That is the question for paid streamers like Netflix, as free services, and YouTube in particular, attract TV viewers. Hollywood giants Disney and Paramount Skydance are exploring adding free tiers to their subscription services to build audiences, grow advertising revenue, and turn curious newcomers into customers, Business Insider previously reported. And Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters said in mid-July that "a free offering could make sense in some markets." Free tiers could define the next stage of the streaming wars as services look to win over consumers sick of stream-flation . YouTube has enjoyed significant growth , as have free, ad-supported TV apps like Tubi and The Roku Channel, which are known as FAST services. Those three free streamers had a 19.1% viewership share on US TVs in May, according to Nielsen, up from 17.2% a year earlier. While Apple TV and Paramount+ let users sample some full episodes, most paid streamers don't have substantial free offerings. "A genuinely free, advertising-funded tier is entirely feasible and could serve as a meaningful differentiator, particularly as consumers become more selective about the growing number of subscriptions they maintain," said media industry analyst Paolo Pescatore of PP Foresight. Free streaming tiers also carry risk, since they could cannibalize a platform's subscription revenue if paid users trade down, said Greenlight Analytics analyst Brandon Katz. Streamers would have to thread the needle in deciding what content to give away for free. "Give away too little, and consumers will not engage," Pescatore said. "Give away too much, and the company risks undermining the very subscription model it is trying to support." The best things in life are free Disney has discussed allowing free access to select Disney+ content , Business Insider reported in July. A source familiar with the company's strategy said streaming leaders often brainstorm ways to better serve audiences. Katz said that making some shows and movies free could help a company like Disney "extract more value from its content investments" by driving viewership years after their releases. Paramount+ is exploring free content as well, through a planned feature known internally as the "free front porch," Business Insider reported last month. This free tier was listed as a "Q3 product priority" during a recent streaming town hall, alongside micro dramas and podcast clips . Paramount+ is planning a free tier to bring in new customers. Business Insider Paramount's presentation said that allowing free access could "drive acquisition and winbacks" of previous customers by getting viewers used to its app and hooked on its content. "I'm surprised that it hasn't happened already," Alan Wolk, a media analyst at TVREV, said of the Paramount+ free tier concept. "I think they should all do it. Otherwise, they're just ceding ground to the FAST services that could be theirs." (Paramount does have its own separate FAST service, Pluto TV.) In a crowded TV landscape, offering free episodes of older shows or samples of new seasons is "a way to keep awareness going," Wolk said. Streamers can get viewers in the habit of watching their libraries, tell them about new originals, and then upsell them on access to the full catalog. "There's not an ambient awareness of what's on TV like there used to be," Wolk said. Being 'thoughtful about cannibalization' While free tiers may seem promising, the risk could outweigh the potential reward for some streamers — especially in certain markets. Netflix has built such a large US subscriber base that it must be "thoughtful about cannibalization of paid tiers," said Peters, its co-CEO, on the company's second-quarter earnings call. If the streaming giant made any of its content available for free, it could give some customers a reason to cancel. "For Netflix, any potential loss of subscription revenue would need to be outweighed by advertising income and incremental reach," Pescatore said. He added that a free tier could be "more compelling in markets where paid penetration is lower or where pricing remains a significant barrier." Peters said Netflix would need "an effective scaled ads business" before launching a free tier in a market. He said Netflix would "continue to consider" a free tier but has "no near-term plans" of launching one. While free tiers could help Disney and Paramount, there could be a "glut" of new supply in the streaming ad market if their rivals followed suit, said John Conca, a media analyst at research firm Third Bridge. "If everyone is offering something free, what happens to the ad economy? I could see a world where that becomes really challenging," Conca said. Streamers would also have to consider whether going the free route would dilute their brand. Pescatore said a free tier could "alter perceptions of a premium service, especially if consumers begin to see its content as something that should be available without payment." items.title: Elon Musk is looking for trades workers to build AI data centers — and his famous 3-bullet-point requirement applies
items.summary: Elon Musk is the CEO of SpaceX. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Elon Musk is looking to hire skilled trades workers for his AI data center buildout. He said in an X post that SpaceX is hiring talent to build data centers "on & off Earth." Applicants were asked to email "3 bullet points demonstrating evidence of exceptional ability." Elon Musk is reviving one of his famed hiring tactics as he recruits skilled trades workers for the AI data center buildout by his rocket company, SpaceX . Musk, in an X post last week, said SpaceX is hiring "exceptional engineering & skilled trades talent to build & operate the most powerful AI supercomputer clusters on & off Earth." The "off Earth" reference reflects Musk's vision of placing data centers in space as a potential solution to AI's soaring energy demands. Interested applicants were asked to email "3 bullet points demonstrating evidence of exceptional ability," along with their resume, to datacenters@spacex.com . SpaceX is hiring exceptional engineering & skilled trades talent to build & operate the most powerful AI supercomputer clusters on & off Earth. If interested, please email 3 bullet points demonstrating evidence of exceptional ability & your resume to datacenters@spacex.com. — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) August 1, 2026 The three-bullet-point requirement has become a hallmark of the world's richest man's recruiting style. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has previously asked potential candidates for white-collar roles at his companies to provide three bullet points "demonstrating evidence of exceptional ability" or three bullet points on the "toughest technical problems" they've solved. Musk's hiring push for trades workers to build data centers comes as SpaceX plays an increasingly central role in his AI ambitions. Earlier this year, SpaceX acquired Musk's AI startup , xAI, which was rebranded as SpaceXAI. SpaceXAI now operates Colossus , the massive AI supercomputer campus built in Memphis, Tennessee, that trains the company's Grok AI models. Read the original article on Business Insider

The "off Earth" reference reflects Musk's vision of placing data centers in space as a potential solution to AI's soaring energy demands.

Interested applicants were asked to email "3 bullet points demonstrating evidence of exceptional ability," along with their resume, to datacenters@spacex.com.

SpaceX is hiring exceptional engineering & skilled trades talent to build & operate the most powerful AI supercomputer clusters on & off Earth.

If interested, please email 3 bullet points demonstrating evidence of exceptional ability & your resume to datacenters@spacex.com.

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) August 1, 2026

The three-bullet-point requirement has become a hallmark of the world's richest man's recruiting style.

The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has previously asked potential candidates for white-collar roles at his companies to provide three bullet points "demonstrating evidence of exceptional ability" or three bullet points on the "toughest technical problems" they've solved.

Musk's hiring push for trades workers to build data centers comes as SpaceX plays an increasingly central role in his AI ambitions. Earlier this year, SpaceX acquired Musk's AI startup, xAI, which was rebranded as SpaceXAI.

SpaceXAI now operates Colossus, the massive AI supercomputer campus built in Memphis, Tennessee, that trains the company's Grok AI models.

items.title: I moved to Japan on a one-year visa. Hopping around short-term rentals is better and cheaper than I expected.
items.summary: My husband and I moved to Japan with just one suitcase and one carry-on each. We've been spending our year here living out of short-term rentals. Alessa Hickman I left Canada, sold most of my stuff, and moved to Japan to spend a year exploring different cities. Moving between short-term rentals has been more comfortable and affordable than I imagined. Living out of a suitcase taught me to be more intentional about what I own and more open to change. Seven months ago, I left Canada after living in Ottawa my entire life. When my apartment lease was coming to an end, I knew I didn't want to make another expensive yearlong commitment in the only city I'd ever lived in — especially as the cost of living kept rising. I'd visited Japan once before, loved it, and couldn't stop thinking about going back. I was also itching to leave my hometown and travel more, so my husband and I sold almost everything we owned and moved there with one suitcase and one carry-on each. Instead of renting an apartment once we arrived, we decided to spend the year living out of short-term rentals so we could experience different parts of Japan . So far, I've lived in Tokyo, Osaka, and Kumamoto, plus visited other cities on day trips. I can confidently say this lifestyle has worked out better than I ever expected. I wasn't sure I'd ever feel at home Moving a lot isn't easy, but I've been able to adapt to new places. Alessa Hickman Before moving abroad, I'd stayed in Airbnbs while traveling, but never for more than a few days or maybe a week. I'd always lived somewhere I planned to be for a while, so I could decorate, organize, and make it feel like home. Here, moving around meant arriving somewhere I'd only ever seen in photos, with a different setup every time. I also knew that once I got comfortable in a new place — learning my neighborhood, finding my go-to grocery stores, or picking a favorite restaurant — I'd eventually have to start fresh somewhere else. I won't pretend it's always easy. Moving day means packing everything back into my bags, dragging them across a city, and becoming best friends with Google Maps all over again. Even so, I've genuinely enjoyed every place I've stayed so far, and I've adapted to each new apartment much faster than I expected. I've found it easy to settle into a routine I thought moving between short-term rentals would be difficult, but it's been much better than I expected. Alessa Hickman When I'm booking a place, I spend a lot of time reviewing the workspace, kitchen, bathroom layout (one of my biggest deciding factors), location, and the price. As long as I'm content with what I find in those categories, settling in has been surprisingly easy. Whenever I arrive somewhere new, I unpack right away. My clothes are organized in packing cubes , so if there's enough closet space, they go straight in. If not, my suitcase becomes my dresser for a while. It's been fun to see different cities and spend time living in them. Alessa Hickman Cooking also looks different depending on the kitchen and tools I have, but I can still make a few meals I love, and every city gives me new local restaurants to try. Thankfully, by booking rentals with bathrooms I know I can work with, I've been able to keep up my hair-care routine and very long wash days, too. As anyone with curls knows, this is basically non-negotiable. I'm spending less on housing than I did in Canada It's nice not having to buy my own kitchen essentials and small appliances. Alessa Hickman Back in Ottawa, I paid more than CA$1,900 a month for my two-bedroom apartment before internet, utilities, tenant insurance, and all the other expenses. In Osaka, I stayed in a two-bedroom Airbnb that cost a little over CA$1,600 a month with everything included. Now I'm staying in a smaller place in Kumamoto for around CA$1,200. Housing costs naturally vary by city, but I've consistently spent less than I did back home. Since these rentals are essentially all-inclusive, budgeting is much simpler. I don't need to worry about varying gas or electric bills, and I'm left with more money for the things I actually care about, like trying new foods and taking day trips . The flexibility has been one of the best parts It's exciting to call a new place home every few weeks or months. Alessa Hickman Instead of spending the entire year in one place, I've lived life in different cities with the flexibility to move when I'm ready to go somewhere new. I also haven't had to worry about buying furniture, signing long leases, or dealing with big security deposits and complex move-out procedures. I can set up my workspace just about anywhere. Alessa Hickman I usually have a rough idea of where I'd like to visit next, but I don't force it. If I can't find a place that checks my boxes, I just look in another city. That's actually how I ended up in Kumamoto on the island of Kyushu. It wasn't on my radar before I moved to Japan, but I found a great place at the right price, decided to give it a chance, and it's one of my favorite places here so far. As someone who naturally overthinks everything , living this way has taught me to be more open and go with the flow when things don't go according to plan. I've realized I need a lot less than I thought I sold a lot of my belongings before I left Canada, which made the move even easier. Alessa Hickman Before moving, I had a closet full of clothes, shelves of beauty products, kitchen gadgets, and more shoes than I ever needed. Even after getting rid of so much before leaving Canada, I still managed to overpack. I actually ended up shipping some things back home, because dragging the extra weight between cities just wasn't practical. I've also been living with a simple capsule wardrobe . Sure, I repeat outfits more, and some everyday products I relied on in Canada aren't available here, but I've learned to simplify my overall routine. Living out of a suitcase made me a lot more intentional about what I own, and I realized I don't need nearly as much as I once thought. items.summary_html:
My husband and I moved to Japan with just one suitcase and one carry-on each. We've been spending our year here living out of short-term rentals.

Alessa Hickman

  • I left Canada, sold most of my stuff, and moved to Japan to spend a year exploring different cities.
  • Moving between short-term rentals has been more comfortable and affordable than I imagined.
  • Living out of a suitcase taught me to be more intentional about what I own and more open to change.

Seven months ago, I left Canada after living in Ottawa my entire life.

When my apartment lease was coming to an end, I knew I didn't want to make another expensive yearlong commitment in the only city I'd ever lived in — especially as the cost of living kept rising.

I'd visited Japan once before, loved it, and couldn't stop thinking about going back. I was also itching to leave my hometown and travel more, so my husband and I sold almost everything we owned and moved there with one suitcase and one carry-on each.

Instead of renting an apartment once we arrived, we decided to spend the year living out of short-term rentals so we could experience different parts of Japan.

So far, I've lived in Tokyo, Osaka, and Kumamoto, plus visited other cities on day trips. I can confidently say this lifestyle has worked out better than I ever expected.

I wasn't sure I'd ever feel at homeMoving a lot isn't easy, but I've been able to adapt to new places.

Alessa Hickman

Before moving abroad, I'd stayed in Airbnbs while traveling, but never for more than a few days or maybe a week.

I'd always lived somewhere I planned to be for a while, so I could decorate, organize, and make it feel like home. Here, moving around meant arriving somewhere I'd only ever seen in photos, with a different setup every time.

I also knew that once I got comfortable in a new place — learning my neighborhood, finding my go-to grocery stores, or picking a favorite restaurant — I'd eventually have to start fresh somewhere else.

I won't pretend it's always easy. Moving day means packing everything back into my bags, dragging them across a city, and becoming best friends with Google Maps all over again.

Even so, I've genuinely enjoyed every place I've stayed so far, and I've adapted to each new apartment much faster than I expected.

I've found it easy to settle into a routineI thought moving between short-term rentals would be difficult, but it's been much better than I expected.

Alessa Hickman

When I'm booking a place, I spend a lot of time reviewing the workspace, kitchen, bathroom layout (one of my biggest deciding factors), location, and the price.

As long as I'm content with what I find in those categories, settling in has been surprisingly easy.

Whenever I arrive somewhere new, I unpack right away. My clothes are organized in packing cubes, so if there's enough closet space, they go straight in. If not, my suitcase becomes my dresser for a while.

It's been fun to see different cities and spend time living in them.

Alessa Hickman

Cooking also looks different depending on the kitchen and tools I have, but I can still make a few meals I love, and every city gives me new local restaurants to try.

Thankfully, by booking rentals with bathrooms I know I can work with, I've been able to keep up my hair-care routine and very long wash days, too. As anyone with curls knows, this is basically non-negotiable.

I'm spending less on housing than I did in CanadaIt's nice not having to buy my own kitchen essentials and small appliances.

Alessa Hickman

Back in Ottawa, I paid more than CA$1,900 a month for my two-bedroom apartment before internet, utilities, tenant insurance, and all the other expenses.

In Osaka, I stayed in a two-bedroom Airbnb that cost a little over CA$1,600 a month with everything included. Now I'm staying in a smaller place in Kumamoto for around CA$1,200.

Housing costs naturally vary by city, but I've consistently spent less than I did back home.

Since these rentals are essentially all-inclusive, budgeting is much simpler. I don't need to worry about varying gas or electric bills, and I'm left with more money for the things I actually care about, like trying new foods and taking day trips.

The flexibility has been one of the best partsIt's exciting to call a new place home every few weeks or months.

Alessa Hickman

Instead of spending the entire year in one place, I've lived life in different cities with the flexibility to move when I'm ready to go somewhere new.

I also haven't had to worry about buying furniture, signing long leases, or dealing with big security deposits and complex move-out procedures.

I can set up my workspace just about anywhere.

Alessa Hickman

I usually have a rough idea of where I'd like to visit next, but I don't force it. If I can't find a place that checks my boxes, I just look in another city.

That's actually how I ended up in Kumamoto on the island of Kyushu.

It wasn't on my radar before I moved to Japan, but I found a great place at the right price, decided to give it a chance, and it's one of my favorite places here so far.

As someone who naturally overthinks everything, living this way has taught me to be more open and go with the flow when things don't go according to plan.

I've realized I need a lot less than I thoughtI sold a lot of my belongings before I left Canada, which made the move even easier.

Alessa Hickman

Before moving, I had a closet full of clothes, shelves of beauty products, kitchen gadgets, and more shoes than I ever needed.

Even after getting rid of so much before leaving Canada, I still managed to overpack. I actually ended up shipping some things back home, because dragging the extra weight between cities just wasn't practical.

I've also been living with a simple capsule wardrobe.

Sure, I repeat outfits more, and some everyday products I relied on in Canada aren't available here, but I've learned to simplify my overall routine.

Living out of a suitcase made me a lot more intentional about what I own, and I realized I don't need nearly as much as I once thought.

I'd choose a year in Japan over 20 extra shirts in my closet any day.

items.title: Anthropic’s AI models accidentally hacked three companies
items.summary: Anthropic has launched an investigation into what went wrong during a recent test of three models that left a trio of companies accidentally hacked. The company was testing how well Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5, and an internal test model could find hidden information about fictional companies in simulated networks. But because of a misunderstanding by one of Anthropic’s partners, the AI models gained access to the internet — and managed to find real companies with the same or similar names as the fictional ones. As a result, three companies were actually hacked. Anthropic said it halted the tests on July 23, and the affected companies were notified four days later. So far, the company has received responses from two of the three companies, according to Reuters . Anthropic is not alone when it comes to renegade models. An OpenAI agent recently went rogue and breached AI platform Hugging Bear and a customer of the cloud platform Modal Labs.

items.title: Poll Finds Overwhelming Majority Disgusted by Trump’s Relationship With AI Industry, Saying He’s Using the Tech to Tear Down Democracy
items.summary: Even before Donald Trump was sworn in for his second stint in the White House, he was promising to unleash “AI innovation” on an unprecedented scale. Despite grumblings from the populist Republican sect , the billionaire-in-chief soon made good on those promises, cozying up to AI moguls like Sam Altman and promising to flip the US power grid on its head in order to feed the growing demand for AI data centers. Now a year and a half into his second term, a growing number of Americans are clearly fed up with the president’s pandering to the tech industry. A new poll conducted by Upswing Research and Strategy in cooperation with the AI accountability group Guardrails Action surveyed Americans in New York’s 12th congressional district, a diverse tract encompassing parts of Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, and the Bronx. Respondents, broadly, are very skeptical of Trump’s AI regime, with an enormous 79 percent saying their “top concern” with AI is that tech companies are “too close to Trump and helping him erode democracy.” A further 81 percent flagged AI companies stealing data and private information as either their “top concern” or a “major concern,” while 71 percent said AI-integrated surveillance of Americans is a top or major concern. While New York’s 12th district is one of the bluest voting blocks in the United States, Trump’s AI strategy wasn’t the only thing catching flack. Nearly half of all respondents also dogged Democrats, saying party leadership sold out to big corporations and special interests to fund their campaigns. Sure enough, Democratic party leadership has accepted millions of dollars from AI super PACs in 2026. The tech industry spigot is evidently so lucrative that incumbent Democratic candidates have been warned by party strategists not to antagonize the tech industry, though an adversarial stance would clearly be massively popular with a huge swath of voters . “With their absurd lobbying spending, PR budgets, and corporate super PACs, these Big AI goliaths think they can buy off our government, our elections, our leaders, and our future and nobody will notice,” Guardrails Action executive director Shaunna Thomas said in a statement. Continuing, Thomas argued that voters “want leaders that won’t sell out to Big AI, corporate donors, or Trump’s fascist agenda. MAGA mega donors and corporate super PACs should not be getting special treatment in closed door meetings on the Hill and in the White House; and they should have no place in Democratic primaries.” More on Trump and AI: The Logo for Donald Trump International Airport Appears to Be AI Slop The post Poll Finds Overwhelming Majority Disgusted by Trump’s Relationship With AI Industry, Saying He’s Using the Tech to Tear Down Democracy appeared first on Futurism .
items.summary_html:
Even before Donald Trump was sworn in for his second stint in the White House, he was promising to unleash “AI innovation” on an unprecedented scale.

Despite grumblings from the populist Republican sect, the billionaire-in-chief soon made good on those promises, cozying up to AI moguls like Sam Altman and promising to flip the US power grid on its head in order to feed the growing demand for AI data centers.

Now a year and a half into his second term, a growing number of Americans are clearly fed up with the president’s pandering to the tech industry. A new poll conducted by Upswing Research and Strategy in cooperation with the AI accountability group Guardrails Action surveyed Americans in New York’s 12th congressional district, a diverse tract encompassing parts of Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, and the Bronx.

Respondents, broadly, are very skeptical of Trump’s AI regime, with an enormous 79 percent saying their “top concern” with AI is that tech companies are “too close to Trump and helping him erode democracy.”

A further 81 percent flagged AI companies stealing data and private information as either their “top concern” or a “major concern,” while 71 percent said AI-integrated surveillance of Americans is a top or major concern.

While New York’s 12th district is one of the bluest voting blocks in the United States, Trump’s AI strategy wasn’t the only thing catching flack. Nearly half of all respondents also dogged Democrats, saying party leadership sold out to big corporations and special interests to fund their campaigns.

Sure enough, Democratic party leadership has accepted millions of dollars from AI super PACs in 2026. The tech industry spigot is evidently so lucrative that incumbent Democratic candidates have been warned by party strategists not to antagonize the tech industry, though an adversarial stance would clearly be massively popular with a huge swath of voters.

“With their absurd lobbying spending, PR budgets, and corporate super PACs, these Big AI goliaths think they can buy off our government, our elections, our leaders, and our future and nobody will notice,” Guardrails Action executive director Shaunna Thomas said in a statement.

Continuing, Thomas argued that voters “want leaders that won’t sell out to Big AI, corporate donors, or Trump’s fascist agenda. MAGA mega donors and corporate super PACs should not be getting special treatment in closed door meetings on the Hill and in the White House; and they should have no place in Democratic primaries.”
