items.title: I put myself through college reselling used clothes. I've made nearly $50,000 so far this year.
items.summary: Courtesy of Hannah Valentine Hannah Valentine started flipping clothes in high school. It's now her full-time job. Her business helped her graduate from college with no student loan debt. She's made nearly $50,000 so far this year. She says her strategy has changed a lot over the years. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Hannah Valentine, 25, cofounder of Drop Soda Market, a monthly vintage market. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. I graduated from Lindenwood University with no student loan debt . After scholarships, my tuition cost about $4,000 to $6,000 a semester, and I paid for the final three years of my degree by reselling vintage clothes. I started selling used clothes on Depop in 2017 as a sophomore in high school. At first, I listed pieces from my own closet that I no longer wore. They sold faster than I expected, so I started buying inventory from thrift stores and reselling it online. I was already used to shopping secondhand because I was raised thrifting. Even now, after moving into my own apartment, almost everything in it — my couch, coffee table, side tables, entertainment center, and most of my furniture — is secondhand. Since graduating, I've been able to devote more time to the business , and I've made about $48,000 in gross revenue so far this year. Today, reselling is my full-time job Hannah Valentine is standing outside the St. Louis Public Radio building. Courtesy of Hannah Valentine I spend about 12 hours a day sourcing vintage inventory , washing and repairing clothes, organizing pop-up markets, creating social media posts, and getting ready for the next event. I don't rely on Depop the way I used to. About 98% of my income now comes from pop-up vintage markets because I've found they're a better use of my time. During market season, I usually have one to three pop-up markets every weekend, where I can sell as many as 250 pieces in a day. I typically price clothing between $20 and $30 an item. I try not to price anything below $20 because I spend time washing, repairing, and restoring many of the pieces before I sell them. Some of the clothes I find have stains, rips, or missing buttons, but I see their potential. I'll sew hems, replace buttons, repair zippers, and patch holes. I have over 1,000 pieces of inventory at any given time, which I keep in my studio. It takes up every waking moment, but I love running my own business, and I wouldn't have it any other way. I spend about $1,200 a month on inventory alone Hannah sells vintage items for about $20 to $30 each, but she made about $400 in profit from a single find. Courtesy of Hannah Valentine I shop at garage sales, browse Facebook Marketplace, and sometimes get clothing from family friends, but I source most of my inventory from Goodwill Outlet stores . You never know what you'll find in the bins at Goodwill. Sometimes I come across used diapers and bloody towels, so I always wear gloves. It's not the most glamorous part of the job, but digging through all of it is part of finding the pieces worth saving. Goodwill charges by weight, which is now about $2.09 a pound. I remember when it cost less than $2 a pound, but like everything else, sourcing inventory has gotten more expensive . Booth fees, which usually cost between $500 to $800, are my next biggest expense, especially when I travel. When I drove to a market in Memphis recently, I paid for a booth, gas, a hotel, and enough inventory to stock it, which added up to about $1,000 before I made my first sale. Every trip is a calculation: Will I break even? How much will I make? Is the drive worth it? Learning what to buy took time A Goodwill Outlet World store in Aurora, Colorado. Andy Cross/The Denver Post via Getty Images One of the biggest lessons I've learned is that knowing what will sell isn't something you gain overnight. It's knowledge that comes from spending years looking through racks of clothing. One of my favorite brands to find is old Forever 21 . Most people think of it as a modern fast-fashion retailer, but I love the pieces it made in the late 1990s and early 2000s. I also look for brands like XOXO, Bebe, Juicy Couture, Baby Phat, and Ed Hardy. One of my best finds came from Facebook Marketplace , where I spotted a blurry listing for a vintage Donnybrook coat priced at $40, in great condition. The coat was especially sought after because Rihanna had worn the same style, so I displayed a photo of her wearing it alongside the coat at my booth. I sold it for $450 at a vintage market in Detroit. I don't think we need to keep making so many new clothes Hannah sells vintage clothing through her business "Ghost Soda." Courtesy of Hannah Valentine I've seen firsthand how much clothing is already out there. At the Goodwill Outlet stores, there are bales of clothes waiting to be put out. Some people may be intimidated by reselling or think it's something that's gatekept, but I think the opposite: We need more people finding homes for clothes that already exist. That's why I encourage people to shop secondhand whenever they can. Vintage isn't the only option — there are plenty of secondhand clothes that are practically new — and every purchase helps keep clothing in circulation instead of creating more waste. items.title: Architectural Properties Before Trust
items.summary: Enterprise AI isn’t just about orchestrating agents. It starts with the architectural properties that make trust possible. Why trustworthy multi-agent orchestration is an architectural problem, not an AI one. The first time I watched two agents work on the same task, the single-agent version of this problem hadn’t prepared me for what went wrong. A single ReAct agent is an easy system to reason about. Whatever it gets wrong stays inside one conversation: you see the mess, you fix the prompt, you move on. The moment a second agent enters the picture, that stops being true. Now one agent’s output becomes another agent’s input, and nobody ever asked the question that actually matters: can the second agent trust what the first one handed it? That question isn’t about intelligence. A smarter model doesn’t answer it. It’s an architectural problem, and it’s the one this article is about. This is not a whiteboard argument. The four-layer architecture from the previous article partially runs: three of four layers deployed on a local Kubernetes cluster, two tenants isolated from each other, one request traveling end to end through every boundary. Identity deliberately remains outside the scope of this implementation. This article is about the architectural properties that have to exist before identity, policy, audit, and trust can emerge. The code is public: github.com/vasiache/enterprise-ai-harness . What follows explains why those boundaries come first, and what they already prove. The first article described the architecture in terms of layers. This one looks at the same architecture through a different lens: the architectural properties those layers are expected to guarantee. Two terms govern the rest of this article. Architectural trust : the ability to rely on execution guarantees that hold independently of the model’s correctness. Enterprise AI Harness : the architectural environment in which multi-agent systems become secure, governable, and engineering-ready. The industry is discussing components, not properties Look at what the field argues about. Models. Prompts. Tools. Frameworks. MCP. Graph libraries. Which agent runtime is faster. These are component choices. The question almost nobody asks is different: what architectural properties must hold for a graph of agents to be trustworthy at all, independent of which model, which framework, which protocol is plugged in? Components are replaceable. Properties are not. So why does the conversation about enterprise AI still feel shallow to me, even when the components being discussed are genuinely good? Because it debates what to install, not what has to remain true after you install it. What we expect from a boundary Authentication checks who’s asking. A boundary is a stronger claim: it holds regardless of whether the code asking is correct. If the code is wrong, if a developer forgets a check, if an agent gets tricked, the boundary is supposed to not care. That’s the whole point of calling it a boundary instead of a convention. If a guarantee disappears the moment someone makes a mistake, it was never a boundary. It was a convention everyone happened to follow until they didn’t. Graph Engineering and the harness Lately the field compares “harness engineering” with “graph engineering” as if they were alternatives. Strange comparison? Not really, once you notice it’s like asking whether a city needs roads infrastructure or traffic rules. The industry is moving toward graph execution as the standard. The 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report predicts multi-agent systems replacing single-agent workflows: an orchestrator coordinates specialized agents working in parallel, each with dedicated context. One node clarifies. Another implements. A third verifies. A fourth decides. Graph Engineering designs the traffic plan. A harness is the road beneath it: the asphalt, the cameras, the lights, the signs. Agents are the cars. Where to place the light is a graph decision. The light itself, the camera, the lane divider. That is the harness. When the infrastructure is complete, the traffic flows. When something is missing (no signs at the merge, no lane markings), agents collide or loop. The graph does not fail because the graph is wrong. It fails because the road does not support the route. What does the harness guarantee? Four things, in two stages. Two hold at the boundary stage: capabilities are bounded per node, and tenant data cannot cross into another tenant’s context. Two arrive with identity: identity survives from initiator to last tool call, and every action is attributable to a principal. The six boundaries below are the mechanisms that hold the two boundary-stage guarantees. The two identity-stage guarantees arrive with the layer this article leaves for next. A harness is more than boundaries. A boundary keeps traffic in lanes. Identity tells you who is driving. Policy tells them where they may turn. Audit records every intersection. Boundaries are the foundation. A harness is the full road. A bounded agent is also the first agent you can bring to review: a named, scoped object instead of a live process you trust on faith. Boundaries before identity Identity is not the first architectural layer. It is the layer that strengthens boundaries that already exist. Consider what happens if you deploy identity on top of nothing: you validate a token at the edge, and then the request enters a space where any agent can call any other agent, where one pod’s compromise reads every tenant’s rows. First you draw the boundaries: runtime, network, data, agent, secrets. Then you add identity to make the trust attributable. Identity without boundaries is a signature on a napkin. The signature is real. The contract is not. Boundaries first. Identity later. The implementation is evidence The rest of this article is supported by a running reference implementation: a local Kubernetes cluster, three of four architectural layers deployed, two tenants isolated from each other, one request traveling end to end. The implementation is evidence. It is not the claim. It is also scoped. The public reference implementation demonstrates the boundary stage: identity out of scope. The purpose is to show that architectural boundaries can be enforced and evaluated before identity exists: that trustworthy execution begins with boundaries, not with authentication. The purpose is not to demonstrate Kubernetes. It is to demonstrate that Enterprise AI Harness is implementable: that the boundary stage of the model already runs. The complete walkthrough, deployment instructions, and source code are in the public repository: github.com/vasiache/enterprise-ai-harness/isolation . I describe it only enough to validate the architectural ideas. The technologies in it are one way to hold the properties, not the properties themselves. If Kubernetes disappeared tomorrow, the properties would still need to hold. The implementation would change. The architecture would not. With that framing, here is what the implementation actually holds. Six architectural boundaries Read each of these as a property, not as a technology. The technology is the mechanism. The property is the guarantee. Each one is what lets a graph node consume another node’s output without re-validating the whole world. Runtime boundary. Each tenant lives in its own Kubernetes namespace: apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: tenant-alpha labels: tenant-id: alpha Agents of one tenant never share a process with agents of another. The property: a compromise in one tenant’s runtime cannot reach another tenant’s runtime by accident. Network boundary. items.summary_html:
Enterprise AI isn’t just about orchestrating agents. It starts with the architectural properties that make trust possible.Why trustworthy multi-agent orchestration is an architectural problem, not an AI one.

The first time I watched two agents work on the same task, the single-agent version of this problem hadn’t prepared me for what went wrong.

A single ReAct agent is an easy system to reason about. Whatever it gets wrong stays inside one conversation: you see the mess, you fix the prompt, you move on. The moment a second agent enters the picture, that stops being true. Now one agent’s output becomes another agent’s input, and nobody ever asked the question that actually matters: can the second agent trust what the first one handed it?

That question isn’t about intelligence. A smarter model doesn’t answer it. It’s an architectural problem, and it’s the one this article is about.

This is not a whiteboard argument. The four-layer architecture from the previous article partially runs: three of four layers deployed on a local Kubernetes cluster, two tenants isolated from each other, one request traveling end to end through every boundary.

Identity deliberately remains outside the scope of this implementation. This article is about the architectural properties that have to exist before identity, policy, audit, and trust can emerge. The code is public: github.com/vasiache/enterprise-ai-harness. What follows explains why those boundaries come first, and what they already prove.

The first article described the architecture in terms of layers. This one looks at the same architecture through a different lens: the architectural properties those layers are expected to guarantee.

Two terms govern the rest of this article.

Architectural trust: the ability to rely on execution guarantees that hold independently of the model’s correctness.
Enterprise AI Harness: the architectural environment in which multi-agent systems become secure, governable, and engineering-ready.
The industry is discussing components, not properties

Look at what the field argues about. Models. Prompts. Tools. Frameworks. MCP. Graph libraries. Which agent runtime is faster.

These are component choices. The question almost nobody asks is different: what architectural properties must hold for a graph of agents to be trustworthy at all, independent of which model, which framework, which protocol is plugged in?

Components are replaceable. Properties are not. So why does the conversation about enterprise AI still feel shallow to me, even when the components being discussed are genuinely good? Because it debates what to install, not what has to remain true after you install it.

What we expect from a boundary

Authentication checks who’s asking. A boundary is a stronger claim: it holds regardless of whether the code asking is correct. If the code is wrong, if a developer forgets a check, if an agent gets tricked, the boundary is supposed to not care. That’s the whole point of calling it a boundary instead of a convention.

If a guarantee disappears the moment someone makes a mistake, it was never a boundary. It was a convention everyone happened to follow until they didn’t.

Graph Engineering and the harness

Lately the field compares “harness engineering” with “graph engineering” as if they were alternatives. Strange comparison? Not really, once you notice it’s like asking whether a city needs roads infrastructure or traffic rules.

The industry is moving toward graph execution as the standard. The 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report predicts multi-agent systems replacing single-agent workflows: an orchestrator coordinates specialized agents working in parallel, each with dedicated context. One node clarifies. Another implements. A third verifies. A fourth decides.

Graph Engineering designs the traffic plan. A harness is the road beneath it: the asphalt, the cameras, the lights, the signs. Agents are the cars. Where to place the light is a graph decision. The light itself, the camera, the lane divider. That is the harness.

When the infrastructure is complete, the traffic flows. When something is missing (no signs at the merge, no lane markings), agents collide or loop. The graph does not fail because the graph is wrong. It fails because the road does not support the route.

What does the harness guarantee? Four things, in two stages. Two hold at the boundary stage: capabilities are bounded per node, and tenant data cannot cross into another tenant’s context. Two arrive with identity: identity survives from initiator to last tool call, and every action is attributable to a principal. The six boundaries below are the mechanisms that hold the two boundary-stage guarantees. The two identity-stage guarantees arrive with the layer this article leaves for next.

A harness is more than boundaries. A boundary keeps traffic in lanes. Identity tells you who is driving. Policy tells them where they may turn. Audit records every intersection. Boundaries are the foundation. A harness is the full road. A bounded agent is also the first agent you can bring to review: a named, scoped object instead of a live process you trust on faith.

Boundaries before identity

Identity is not the first architectural layer. It is the layer that strengthens boundaries that already exist. Consider what happens if you deploy identity on top of nothing: you validate a token at the edge, and then the request enters a space where any agent can call any other agent, where one pod’s compromise reads every tenant’s rows.

First you draw the boundaries: runtime, network, data, agent, secrets. Then you add identity to make the trust attributable.

Identity without boundaries is a signature on a napkin. The signature is real. The contract is not.

Boundaries first. Identity later.

The implementation is evidence

The rest of this article is supported by a running reference implementation: a local Kubernetes cluster, three of four architectural layers deployed, two tenants isolated from each other, one request traveling end to end.

The implementation is evidence. It is not the claim.

It is also scoped. The public reference implementation demonstrates the boundary stage: identity out of scope. The purpose is to show that architectural boundaries can be enforced and evaluated before identity exists: that trustworthy execution begins with boundaries, not with authentication.

The purpose is not to demonstrate Kubernetes. It is to demonstrate that Enterprise AI Harness is implementable: that the boundary stage of the model already runs.

The complete walkthrough, deployment instructions, and source code are in the public repository: github.com/vasiache/enterprise-ai-harness/isolation.

I describe it only enough to validate the architectural ideas. The technologies in it are one way to hold the properties, not the properties themselves. If Kubernetes disappeared tomorrow, the properties would still need to hold. The implementation would change. The architecture would not.

With that framing, here is what the implementation actually holds.

Six architectural boundaries

Read each of these as a property, not as a technology. The technology is the mechanism. The property is the guarantee. Each one is what lets a graph node consume another node’s output without re-validating the whole world.

Runtime boundary. Each tenant lives in its own Kubernetes namespace:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: tenant-alpha
  labels:
    tenant-id: alpha

Agents of one tenant never share a process with agents of another. The property: a compromise in one tenant’s runtime cannot reach another tenant’s runtime by accident.

Network boundary. The default is closed. deny-all for ingress and egress, opened only to destinations the work requires:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all
  namespace: tenant-alpha
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-platform-egress
  namespace: tenant-alpha
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: platform

The property: a pod that should only talk to the database cannot, by construction, talk to another tenant’s pod. Isolation here is enforced, not declared. I made deny-all the default after a pod reached another tenant’s service by accident; declared isolation wasn’t isolation.

Data boundary. Tenant-scoped rows are filtered at the storage layer by PostgreSQL Row-Level Security:

ALTER TABLE orders.leads ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_rls ON orders.leads
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true));

The property: even if the application asks for everything, storage returns only rows belonging to the current tenant. If the context is missing, storage returns nothing, not everything. A fail-safe ensures a forgotten context returns zero rows:

ALTER DATABASE postgres SET app.tenant_id = '';

RLS alone is not enough. The application must set the context inside an explicit transaction, or asyncpg silently breaks it. I assumed RLS would be enough. It wasn't: asyncpg dropped the context outside an explicit transaction, and the leak took a day to find. The wrapper forces this:

async with conn.transaction():
    await conn.execute(
        "SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)", tenant_id
    )
    return await conn.fetch(sql, *params)

set_config(..., true) is used instead of SET LOCAL because SET does not take bind parameters, so interpolating tenant_id into SQL text is an injection even when the value comes from config. The wrapper also disables prepared-statement caching (statement_cache_size=0), so RLS does not remain a checkbox.

Trade-off: a database per tenant vs. shared + RLS. The strongest isolation is a separate database per tenant: get RLS wrong and there is no leak, because there is no RLS. The cost is N databases, N backups, N connection pools, so operational complexity grows linearly. This reference takes the compromise: one platform database, RLS, the wrapper, and the fail-safe.

Agent boundary. An agent can be invoked as a tool only from within its own namespace:

apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: echo-agent
  namespace: tenant-alpha
spec:
  allowedNamespaces:
    from: Same

The property: a tenant’s agents cannot be composed into another tenant’s loop. The agent system enforces the deny, with the network boundary as a second layer.

Secret boundary. Credentials live in the tenant’s own namespace and never pass through the deployment’s value chain. The property: a tenant’s secret is not present in Helm values, release history, or any shared configuration where another tenant’s process could read it. Per-tenant Vault paths arrive with the identity layer.

Operational boundary. The five above are only real if deployed in the right order. One command spins up the whole stack:

up: ## Spin up Kind cluster + platform stack
    scripts/setup-kind.sh
deploy-tenant: ## Deploy a tenant
    uv run python scripts/admin/tenant.py deploy --tenant $(TENANT)

The property: a data boundary that depends on a migration has that migration applied before any pool opens; a data boundary that depends on a wrapper has that wrapper on every code path. The operational boundary is the discipline that keeps the other five from being a checkbox.

Six boundaries, six guarantees. None of them authenticates anyone. All of them are required for what comes next.

Boundary What enforces it What it guarantees Runtime Namespace per tenant One compromise cannot reach another tenant’s processes Network NetworkPolicy deny-all by default A pod cannot talk to another tenant’s pod by accident Data PostgreSQL RLS + TenantDB wrapper Storage returns only this tenant’s rows, even if the app asks for everything Agent allowedNamespaces: Same Agents cannot be composed into another tenant's loop Secret Per-namespace secrets Credentials never pass through shared Helm values or release history Operational Ordered deployment (migration before pool, wrapper on every path) Boundaries hold on every code path

A boundary you can test. Deploy two tenants against the same database. Query without setting app.tenant_id. The result must be zero rows. If you get data, your wrapper is broken and your RLS is a checkbox.
One request, end to end

One Telegram message shows what the boundaries actually do. The route crosses every boundary, and each one holds:

The tenant identity for the tool isn’t a parameter the caller passes and could forge; it’s a property of where the tool was deployed. The query returns only this tenant’s rows, and would return zero rows if the context were ever forgotten.

Five boundaries get enforced along that one route, and none of them get merely checked or merely logged. The whole point is that nothing about it was exciting to watch. At no point did the request’s safety depend on an agent being smart, a prompt being careful, or a developer remembering a check that day. That quietness is the actual product.

Where boundaries stop

Honesty matters more than a clean story.

These boundaries separate tenants, not roles within a tenant. A user and an admin inside the same tenant are the same principal to the system.

A pod compromised inside a tenant’s scope opens everything inside that scope. Privileged containers and hostPath mounts escape Kubernetes-level isolation entirely.

A data boundary can fail silently. A developer deploys a hotfix on Friday evening, uses asyncpg directly for speed, forgets the wrapper. Monday morning the dashboard shows leads from every tenant mixed together. No error thrown, no alarm triggered. The wrapper exists because this scenario is not hypothetical.

Shared tools are a shared blast radius. A stateful, privileged component shared across tenants is a single point of compromise for all of them.

There is no audit trail yet. The system can show what happened. It cannot show who initiated it.

Why identity becomes necessary

Identity is introduced because the moment a multi-agent process includes an approval, the system has to answer a question boundaries alone cannot answer: who performed this action, and were they permitted to?

Identity converts a boundary-protected space into an attributable one. It attaches a principal to every action, a policy to every capability, and a record to every decision. It does not replace the boundaries. It makes them meaningful at the level of people and rules.

Why this unlocks graph engineering

The purpose of an Enterprise AI Harness is not running agents. It is enabling trustworthy enterprise orchestration: the ability to design, run, and evolve complex multi-agent processes without destroying trust between nodes.

A graph is the shape of such a process. One node clarifies a task. Another implements. A third verifies. A fourth decides whether to retry or to ship.

Each arrow in that graph is a transfer of trust. The verifier trusts that the implementer’s output is what was committed. The judge trusts that the verifier actually ran. Every one of those trusts is only valid if the nodes operate inside boundaries that make forgery and cross-contamination impossible.

A graph node without its tenant, its initiator, and its policy is a leak with a nice diagram drawn around it.

The evolution is not accidental. You do not arrive at graph execution by making agents smarter. You arrive there by making the environment trustworthy enough that a graph can be allowed to run.

There’s a payoff in all this boundary work that the boundaries framing was never marketed for. Once an agent is a namespaced, bounded YAML object, it stops being a live process you trust on faith and becomes something you can diff, review, and ship. Two versions of an Agent CRD are just a diff. Promoting one to production is a merge. Rolling it back is a revert.

That’s boundaries doing something they were never sold on: turning an agent into the kind of thing you bring to review the same way you’d bring a pull request. “I tested it, trust me” becomes a diff a second reviewer can actually read before it ships. A reviewer can challenge a capability, an approval gate can block the promote, and the team ships the agent the same way it ships code: through a pipeline, not through a person’s word.

What a full review pipeline for agent graphs looks like is a later article. For now, even this boundaries-only stage already buys you that.

Where this leaves me

An enterprise AI system doesn’t become trustworthy by choosing better components. It becomes trustworthy by acquiring architectural properties. Two orders matter, and both resist skipping.

Evolution (how a system grows toward graph execution):

single agent → multiple agents → cooperation → approvals → verification → graph execution

Dependency (what each stage needs underneath it):

architectural boundaries → identity → trust → graph execution

They meet at graph execution. One describes how you get there, the other describes what has to be holding when you arrive. Architectural boundaries are where the dependency chain starts, which is where the rest of it actually starts.

The implementation behind this argument is temporary; I expect most of it to be replaced within a year. The properties it’s demonstrating, I don’t expect to change.

Where the earlier article framed the harness as four layers, I’m not fully settled on that framing anymore. Some days I still think in layers; other days the properties feel more real: boundary, identity, audit, whatever comes after. Both may be two ways of looking at the same thing, and I may have a cleaner answer by the next article. I’d rather say that plainly than pretend the model is more finished than it is.

What I’m sure of, in whatever order I end up drawing it:

Graph Engineering needs trust.

Trust needs identity.

Identity needs boundaries.

All of it together is what I’ve been calling an Enterprise AI Harness.

If you’ve built something like this yourself, or you’d draw these boundaries differently, I’d genuinely like to hear it: in the comments, or on the repo.

items.title: Devtools must be open source (exe.dev)
items.summary:
My comment on Devtools must be open source (exe.dev) — Hacker News. One of the arguments for open source software for end-users has always been the freedom to examine and modify how that software works. The reality for most people - even expert programmers - has been that the freedom is more about being able to lean on other people to do that. Most people can't justify the time commitment needed to read and then modify the code for tools they use very often. I think LLMs have changed that equation in a way that makes the original dream much more feasible.
Several times a day I'll prompt regular Claude chat to "Clone x/y from GitHub and tell me how Z works". Getting software to compile in order to start hacking on it used to be enough friction that I often wouldn't bother. Now I treat that as a zero time investment challenge: tell Codex or Claude Code to checkout and build X and then come back ten minutes later and see how it got on. I'm not habitually modifying the software I use yet, but I can see a path to that which didn't exist a year or so ago. Tags: hacker-news , open-source , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-programming

items.title: Interior designers share 5 of the best and 3 of the worst ways to use extra space in your home
items.summary: Designers said there are some smart ways — and riskier ways — to utilize extra space in a home. sl-f/Getty Images/iStockphoto Interior designers told Business Insider the best and worst ways to use extra space in your home. Bookshelves can provide extra storage, TKTKTKTKT Sometimes a built-in storage unit or cabinet can lower the resale value of your space. Whether you rent an apartment or own a house, it's essential to consider how your design choices allow you to make the most efficient use of your space. So, Business Insider asked interior designers for tips on the best and worst ways to take advantage of extra space in your home. Declutter your closet by efficiently storing clothes you don't need Mark Cutler, an interior designer at CutlerSchulze , told BI that he recommends storing clothing you don't regularly wear separately rather than cluttering your closet. For example, you can also swap your clothes out seasonally and store not-often-worn items , like wedding-guest dresses, in another spot. "Just because you have a large closet, it does not mean you have to fill it or occasionally purge," Culter said. "Having all that extra space means you should be able to space out your wardrobe." He suggested using vacuum bags that can fit under the bed since they're protective and easy to tuck away. Consider adding more shelving to your space, especially if you love books You can also use bookshelves to store miscellaneous items. MagicBones/Shuttershock Different people have specific needs for their space, so avid readers may require a place to store more books efficiently, said Betty Brandolino , founder and creative director of design firm Fresh Twist Studio . Shelving units with cabinets or drawers at the bottom can be especially versatile. "Bookshelves can add extra storage space by incorporating lower cabinets, and we utilize baskets as hidden storage on a bookshelf," Brandolino said. When styled correctly, these shelves can also be beautiful centerpieces in a room. "We love to style bookshelves with decor items, baskets, picture frames, and, of course, books. It's all about scale, color, and texture," she added. She said that you can even add wallpaper to the back of the bookcase for "extra definition" or a pop of color. Turn the extra floor space near your bedroom window into a meditation nook Primary suites often feel like they have a lot of extra space for more shelving and furniture. However, Amanda Oninski , an interior designer at FLOOR360, suggested creating a meditation area with a rug instead. "The area rug can be selected to match the rest of the decor and custom cut to fit the designated space," she said. "The area rug serves as the floor cushion to relax." Oninski also recommended installing window treatments in the space to adjust the lighting and create a soothing mood. Add visual interest that isn't furniture to your space You can elevate a space with art. Followtheflow/Shuttershock Charli Hantman, owner of luxury firm August Black Interior Design , said it can be tempting to fill your extra space with additional large pieces of furniture — but there are other options worth considering, like wall art and sculptures. "Extra space doesn't necessarily have to be filled corner to corner. It's nice to have a variety of things to look at to create depth and visual interest," Hantman said. "I love finding art and wall sculptures that work together but have their own personality." For example, gallery walls can be a stylish and eclectic way to bring unique pieces to a room without adding more furniture. Put the space under your stairs to work Interior designer Brenna Morgan told BI that the space under neath a staircase is a great place for added storage that's often forgotten. "People typically avoid using it because it isn't a 'walk-in' space and has awkward angles," Morgan said. "[But] I have seen drawers and cabinets installed. I have seen it hollowed out to allow for a dog house. I have seen it used for wine storage." Morgan advised using careful measurements and working with the odd shapes and angles of your stairs to best incorporate extra storage. On the other hand, defining extra space with permanent features can lower the resale value Built-in cabinetry is not always very versatile. Breadmaker/Shuttershock Although it can be tempting to permanently tailor your space to your needs, Renee Croome , a designer at Northeast Kitchen and Flooring Center, advised against built-in furniture. "In a bonus room, I've seen a homeowner use cabinetry to build in a custom hobby or craft area," she told BI. "Although it was a beautiful space for crafting, the room didn't have the same versatility it would have if they had simply used furniture pieces instead of built-in cabinetry." Croome added that a permanently customized space is "not always the best option for resale value," so consider temporary or movable options first. Avoid adding single chairs as filler Hantman told BI one of her interior-design pet peeves is seeing single chairs placed in small, empty spaces without a purpose. "A chair can be placed just for visual appeal, but it should be surrounded by some other element like a lamp or a side table, to create a 'moment,'" Hantman said. "If it's only going to clutter the space and doesn't add any value to conversational seating, it will only make the space feel smaller and incohesive." The designer added that empty corners are OK since they allow the eye to focus on the more interesting pieces in the room. Don't use your empty space without some sort of plan Designer and stylist Heather McKeown of Land and Sky Designs told BI that "one of the worst ways to go about using extra space is to be a man without a plan." "A room without a sense of purpose or organization is like a lost ship at sea, floating aimlessly in the waves waiting for a storm to hit," McKeown said. "In this scenario, you are the storm, and the chaos of disorder is that lack of direction." Without a clear vision, rooms can become a cluttered, stressful mess, according to the design pro. So, before tackling your extra space, think about what function your home is missing and ways it could serve you better. Maybe you need extra toy storage, or your family could benefit from having a bench by the entryway for putting on shoes. When it comes to using extra space, focus on what could work best for your household. This story was originally published in September 2021 and most recently updated on August 3, 2026. items.title: Bluesky’s new CEO wants a big tent, not a bubble
items.summary: Today, I’m talking with Toni Schneider, who is the brand new CEO of the social platform Bluesky — he formally took over after a short stint as interim CEO. This is one of my favorite kinds of interviews to do on Decoder , because a couple years ago, we had Bluesky’s prior CEO, Jay Graber, on the show — she’s now the company’s chief innovation officer, and all of that kind of shuffle is pure Decoder bait. And a new CEO often brings with them new priorities, which is perhaps the most Decoder subject of all. Bluesky in particular is a company pulling in a lot of different directions: There’s a Twitter-like social media app, which is what most people are familiar with, and then there’s the underlying technology behind that app call AT Protocol, which allows anyone to build social networking products that interoperate with Bluesky. As you’ll hear Toni say, that ecosystem is vibrant and growing — it’s called the ATmosphere, which is adorable. But the users of Bluesky the app are not the same as the people building on AT Protocol, and the goals of a company founded to push forward the ideas of open and interoperable social standards are not necessarily aligned with the things all those users might need or want. This is a fight that bursts into view on Bluesky itself all the time, and I wanted to know how Toni thinks about balancing all of that with what remains a fairly small team. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Toni was formerly the CEO of Automattic, which makes the huge WordPress web content management platform, and you’ll hear him make the case that this period in social networking feels a lot like the early days of the web, and that success looks like a vibrant ecosystem with lots of big players that might take a decade to fully develop. That’s quite a vision, but here and now, the open web is falling apart, and the social products of today are fragmenting and in many cases either get smaller or full of AI slop. So we talked about all of that, and about Bluesky’s reputation as a bastion of leftists insulated in their own little bubble sitting next to the increasingly hard right bubble of X. And of course, we talked about how Bluesky might start to generate revenue — and interestingly enough, it’s not just ads. This is a fun one that touches on almost every Decoder theme there is. I think you’re gonna like it. Okay: Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Toni Schneider, you are a venture partner at True Ventures, and more importantly, the now permanent CEO of BlueSky. Welcome to Decoder. Thank you. Thanks for having me. I am very excited to talk to you. What is happening with the open social web is maybe the most important thing happening for media. It does not get as much attention as AI, but there’s something very big happening on these interoperable social networks. I know that you are a believer in it in the same way that you believed in the web when you were the CEO of Automattic, which is the company that makes WordPress. So let’s just start at the very start. Describe what you think BlueSky is today and what you think the opportunities with these new kinds of networks are. BlueSky today is really two things. There’s the BlueSky app, which is what a lot of people are familiar with. It’s a social network. We think it’s a better social network. It’s more human focused, doesn’t have ads. It doesn’t have algorithms. But more importantly, underneath BlueSky is an open protocol called AT Protocol. And BlueSky is only one of now over a thousand apps built on that protocol. The whole point of BlueSky was to demonstrate that this open protocol could scale and attract other builders, building lots of apps, lots of social experiences that all interoperate and connect with each other, which is what we believe the future of social media should look like. It’s what is actually going to make social media something that we believe in, which is that the future of social media should serve the public good. That is what motivates us, and that’s why we built the protocol first and then the app. There’s a lot in there already that is just pure Decoder bait, including the notion that BlueSky, the product, and the ATmosphere and AT Protocol, the standard, are all intermixed in one company that you now run. Right next to that is maybe the purest Decoder bait of all: the fact that Jay Graber, who was the CEO of BlueSky – she was on the show about two years ago – stepped down into the role of chief innovation officer. You were the interim CEO, and now after four months, you are the full-time CEO. Fundamentally, that is just the story that Decoder loves to tell the most. Talk me through that. What made you step in as the interim CEO, and why did you decide to become the full-time CEO? It’s actually really cool and inspiring that a founder, after she worked on this for six years, got it off the ground. She started inside Twitter, got it out of there, made it an independent thing. There are a lot of reasons why BlueSky is facing long odds and she got into this place, and then felt like it’s at a scale now where [it’s in] her sweet spot, the things that she loves working on, which is vision, innovation, new ideas. She felt pulled back towards building, especially also because of the advent of AI and how AI and AT Proto can interoperate. She felt like that’s what she wants to go work on, and it’s time to find somebody else for the CEO job. I was already involved with this project because I met the team a little bit over two years ago, probably around the same time Jay was on your podcast. We became investors through True Ventures. So I’ve been following it as an investor, supporting it. The team approached me and said that my background with WordPress and open source was a really good fit. This went over really well to the point where now WordPress is supporting Standard Site and lots of other publishing platforms. About 50 people, all remote, structured into small teams. I’m a big believer that six to eight person teams, highly aligned, highly incentivized, and motivated are the way to get things done. I would say it’s a team that’s a very low ego, high agency. That is kind of the ethos. Low drama, just a lot of get-shit-done energy. Really collaborative. Whenever I think about new social products and how they might scale, especially with explosive user growth – up until recently, the conventional wisdom is you’ve got to scale trust and safety and moderation linearly with the size of your user base. Maybe we’re going to add AI to this and that linear relationship will break, or maybe it’ll actually get even more costly because token spend will get more costly than having human moderators, or there’ll be more false positives and we’re going to be even angrier. So you have to have more humans in the loop. It’s really unclear to me how that’s going to work. You’ve obviously been scaling BlueSky as a consumer social product. Then you have the complexity of, “We’re hooking onto lots and lots of other products that are putting content in front of people.” How does the moderation layer work? And have you seen it be a linear increase in cost with the size of the network and the user base? Moderation is huge in any social product. In addition to our 50-person team, we do have contractors that help us with moderation. What we’ve done differently is that our whole moderation system is composable or pluggable. It’s not just us that can label content and moderate it. Anybody can do it and add labels. It’s part of the protocol. Anybody else who builds products can decide if they want to use those labels or not. So if somebody on our moderation team labels something as, let’s say, AI slop, everybody else who’s building in this ecosystem can take advantage of that piece of data. They don’t have to, but they can. So what we’re seeing and what we’ve seen is we have our moderation team, but then there are other teams that have decided to moderate label content the way they want. For example, maybe the first non-BlueSky project on the protocol was BlackSky. And it’s now become a thriving company on its own. It’s a team building all kinds of interesting things. And they started out by saying, “Hey, we want to build a version of this network that is optimized for Black users and their needs. And we want to have our own moderation policies.” And they are able to do that and plug that in. But everything they’re doing is still part of the larger network. And now there are hundreds and thousands of these kinds of systems. This has really helped where the moderation burden isn’t all on one team that has to scale and look at everything. There should be lots of different teams and lots of different systems because each network, each community has its own idea of what moderation should look like. So we feel like this kind of distributed moderation approach is more powerful. That said, yes, we’re continuing to scale up ours, but it’s manageable. It’s a lot of work, but it’s manageable. It’s worth it when the whole network can benefit from it. The next part of that story that’s going to be really interesting is that the biggest thing we’re actually working on with AT Proto, the next evolution of the protocol, is private data. We all know that the public square, public social networking has reached a certain scale. And there are a lot of people who want to retreat into more private spaces. We’ve seen explosive growth in group chats. We’re all in a million group chats. This has been the number-one request from our community, from our developers: “Let us build more private, membership-based, various versions of private spaces on this protocol.” We’re in the middle of building that. It’s a community effort. It’s rolling out very soon. Now, moderation moves and gets broken up into even more and smaller spaces. People can decide, “If I don’t like a network or I don’t like the way it’s moderated, [I can] go start my own.” Go start your own community. That’s the most interesting thing ahead of us, because right now everything on AT Proto is public. It can only be used for a completely public product. Once we enable private data, I think that it’s like 10 or 100X the number of use cases we can serve. Not to be reductive, but I think it’s useful to talk about this in comparison to other social products people might be more familiar with. With AT Protocol right now and the ATmosphere, everything is very public. The models in my head are Twitter, and RSS, and massive broad-based publishing platforms, right? One-to-many. I think what you’re describing is much more like a Reddit style approach, where you have smaller, closed communities. Some of them can be totally private unless you’re invited in. And yet, they’re still on the ATmosphere in some way. Is that right? That’s right. The trade-off has traditionally been that if you want to be on a launch network, you have to be on a public network. Or if you want to control, have ownership over your own community, you have to set up your own thing. You have to run your own server or you have to run your own forum. There’s clearly a need for that because there are lots of those out there. But the challenge is each one of those is now a little island. And you have to convince people. We think we can pull off as the best of both worlds. When you build a community or private space on AT Proto, it’s absolutely 100% owned by you. It’s not owned by BlueSky or by any company. It’s just like everything else on a protocol. It’s owned by the users, not by the platform. So it’s really truly yours. You can move it around. You can make all the decisions. But because it’s on a shared protocol, all of these communities plug together. You can go to a place like BlueSky and get all your notifications in one place. You can see what’s going on across everything. You just need one login, one place to check, but you still have the independence and the identity of these individual communities. That is something that no other platform can do right now. You’re either on the large platform owned and controlled place, or you run your own and you’re a little siloed. We think we can solve that. We see the energy behind this idea and the number of things people are already prototyping is very palpable. I have to ask you the other Decoder question because I’m very curious where this idea came from and how you decided to bet on it. How do you make decisions? What’s your framework for making decisions? I already talked a little bit earlier about the reversible and irreversible decisions. The hardest thing about running any project is that, especially if it’s successful, it’s just an endless flow of things you have to prioritize and decide on. I find you could make that a lot less daunting and exhausting if you move a lot of decisions into this category of “they’re not that big a deal.” Let’s make it easy to experiment and reverse things, and really only focus on the truly long-term impactful things that we have to get right. You have this lightness or almost playfulness about some of these things, where it’s just not that big a deal. Let’s just try something. Let’s be creative and improvisational about it. This is a lot of how Automattic runs. I actually credit a lot of that to Matt Mullenweg’s approach to first running an open-source project. Inside Automattic, there are a lot of jazz analogies because Matt started out as a jazz musician. One of the things that I feel like we’ve gotten better at in the last few months is to do that out in the open. Alex Benzer, who’s our head of product, who makes those decisions around what goes in the app and what doesn’t, has been posting about it and inviting feedback and saying, “Look, this is coming. What do you think? What kind of communities do you want? Do you want them? How similar should they be to the current app? How different?” I think we have 500 people who’ve signed up to give us feedback. We’re going through user interviews. You get to make your own. You can plug in your own. People have made over 100,000 feeds. Some of those are really communities themselves. There are things like BookSky and AstroSky, where it’s just communities of people talking about a certain topic within a custom feed. People have taken what we have to bend it into a community shape. It’s already happening on a network. That makes it a lot less scary. It’s not like we’re going to stop one thing and pivot somewhere else. We’re just doing more of a thing that some users are already doing. I think we can do it in a way that doesn’t disrupt. If you never want to join a private community, you don’t have to. BlueSky the app as it stands today isn’t going to change. The public part of it is popular, it’s growing. So we’re not going to mess with that. Let me ask you about BlueSky the app not changing, because I think that’s the thing that I’m poking at. It feels like every other social network evolves into a crab . Everything is evolving into TikTok. We can see it happening every single day. Meta today announced a test in which the big blue Facebook app will open for some set of users into full-screen video. “Screw it. We’re just going to turn Facebook into TikTok.” Everything heads in that direction. X has headed in that direction. That’s the competition, and maybe that’s the thing the market wants. You’re saying, “We’re going to build private data. We’ll have a more Reddit-like experience.” BlueSky may be the last really text-first social platform of its kind that exists. Do you feel that pull into different directions, into different formats? Because that’s a thing that your user base also pushes against. This is the beauty of an open protocol. Let somebody else build the TikTok of AT Proto. Let somebody else go push into new formats. We’re perfectly happy with a text-first, microblogging network. We love it. Honestly, I’m glad if others are chasing off in other directions because we like what we have. We talked earlier about traffic. A lot of these other networks, as you know… You’ve coined the term Google Zero right there. All these walled gardens, all these other platforms are getting more and more walled. They say, “Once we’re open enough to attract an audience, and then once you’re here, we’re not going to let you go. We’re just going to keep trying to find ways to keep you in there.” BlueSky’s the opposite. Because of the protocol, it’s locked open by default. We couldn’t keep you in it even if we wanted to. We want people to build other apps and experiment with other things. We want people to find great content on BlueSky and leave. We’re still a place where we don’t downrank links. I’m curious, if someone wants to build the TikTok of the ATmosphere, is there a bunch of protocol-level work that needs to be done to support it? I know there are attempts to do this. Skylight, I think, is a TikTok-like app on the ATmosphere. There are others. But all of your technical innovation on the standard itself is pointed at text. I’m wondering if there’s something you need to do to be better at video to compete with what all of the closed platforms are chasing at a much larger scale. No, I think at the protocol level, it’s easy to do. You can define your own records on the protocol. Yes, ours are text-focused or posts, they’re follows, they’re likes, things like that. But there are already people publishing all kinds of different things within a protocol. I saw yesterday that somebody’s publishing a patent database onto AT Proto, so everybody else can just tap into that patent information. There’s somebody who’s publishing the health data off of their Apple Watch onto their PDS. So they’re just live-streaming their health data onto the protocol. People are putting out all kinds of things. The protocol can be used for anything. What’s harder is that you need people there, so that when you build the next TikTok on AT Proto and you launch that app, it launches into millions and millions of people who are already there. That’s what we’re working on, to just keep getting more and more people onto the ATmosphere so that you don’t have that cold start problem as a new developer where you want enough people. Eventually our 10-year goal is a billion people on AT Proto. You don’t need a billion to have success with a new product, but you need a critical mass so that when people show up, then they ask, “Oh, where are my friends?” This is the dynamic that I’m really interested in with the BlueSky app and then the protocol itself. One of the issues here is we publish in a lot of formats in a lot of different places. If I just immediately federate The Verge tomorrow, we have a lot of video. Where’s the video going to go? It’s going to go out on the network. Maybe I can convince a lot of people to download a Verge app and they’ll see a bunch of stuff in it, and that would be great. But if what you’re describing is that BlueSky the app will be the entrance point for a lot of different people, and BlueSky the app has not prioritized video as part of the core part of the user experience – for any number of reasons why you might not prioritize video – then that part of the network won’t get that effect. It won’t get what feels like a network effect, which is, “Oh, there are lots of people here.” The way that if I federate The Verge , I’d say, “Look at all these great posts from other tech writers,” I could do that tomorrow. It’s almost easy to do. It’s easy to vibe-code that prototype, I will tell you. It’s hard to get it all the way to the finish line. That’s the dynamic. If you want BlueSky, the consumer app, to be the entry point to the diversity of the network, the app itself has to be diverse in a way that might dilute the app and make it lose its product market fit. How do you think about that back and forth? I think what we’re seeing works well, and I’ll go back to the Standard Site example. If the other piece of content that’s not text is something that can show up inside a post, we call them link cards, and that could be a video. It could be a game. It could be something where somebody can post about it and say, “Hey, check out this new game.” Somebody can see it and then go there. That’s a perfect fit because then it fits our mode of how people discover things. But then when they want to engage with it, we send them off to that place. Same with video. As long as somebody can embed it and promote it on our end, we’re not going to try and become a video network where we then say, “Oh, all video has to be watched on BlueSky.” No, no, no. Go off to The Verge , go somewhere else, go explore. I think BlueSky as an app is a great place to surface things and notify people of new things, but it does have to somehow fit inside the post. You can give people a preview essentially and say, “Okay, now go play this game. Go subscribe to this publication. Go donate to this cause.” That’s the kind of action we’re trying to surface for everybody else in the ATmosphere and then just send people off on their way. I want to ask you to compare your role at BlueSky to when you were the CEO of Automattic. These are big companies, or we want them to be big companies that operate on standards and protocols and the open web in different ways. At BlueSky, you control the standard itself. This is a very important piece of the puzzle that the standard is in development. And you’re making products on top of it and you want other people to build on top of the standard. A lot of people can say a lot of things about Automattic’s relationship to the web, but technically you don’t control the standard. And maybe it has enough scale so that the way Automattic does it becomes the way everyone else does it. But at Automattic, you didn’t make the browsers. You weren’t on the steering committees of the big standards in a way that allowed you to actually dictate what they were. You were making a web-server product that interacted with an ecosystem of other open products. Do you want BlueSky to get there where it’s just one player among many, or do you want to retain control of the standard too? And how do you think that’s different from how Automattic exists in the web ecosystem? We 100% do not want to control the standard at BlueSky. We are actually very actively doing everything in our power to divest control of it. First was to design the network in a way that if BlueSky goes down or goes away, the rest of the network is fine. That’s a big test case for us. It actually got tested a couple of months ago, not the way we had hoped, but we got a DDoS attack on the BlueSky network. A very, very massive one. It did take us down for several hours. Other parts of the network, like I mentioned BlackSky earlier, operated just fine, totally independently. That’s a big part. Just the practicality of it is, can other nodes in this network operate independently? Are there things left that BlueSky runs that everybody else is dependent on? And if so, what can we do to fix that? A big part of that, too, is that – this gets a little nerdy into the whole stack and the protocol – when people look at the design of this network and they like to find out, is it truly decentralized or not? There is one thing at the heart of it that absolutely no company should control, and that’s the identity directory, the lookup. When you log in your identity in the ATmosphere, where does that lookup actually happen? It’s like DNS on the web when somebody looks up a URL. We have been running that core directory, and we’re actually in the process of setting up a Swiss nonprofit with a separate board, a completely separate entity, to which we’ve handed over that directory. We’re in the process of handing over the domain to it. So that’s one example. We’re also handing the protocol spec itself to the IETF. Last week, the IETF met in Vienna, and AT Proto is now a work stream, an official work stream to take that out of BlueSky and hand it to the IETF. It’s going to become a blessed internet standard run by a completely separate entity. We’re constantly taking all the pieces that we had to bootstrap and handing them off to other entities. We’re super serious about that. The end state is that, yes, we are one app of many, one company of many running in this protocol, and we won’t control the protocol. The parallel to Automattic is that WordPress, the core software that Automattic is hosting, is open source and it’s GPL. Anybody can use it, but anybody who uses it and changes it has to give back to open source. In our case, it’s AT Protocol where anybody can build on AT Protocol. The beauty of building on AT Proto as a developer is all the data is owned by users and it’s accessible to any other app. But as an app, then your data also goes into those user repositories. So it makes it better for everybody else on the network. It’s similar to the way open source gets better through collaboration. This network gets better through everybody having their data shared and remixable and interoperable. When you get that balance right – or you have a company that helps bootstrap the whole thing, but by definition keeps itself separate and makes sure it can’t control the shared resource – then it can work. We did this successfully with Automattic and WordPress. Automattic became a big company. WordPress became a huge open source ecosystem, and then tons of other companies formed around it. Our test case was always, “What if Automattic goes out of business or gets acquired by somebody evil? Is WordPress going to be okay?” That’s why we put the WordPress trademark into a foundation so the company couldn’t mess with it. It’s complicated to set those things up. This is one of those, not even five years, like 20 years out decisions. If this thing gets big, will it be truly independent? Or could somebody come in and change their mind and mess with it? We think about that constantly at BlueSky and getting that balance right. Handing off pieces so that this – because it’s not going to work if one company tries to control it, we’re right back at square one and we’re just another walled garden, which is completely the opposite of what we’re trying to achieve. There’s a lot of drama with WordPress and the open-source community and other companies monetizing open-source in different ways. There’s drama with the foundation . I’ll set that all aside. People can go listen to Matt’s episodes . We did it in detail, and certainly will have him back. I like talking to Matt a lot. But that’s all coming for you too, because at some point all of this has to make money. A real theme on Decoder is we’ve set up complicated structures so that capitalism can’t ruin everything. We just had Proton on the show . Complicated Swiss foundation structure so that capitalism can’t ruin everything and all the promises they make to their customers. You don’t have that problem yet. As far as I can tell, there’s no revenue flowing into this and probably thus no push to make that revenue number go up in bad ways. At some point there is going to have to be some revenue. You’re an investor. I’m assuming you want to get paid out into your own fund. How is BlueSky going to make money on the app level, and how is the protocol going to make any money? The way we’re going to make money as a company, we’re only interested if that economic model works for the entire ATmosphere. We make money when everybody else makes money. That rules out a bunch of things that will be purely app-based. I’m not ready to announce the specifics, but we will start monetizing this year. The way I look at it is there’s already money being made on this network. We’re sending lots of traffic to people who then convert that traffic into subscriptions.. I think our job is to just help more of that happen. Right now it’s just organic, and we can build things into our app and into the protocol that make it easier for people to start making a livelihood on this protocol and start doing ecommerce with each other. That’s the direction we’re headed in. We’re going to do it in a way where the whole idea is for the pie to get huge and for us to be a small slice of a big pie and for everybody to make money. If we can help you as a publisher make more money, then we can do business together. I know you said you weren’t going to do specifics, but I have to poke at this a little bit. Your options, if you want a small piece of a big pie, are “We’re going to let you run ads for your subscription newsletter and then that’ll convert.” That’s Facebook’s model, right? “We’re going to let you run ads at whatever CPM, and your return on ad spend will be high enough so that enough subscribers signed up based on how many ads you were on.” And the other one is, “We’re just going to take a percentage of every signup fee.” Which direction do you think you’re headed in? It would definitely be the latter, but we would only take a percentage of anything that we actually enable. If we send extra traffic to you, then it would be a percentage of that. So basically affiliate-style monetization. If I’m selling a newsletter for $10 a month and you send me a new subscriber, you’re going to get some of that back. Affiliate style and in a way that works for the entire network. Anybody on the network that sends you traffic can participate. We want everybody to have a part in it. Can you decentralize the billing and financial layer of that? We can make it work in a decentralized network. Billing does require some centralized trust, and that’s certainly something we’re looking at. I asked you that question because I was terrified of a crypto scheme basically, but it does not sound like you’re going to do crypto schemes. No, no. Similar intentions, but definitely not a crypto approach. One of the things that you’ve been describing is, “We have to build all these structures to withstand the bad incentives. If somebody shows up and buys BlueSky, and they’ve got bad intentions or they just want to use it to do crypto schemes, we have to build the structure that will withstand it.” Adding monetization in whatever form – and I agree the network should be monetized in some way – creates a bunch of these incentives at first launch. It will be your first contact with those incentives. You have some experience with this, certainly even thinking about it. How do you expect that to go both with your team and with the user base of BlueSky itself? The team is eager to figure this out because we realize that there has to be an economic model for this network. Otherwise, we’re in the early bootstrap phase still and lots of people are getting excited to build on this. But it’s the number-one question for my team, from all the people building. “What’s that model going to be?” Everybody’s eager to figure this out and to do it in a way that we don’t fall into the traps of trying to create the incentives that we’ve seen in other networks, which just cause all kinds of unintended consequences. Looping back on the WordPress example, it can work really nicely. WordPress is a slightly different model because it’s a hosting model. But there are thousands and thousands of WordPress hosts out there that are doing just fine and it just works. You can host your site anywhere, you can move it anywhere. They compete to be the best host for your content, but it’s a very good model. As far as I can tell, it hasn’t created anybody to take all the market share or create these weird incentives where the product gets worse. There’s a very nice dividing line there between “I’m your host” and “you go and do whatever you want.” You can build an ad network if you want. You can build a store, you can build something else. Our business model doesn’t dictate what your business model should be, which is kind of what happens in these other networks when it’s only ads. “Oh yeah, come here, build your following on here and then we’re going to put ads on it. If you want to do anything else, no, no, no, it’s going to be ads.” Those are the kinds of things we think about. Talking about irreversible decisions, that’s going to be a huge one when we start to zero in on the right model to make sure that we can picture this scaling to billions of users and all kinds of businesses emerging on this network, not just one type that we happen to think about. You’ve mentioned BlackSky a handful of times in this conversation. I’ve been lucky enough to be at a dinner with Rudy [Fraser] who runs BlackSky. He’s prolific in talking about what it’s like to actually build on the ATmosphere and what a lot of the challenges have been. Because it hasn’t yet really, truly been decentralized. Now it’s my turn to say, I won’t go into the weeds of the protocol, but there are parts of the BlueSky stack and parts of the ATmosphere that have been pretty heavily centralized up until fairly recently. Is it easy to stand up a competitor, in the way that you’re describing people can stand up competitors to WordPress and operate in their own universe using the same tools and same access to end customers? Or is there still work to be done there? Because it hasn’t been easy up until now, at least using the example of BlackSky. Rudy deserves a lot of credit for taking those early risks when it was much harder to build and being the first to prove that it can be done, but it’s getting easier and easier. We are seeing more and more BlueSky- and BlackSky-style networks pop up pretty often. We’re actually seeing a whole bunch of energy in Europe. We’ve got EuroSky. W Social just launched. There’s another one I think that’s about to launch. It’s getting easier, and we’re investing a lot to make it as easy as possible. In addition to being an open protocol, all of BlueSky’s open source. You can take the BlueSky app and just fork it and go do your own BlueSky. That’s great, but we’re really also interested in people building other things that are microblogging on the network and making that super easy. We’re seeing Tangled as an example that a lot of people like to use recently because it’s a great project. They raised VC funding. It’s a social coding platform, like a social GitHub that’s growing really nicely using AT Proto for the social layer of the social coding aspect. Has nothing to do with microblogging, but it’s another thing that we can collaborate and integrate. People use both Tangled and BlueSky. It all just works together. But those are examples where it’s getting really easy to just build a new app on AT Proto and have it have social functionality. It doesn’t have to be an entire BlueSky-style network that you have to run. We put effort into making it easier. When BlackSky started two or three years ago, it was a big lift. You had to be very technical to do it. Now it’s gotten easier and easier. Finally, we haven’t talked about AI yet. AI makes it even easier. A lot of the growth we’re seeing now is that you can point to one of the AI coding tools on AT Proto and say, “Hey, build me a social app, build me a community.” And that makes it that much easier. Those are some of the tools and integrations that we’re working on on Jay’s new team, but that really changes the game pretty substantially for just how easy all this stuff is getting. I do have to ask you the AI question. You’re a software CEO again. How do software companies work in the age of AI? Have you rethought your teams? Do you have the traditional product-manager-designer-engineer trio? Or is everybody doing everything? It’s a small team and you’re the new CEO. So you have lots of opportunity to rethink everything. It is very empowering once you get it right. We have to use our exploration team as an example. That’s a three- to four-person team that’s launching at very high velocity, launching brand new products. It’s really fun when you have an existing company with existing resources and very senior talented people can then go after a new greenfield opportunity with these new tools. That’s when you see a ton of velocity. If you have an existing product with all the complexity of how it’s been built, AI helps, but you’re still dealing with that same complexity for a while. I see it accelerate everything in terms of the development pace. You still need great product managers, you need great designers. You need [to know] how to build. The building part is faster than what to build. The ideas are just as hard as ever, in a way harder because there’s so much noise out there and so many things popping up every day. Setting yourself apart, building something really great that lasts. Just because it’s faster with AI doesn’t make it any easier. We’ve talked a lot about standards and making AT Protocol and the ATmosphere a more standardized project at the IETF and whatever Swiss foundation is going to do name lookups. It feels like we’re going to recapitulate ICANN. But that’s a totally different episode of Decoder , and we’ll come to that drama when everything is successful. There is another standard that has already gone through all this. There’s ActivityPub. Mastodon runs an ActivityPub. Famously, Threads runs an ActivityPub, to whatever extent Threads runs on ActivityPub. There’s an argument that Meta did all of that just to satisfy European regulators, and that’s all it’s there for. Have you talked to the Threads team about integrating with ActivityPub or moving them to the ATmosphere? Once you become an official standard, I imagine that must be easier for them to continue throwing bones to European regulators. That would be the big unlock, right? That is the hundreds of millions of users on a nominally open network. Have they shown any interest? We have not talked to Threads. We’re definitely talking to Mastodon and ActivityPub. They definitely feel we’re very aligned. Our missions are very aligned. We’re all on Team Open together. These are two different standards that do slightly different things. And some use cases for ActivityPub are great and some are great for AT Proto. What are use cases that are good in ActivityPub and what are use cases that are better in AT Protocol? ActivityPub is based around this notion of a server. At the heart of it, you set up your own server, you control it, you run it, that’s your community, and then all the servers can federate if you want. You don’t have to, you can just run it by yourself, or you can plug into the federation, into the Fediverse. That’s how their system works. It works really well. They have a lot of successful governments who want to set up their own server infrastructure and run their own community infrastructure. AT Proto has a different goal. We don’t have a server at the heart of it. We have the PDS, the personal data server that is your data. The heart of AT Proto is personal identity and portability and ownership of that so that whatever you create and the social graph that you create is owned by you and lifts wherever you want to host it. It’s really a federation of millions and millions of these tiny little personal servers that can all talk to each other. That works if your social product is focused on people, not on an entire server with a community on it. So a slightly different shape. They interoperate too. There’s something called Bridgy Fed that connects these two worlds together. So if you’ve built products on this yourself, if you want to post or publish across all of it, you can and the end user doesn’t even have to know. That’s the beauty of an open protocol: you shouldn’t have to. Consumers of this should never even hear about these new protocols. Because it’s one of these things where you have to get the protocol right and it has to be open, but then people should just forget about it. It should just disappear. The examples we use a lot are email and websites. If I’m on Outlook and you’re on Gmail, we can just email each other. You never think about the fact that those are two completely separate systems. It just works. But on social media, it just doesn’t work that way. If you’re on Instagram and I’m on TikTok, we can’t talk to each other. You have to do everything five different times and on five different apps, and it’s crazy making. If we get this right at the protocol level, that just goes away. All this stuff just works just like email does or just like websites do. Our job is to make all of that work under the hood, but nobody has to think about it.
