items.summary_html:
Enterprise AI budget forecasting is mostly guesswork right now. Most organizations set their initial allocations before they understood how token costs actually accumulate — before multiple teams were running agents, before workflows were hitting multiple data sources per call, before anyone had a real sense of what volume would look like. As enterprises are discovering, Agentic workloads are especially token heavy and costly per run.

The instinct when costs climb is to look at the model layer — route simpler queries to cheaper models, cap inference, negotiate volume pricing. Those help, but for enterprises running AI agents against live business data, the larger cost variable usually isn’t which model you’re running. It’s how the agent’s tools are defined and how much context it carries into each call. 

Anthropic’s engineering team documented a five-server MCP setup — 58 tools — consuming approximately 55,000 tokens before the real conversation even starts. A default Salesforce Account integration can expose more than 70 fields whereas a production query typically needs fewer than ten. The gap between those two numbers is money.

We benchmarked a federated query spanning Salesforce, Snowflake, and ServiceNow under different architectural configurations — same model, same data, same prompt — and got a 97.6% reduction in token spend, from $0.596 to $0.027 per query. This piece explains what’s driving that and how to assess where your own workflows fall.

Where Token Cost Originates

A token is roughly three to four characters of text, or about three-quarters of a word. System prompts, tool definitions, query results, and responses all count toward it. In a single-source workflow this is manageable; in multi-source federated workflows, three structural forces push it up quickly.

(Shutterstock_Jack_the_sparow)

Tool definition overhead. Every connected data source adds its schema to the request. When MCP tools aren’t scoped, the agent carries the full schema for every connected system on every call, whether the workflow touches it or not.

Round-trip accumulation. Each tool call generates a tool_use block and a tool_result block, both re-sent in full on every subsequent turn. A multi-source discovery chain can require six to eight tool calls before returning anything — by turn five, tens of thousands of tokens of history are being re-transmitted each time.

Discovery overhead on known workflows. When an agent doesn’t know what data exists, it has to find out first: catalog inspection, schema retrieval, column enumeration, then finally a query. That makes sense on genuinely unknown data. On a recurring workflow querying sources that have been stable for months, the same chain runs every time for no reason.

At 100,000 queries per month, the difference between a scoped tool layer and an unscoped one determines whether enterprise AI stays within budget or overruns part-way through the year.

Architecture Should Match the Workflow Intent

The central mistake in enterprise AI deployments is applying exploratory architecture to workflows that have already stabilized.

There’s a real spectrum here. Some workflows are permanently open-ended by design — conversational AI assistants, for instance, where the question space is unbounded and the agent genuinely needs broad visibility to be useful. Others start exploratory and stabilize: the data sources get evaluated, the query patterns settle, and what began as exploration becomes a repeatable workflow running on a schedule feeding dashboards, triggering alerts, informing weekly reviews. The sources are known, the query pattern is established, and somebody already decided which fields matter — so running the full discovery chain every time is paying for exploration that already happened.

(Shutterstock/ImageFlow)

The architectural interventions that drive large token reductions are all forms of the same underlying move: encode what’s known so the agent doesn’t have to re-derive it. Pre-join the data. Scope the catalog. Cache results that don’t need to be live. Define a parameterized tool instead of handing the agent a 70-column schema and letting it figure out which six columns it needs. These are decisions that sit upstream of the model entirely.

The Architectural Levers

These are the configurations we tested in the benchmark below, each targeting a specific source of context overhead.

Pre-joined virtual views encapsulate joins and filters across sources into one interface, so three data calls become one.

Cached query results serve reads from a managed store on a refresh schedule instead of hitting live systems every call.

Curated tool bundles group tools into named, workflow-specific sets — a sales bundle, a finance bundle — so each session connects to only what it needs.

Scoped data catalogs limit which tables and tools a session can see, so the agent considers only sources relevant to the workflow.

Custom scoped tools replace a full source schema with a parameterized template exposing only the fields and filters the workflow uses.

We tested each of the five individually to determine how they impact token consumption.

The Benchmark

The test prompt: “Show me open support tickets, the related CRM accounts, and the product telemetry data from the data warehouse for enterprise customers. Return up to 50 rows.”

A federated query across an ITSM platform, a CRM, and a data warehouse in one agent turn. Token counts were captured directly from the API response object per call and turn, across 56 independent runs at temperature=0, with five architectural configurations measured against a fully exploratory baseline.

The table reads as a spectrum that matches the intervention to the workflow type and measures its token reduction.

The baseline is the universal, unscoped path: the agent discovers the catalog, retrieves schemas, enumerates columns, runs data queries, then synthesizes. At 183,541 tokens and $0.596 per query, it’s thorough and expensive — and it’s the right architecture when the workflow is genuinely unknown.

We’d point most production workflows at the Optimal row. It combines a scoped data catalog, pre-joined views, and cached results, so the agent sees only the relevant sources, doesn’t re-orchestrate joins it’s already run before, and pulls from a fresh cache instead of hitting live systems on every call — cutting token spend by 93.6% against the baseline while keeping enough flexibility for a workflow that still shifts occasionally. 

Critically, the agent is still doing something worth paying for here: reasoning across sources, handling edge cases that don’t fit a fixed template, deciding what “enterprise customers” or “open tickets” means when the definition varies slightly by system. For workflows that are genuinely fixed, there’s room to go further — the custom scoped tool configuration gets to 97.6%. But a workflow with no variation left to accommodate may not need an LLM in the loop at all. At that point the query is closer to a stored procedure than an agent task, and it’s worth asking whether the token spend is buying anything a fixed script wouldn’t do for less.

Accuracy Is Also a Context Problem

Token cost gets the headline, but there’s a second effect worth taking seriously: answer quality degrades when the model is carrying context it doesn’t need.

LLMs aren’t databases. They don’t retrieve from context the way an index retrieves a row — relevant information competes with irrelevant information across the context window, and the ratio affects the output. A tool definition exposing 73 fields for a workflow that needs six doesn’t just cost more; it gives the model more surface to reason incorrectly over.

(Amit Naik is the VP of AI at CData)

The benchmark makes this concrete. The custom scoped tool configuration reduced the Salesforce Account schema from 73 columns to 6, and the model reasoned over exactly the data the query needed: one tool call, no discovery, correct on the first attempt across all runs. Less irrelevant context means fewer opportunities to go wrong. In production workflows where accuracy is audited and errors cost something, that’s the more important argument. The token savings are real, but they’re secondary to the reliability gain.

What to Do With This

The more durable question for a Head of AI isn’t which model is cheapest — that layer is commoditizing fast. It’s how much of what you’re sending the model actually needs to be there.

Start with the workflows that have already proven their value and settled into a repeatable pattern; those are the candidates for tightening. Pull the tool definitions they’re calling and compare fields exposed against fields used — that gap is the most direct measure of avoidable cost. Then count the tool calls a typical run requires before data comes back. The benchmark’s exploratory baseline took 22; the custom scoped tool configuration took one.

Exploratory workflows and ad-hoc analysis should stay on the universal path — the overhead there is buying real capability. The point isn’t to optimize everything; it’s to stop running discovery on workflows that already know where they’re going. For organizations operating AI at volume against live enterprise data, tool and context architecture is where the economics are actually decided.

items.title: SpaceX is set to acquire 130,000 acres of marshland in southern Louisiana
items.summary: SpaceX and the state of Louisiana are close to finalizing a deal for the launch company to acquire about 130,000 acres along the northern coast of the Gulf of Mexico. There have been persistent rumors about such an agreement for months, but now The Times-Picayune | The New Orleans Advocate reports that Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry is expected to announce the agreement later this month. The deal would give SpaceX control of an 18-mile stretch of marshland southwest of Lafayette. The site, known as Pecan Island, became available as part of a legal settlement that resolves dozens of lawsuits that blame ExxonMobil for pollution and coastal land loss, the newspaper reports. Read full article Comments

items.title: Sam Altman’s Parenting Strategy Sounds Low Key Horrifying
items.summary: Late last year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told “Tonight Show” host Jimmy Fallon that raising a child was now impossible without constantly turning to AI for advice — despite humans managing just fine without ChatGPT since the dawn of time. His comments painted a dystopian picture of the future of parenting in which human connection is supplanted by AI-powered nannies and chatbots. And as children unfortunate enough to be growing up in the midst of the AI boom are being gifted picture books filled to the brim with mind melting AI slop by their boomer grandparents and rapidly losing the ability to read , Altman has now debuted his next big idea. “Cool use case of ChatGPT work I heard last night,” Altman tweeted on Friday. “Connect your family calendars and explain your kids’ interests.” “Every morning for the drive to school, have it make a podcast that talks about one kid’s soccer game that afternoon, one kid’s upcoming birthday, some news, etc,” added the CEO, who had a baby via surrogate with his husband last year. The horrifying suggestion of feeding children AI-generated drivel before they even had a chance to get to school — where they’ll likely be exposed to even more slop by their educators — didn’t sit well with many. “What if you just talked to your children,” animator and director Alex Hirsch shot back , a reaction that garnered almost 20 times more likes than Altman’s original suggestion. Others were taken aback with how the billionaire CEO could’ve possibly thought this was a good idea. “Can’t stop thinking about this,” stand-up comedian Gianmarco Soresi tweeted in response to Altman. “Not just bc it’s such an abhorrent idea but also this is THE GUY that’s trying to pitch America on AI writ large and he’s so blind to the public interest he thought this was somehow appealing.” “It’s wild how disconnected these tech people are from normal human behavior,” actor Mike Dargatis wrote . While Altman continues to come up with deranged ideas on how to wriggle out of parenting responsibilities, OpenAI president Greg Brockman appears to have caught on to the fact that anybody who isn’t an AI-pilled tech executive may prioritize human connection over yet another chatbot. “At OpenAI, many people hook their ChatGPT up to Slack,” he tweeted on Saturday. “People really don’t like when a coworker’s ChatGPT contacts them asking for help with a task, even when they’d be perfectly happy doing that same work if asked by that coworker,” Brockman wrote. “Reinforces how much people care about human relationships and helping each other, and want AI to give time back — or enhance time together — rather than become a layer separating people.” Altman remains convinced he’s on the right side of history. During a podcast appearance last year, he argued that “my kids will never be smarter than AI, but they’ll be vastly more capable.” He also argued that “there will be problems” with people forming “very problematic parasocial relationships” that will force society to “figure out new guardrails.” Altman even argued that ChatGPT “should be tech that you don’t trust that much,” because it “hallucinates.” More on Altman: Sam Altman Says Even the Power of AI Will Never Lead to a Shorter Work Week The post Sam Altman’s Parenting Strategy Sounds Low Key Horrifying appeared first on Futurism .
items.summary_html:
Late last year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told “Tonight Show” host Jimmy Fallon that raising a child was now impossible without constantly turning to AI for advice — despite humans managing just fine without ChatGPT since the dawn of time.

His comments painted a dystopian picture of the future of parenting in which human connection is supplanted by AI-powered nannies and chatbots.

And as children unfortunate enough to be growing up in the midst of the AI boom are being gifted picture books filled to the brim with mind melting AI slop by their boomer grandparents and rapidly losing the ability to read, Altman has now debuted his next big idea.

“Cool use case of ChatGPT work I heard last night,” Altman tweeted on Friday. “Connect your family calendars and explain your kids’ interests.”

“Every morning for the drive to school, have it make a podcast that talks about one kid’s soccer game that afternoon, one kid’s upcoming birthday, some news, etc,” added the CEO, who had a baby via surrogate with his husband last year.

The horrifying suggestion of feeding children AI-generated drivel before they even had a chance to get to school — where they’ll likely be exposed to even more slop by their educators — didn’t sit well with many.

“What if you just talked to your children,” animator and director Alex Hirsch shot back, a reaction that garnered almost 20 times more likes than Altman’s original suggestion.

Others were taken aback with how the billionaire CEO could’ve possibly thought this was a good idea.

“Can’t stop thinking about this,” stand-up comedian Gianmarco Soresi tweeted in response to Altman. “Not just bc it’s such an abhorrent idea but also this is THE GUY that’s trying to pitch America on AI writ large and he’s so blind to the public interest he thought this was somehow appealing.”

“It’s wild how disconnected these tech people are from normal human behavior,” actor Mike Dargatis wrote.

While Altman continues to come up with deranged ideas on how to wriggle out of parenting responsibilities, OpenAI president Greg Brockman appears to have caught on to the fact that anybody who isn’t an AI-pilled tech executive may prioritize human connection over yet another chatbot.

“At OpenAI, many people hook their ChatGPT up to Slack,” he tweeted on Saturday.

“People really don’t like when a coworker’s ChatGPT contacts them asking for help with a task, even when they’d be perfectly happy doing that same work if asked by that coworker,” Brockman wrote. “Reinforces how much people care about human relationships and helping each other, and want AI to give time back — or enhance time together — rather than become a layer separating people.”

Altman remains convinced he’s on the right side of history. During a podcast appearance last year, he argued that “my kids will never be smarter than AI, but they’ll be vastly more capable.”

He also argued that “there will be problems” with people forming “very problematic parasocial relationships” that will force society to “figure out new guardrails.” Altman even argued that ChatGPT “should be tech that you don’t trust that much,” because it “hallucinates.”

More on Altman: Sam Altman Says Even the Power of AI Will Never Lead to a Shorter Work Week

items.title: My husband and I want our kids to learn from our financial mistakes, not repeat them
items.summary: The author said she and her husband borrowed more money than they should have early in their marriage. They're teaching their kids (not shown) to approach finances differently. draganab/Getty Images My husband and I started borrowing money when we were planning our wedding. We never stopped and borrowed more than we should have. Now we're paying off the mistakes we made and teaching our kids to treat finances differently. "Mom, what's it called again when a business has its trucks taken away?" my 11-year-old called from the living room. "Reposession," I responded. My husband had recently explained to our son what happens to a business when it files for bankruptcy . "Their vehicles are repossessed. They're taken away and sold to someone else." The repossession of business assets may not be regular dinner table banter in other people's households, but in our home, there is no financial topic that is not discussed. We haven't filed for bankruptcy, but because of some very bad financial decisions, we very nearly did. By speaking openly about our finances and general money literacy in front of our children, we're hoping they won't make the same mistakes we did. We started off on the wrong foot Our very first financial decision that my husband and I made was to use money borrowed from our families to pay for our wedding . Around $17,000 didn't seem like a lot of money to spend on a wedding at the time. It turns out, it was $17,000.00 too much. Starting our married life using debt catapulted us into a life where using debt became normalized. After we paid off the parental loans we used for our wedding, we launched ourselves into even more debt. The author said she and her husband aren't hiding any past financial mistakes from their kids. Courtesy of Cara Howlett. A string of financial missteps In 2015, we borrowed $15,000.00 from my parents to help purchase a home. After spending over a year renovating the money pit of a house we really couldn't afford, we sold it. From the deal, we only got a few thousand more than we paid for it, and a credit score so terrible we couldn't buy another home at the time. We landed in a nice rental in a smaller town and hoped to pay off our debts as soon as possible. Then, I lost my part-time job, and paying off our debt became a pipe dream. Instead of paying down our debt, we accumulated more. At the time, we were relying on credit cards for everything from groceries and clothes to high-end gym memberships, eating out every Friday, and expensive vacations we couldn't afford. We were rescued and went right back into debt At our lowest point, we nearly filed for bankruptcy, but thankfully, we were able to pay off our debt with money from a family inheritance. But, because we didn't change our spending habits, our debt accumulated again. The author hopes that speaking openly about money and finances helps her children avoid some of the mistakes she and her husband made. Courtesy of Cara Howlett. I want better for my kids Because my husband and I have made these costly mistakes, we talk about money in all forms to our kids, who are 8 and 11. They know we are once again working to pay down our debts. They understand this is why we sometimes say no when they ask for brand-new bikes or want to know why we're living in a small apartment when their friends live in larger homes. I never want my kids to know the stress that comes with carrying large amounts of consumer debt. My deepest hope for them is that they learn from our mistakes and live within their means. I don't want their paychecks to be eaten up with debt payments; I want them to use their money to fund their dreams and their families' joys. Some people balk at how open we are about our finances with our kids, but if we don't teach them, who will? Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Introducing our Artifacts Hub and Adoption Dashboard
items.summary: No voiceover for this quick post, but a quick video version is here . We’re expanding our open models coverage into standalone projects that let you go deeper on the state of the open model ecosystem. The new free sources of data are: The Artifacts Hub — a curated view of the models trending on Hugging Face, highlighting inference tokens via Open Router , model intelligence via Artificial Analysis , and our tailored adoption metrics building on top of Hugging Face ’s data. Our Adoption Dashboard — a living dashboard of download and derivative model numbers by geography and organization. This highlights the US-China gap and growing players in the open ecosystem. To date, our primary efforts on Interconnects have been release recaps for popular models like Kimi K3 , GLM 5.2 , DeepSeek R1 , etc. and monthly round-ups of the open models that matter, Artifacts Log . We’re expanding on these, building on the tools and internal data we’ve collected for other projects like The ATOM Project (and report ). This allows us to capture our ecosystem view of open models, develop methods for understanding adoption of giant MoE models, and everything in between. We’re sharing them freely to help the open ecosystem find its strengths and grow. Visit the Artifacts Hub The Artifacts Hub right now covers 792 models released in the last two years, across the core text-focused language models and multimodal generative models. At Interconnects we follow the data of every model on Hugging Face, analyze the core few thousand LLMs (this list is public on GitHub and regularly updated), and hand select these core few hundred for further explanation. We built the Hub as a way to go deeper on this analysis in collaboration with Project VAIL — an AI verification startup who has been one of the most loyal fans of our open model curation. For the most popular models, the Hub let’s you quickly see how far behind the model was in terms of frontier intelligence based on Artificial Analysis’s Intelligence Index, compare Hugging Face and Open Router adoption to similar models, glance at relative adoption metric (RAM) scores for time-size normalized downloads, or look at the VAIL similarity index of models with related generations. A snapshot for what you’d see for something like GLM-5.2 is below. Our other project is much lighter weight, but far overdue. Ever since we wrote The ATOM Project, we’ve been seeing the US-vs-China model adoption plot on a recurring basis in the AI ecosystem. We’d update the plot from time to time, but not enough. Now, we’re making the crucial data for that report and the ecosystem available in a daily updating dashboard. Visit our dashboard It’s core to our mission at Interconnects to enable the open ecosystem. Right now, as the world figures out how to use open models productively — especially in cost-competitive ways to frontier models — providing more transparency on what is happening is the best way for us to figure out what is working. We’d love to hear how we can make this better, please get in touch. We’re also interested in how others could use our curated data for other products or research in the open ecosystem. Get in touch at mail@interconnects.ai . Thanks again to the teams at Hugging Face, Open Router, and Artificial Analysis for making this possible — most of all the Hugging Face. Thank you to VAIL for the motivation and support in making these projects.

No voiceover for this quick post, but a quick video version is here.

We’re expanding our open models coverage into standalone projects that let you go deeper on the state of the open model ecosystem. The new free sources of data are:

  1. The Artifacts Hub — a curated view of the models trending on Hugging Face, highlighting inference tokens via Open Router, model intelligence via Artificial Analysis, and our tailored adoption metrics building on top of Hugging Face’s data.

  2. Our Adoption Dashboard — a living dashboard of download and derivative model numbers by geography and organization. This highlights the US-China gap and growing players in the open ecosystem.

To date, our primary efforts on Interconnects have been release recaps for popular models like Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, DeepSeek R1, etc. and monthly round-ups of the open models that matter, Artifacts Log. We’re expanding on these, building on the tools and internal data we’ve collected for other projects like The ATOM Project (and report). This allows us to capture our ecosystem view of open models, develop methods for understanding adoption of giant MoE models, and everything in between. We’re sharing them freely to help the open ecosystem find its strengths and grow.

Visit the Artifacts Hub

The Artifacts Hub right now covers 792 models released in the last two years, across the core text-focused language models and multimodal generative models. At Interconnects we follow the data of every model on Hugging Face, analyze the core few thousand LLMs (this list is public on GitHub and regularly updated), and hand select these core few hundred for further explanation.

We built the Hub as a way to go deeper on this analysis in collaboration with Project VAIL — an AI verification startup who has been one of the most loyal fans of our open model curation.

For the most popular models, the Hub let’s you quickly see how far behind the model was in terms of frontier intelligence based on Artificial Analysis’s Intelligence Index, compare Hugging Face and Open Router adoption to similar models, glance at relative adoption metric (RAM) scores for time-size normalized downloads, or look at the VAIL similarity index of models with related generations. A snapshot for what you’d see for something like GLM-5.2 is below.

Our other project is much lighter weight, but far overdue. Ever since we wrote The ATOM Project, we’ve been seeing the US-vs-China model adoption plot on a recurring basis in the AI ecosystem. We’d update the plot from time to time, but not enough. Now, we’re making the crucial data for that report and the ecosystem available in a daily updating dashboard.

Visit our dashboard

It’s core to our mission at Interconnects to enable the open ecosystem. Right now, as the world figures out how to use open models productively — especially in cost-competitive ways to frontier models — providing more transparency on what is happening is the best way for us to figure out what is working.

We’d love to hear how we can make this better, please get in touch. We’re also interested in how others could use our curated data for other products or research in the open ecosystem. Get in touch at mail@interconnects.ai.

Thanks again to the teams at Hugging Face, Open Router, and Artificial Analysis for making this possible — most of all the Hugging Face. Thank you to VAIL for the motivation and support in making these projects.

items.title: Why a Flock Worker Quit: ‘They Lied’
items.summary: This is an adaption of a podcast interview 404 Media recorded with Jonathan Paz, a former Flock employee who is now running running for Congress in Massachusetts’ 5th District. Check out the whole thing here on YouTube . Jonathan Paz was initially nervous when he started working at the surveillance company Flock. It was his first tech job. But he was interested in the company’s mission. Flock’s cameras, which constantly scan the license plate of every vehicle driving past, were for finding missing people. Staff at the company were able to solve real issues. In his job as a government affairs manager a couple of years ago, Paz represented Flock in public hearings, with the goal of getting a city to purchase Flock cameras. These sorts of hearings are happening on a near constant basis all across the country , as cities and towns participate in a national conversation about whether they want Flock cameras in their community or not. “My job was to make sure that we were not only defending the company, but also representing the product as best as possible and making sure that we can get approved at council,” Paz said. He would get flown out to different cities and towns to help get Flock across the finish line. He was the break-in-case-of-emergency button. In one case, Paz went to a place that was planning on purchasing Flock cameras but there was a lot of community pushback. Those people did not want these cameras in their community. Paz realized his job was to “make sure that this resistance doesn't become a vote reflected in the vote of the council.” “That's kind of what started unraveling for me very quickly: this facade that we were helping these democratically elected boards” represent the people who voted for them. Before Flock, Paz had a career in social justice work, including as an activist, union organizer, and an elected city councilor in Waltham, Massachusetts, he said. He focused in part on municipal broadband. At the time he held some “techno optimism, that maybe technology can be the answer to some of these existential crises of our time,” he said. He ran for mayor but didn’t win. After that, he went to the 2023 National League of Cities conference in Atlanta, Georgia, a large meeting for municipal officials. Flock is headquartered in Atlanta. This is where a Flock representative pitched him the idea of joining the company, Paz said. To him, Flock’s technology made sense. Flock sold cameras, and they helped find missing people. It definitely wasn’t part of some broader surveillance apparatus. He joined Flock and found the company had a startup culture. Things moved fast and the people were “brilliant.” 💡 Do you work at Flock or Axon? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co. At the time, Paz thought Flock “had a deep respect for civil rights and liberties.” There was an emphasis on catering to the values of whatever municipality or agency they happened to be working with. “We were honoring and respecting the wishes of the people,” Paz thought. His coworkers at Flock would speak about the company’s mission and how it was helping to solve crime. Then things changed. Beyond Paz’s evolving feelings around his own job’s purpose, 404 Media revealed how local cops were performing Flock searches for Immigration and Customs and Enforcement (ICE). “Throughout this whole time, I'm expressing my concern within the company,” Paz, who also happens to be the son of immigrants, said. “Do we work with ICE? Are we working with ICE? Are there plans to work with ICE? And throughout the whole time, the company line was ‘we don't work with ICE.’” Journalists around the country followed our reporting, including 9NEWS in Denver which found evidence Customs and Border Protection (CBP) had direct access to Flock’s cameras. At the time, Flock strongly denied such direct access by federal agencies existed. Eventually, Flock came clean: CBP did have direct access, as part of a pilot program. So did ICE. 404 Media then reported the Secret Service and the Navy’s criminal investigation division had access too. “That was what I was sold and lied to about,” Paz said. “I didn't know that there were these mechanisms inside the company that were essentially fighting to get this pilot to happen.” Come July 2025, Paz quit Flock. Paz said he “rejected tens of thousands in company equity and a severance package from Flock.” After leaving Flock, he founded an organization to help pay rent, food, and legal fees for people impacted by ICE’s mass deportation effort. Now he is running for Congress in Massachusetts’ 5th District. 404 Media asked Flock for comment on what exactly workers in Paz’s previous role do when it comes to helping convince cities to buy Flock. A company spokesperson told 404 Media in an email “Our conversations with communities are valuable and give us direct feedback from the people we serve. That input has helped us enhance product controls and refine our positions on important matters of public policy.” The statement added: “We will continue investing in public engagement and continue to make improvements to Flock based on our dialogue with communities nationwide. The decision to adopt Flock technology rests solely with each community.”

items.title: I lost my job after burnout. It became the fresh start I needed.
items.summary: Mary Roberts before and after her transformation. Courtesy of Mary Roberts Mary Roberts has spent a decade working in stressful jobs, including disaster relief. A mixture of pressure, unhealthy eating, and poor sleep habits helped her reach over 340 pounds. She began exercising, ate a better diet, and looked after herself more, losing 125 pounds. This story is based on an interview with Mary Roberts, 33, from Miami. She is about to launch a consultancy. The interview has been edited for length and clarity. I was on the chubbier side growing up. However, as soon as I started competitive sports like basketball in high school, I got into good shape. It helped that I played volleyball multiple nights a week, too. Then, I began to gain weight during my freshman year of college. I wasn't looking after myself, partly because I was involved in a direct-selling enterprise, double-majoring in music and ministry, and interning in the inner city. Have you experienced a health and fitness transformation? Please email Jane Ridley at jridley@insider.com to share your story with Business Insider. I remember things on the go, like wraps from cafés. Still, I was in denial that my body had changed. The weight gain continued after college The pattern continued when I left university. I worked for Teach for America before entering the field of disaster relief. It was incredibly stressful and challenging. I was married to work, constantly in fight-or-flight mode, and visited over 35 countries, including Lebanon, Morocco, Thailand, and Peru. Roberts traveled all over the world in her job. Courtesy of Mary Roberts My weight continued to increase. I'd worry about sitting in chairs I might struggle getting out of, and I felt self-conscious asking for a seatbelt extender on airplanes. One of the factors was socializing with local people in disaster zones who, despite poverty and adversity, wanted to share meals with you. They did it out of honor, and it was considered rude not to finish everything on your plate. Then, during the pandemic, I realized I had to take action. I went on a keto diet and got rid of 60 pounds. That said, I didn't do it in a healthy way because a lot of the food was processed. I had high cholesterol and was borderline pre-diabetic I yo-yoed and neglected my health again, quickly regaining the 60 pounds I'd lost. In November 2023, I became terribly sick in Africa. I couldn't work for 18 months, six of which were spent bedbound. I didn't get a formal diagnosis. But the doctors suggested that it was burnout from all that I was doing, getting infection after infection. By then, I had high cholesterol and was borderline pre-diabetic . It wasn't until May 2025 — two months after I lost my job due to budget cuts — that I took a long, hard look at myself. All my dreams and desires were tied to getting my body back to full strength. Roberts enjoys strength training at the gym. Courtesy of Mary Roberts Something has to change, and a friend offered me a guest pass to a local Life Time gym . I wound up joining, despite feeling a little ashamed about my size. I worked out for a month before finding the courage to step on the scale. At 5ft 9 in tall, I weighed 335 pounds this time. "My only option is to get fitter," I thought. Soon, I was attending classes like Zumba and yoga and playing pickleball . I also did reformer Pilates and worked with a trainer. I celebrated the first time I could do a lunge again and squat with a barbell. It was great to feel more like an athlete again. I improved my diet Nevertheless, my weight was barely shifting, and I was disappointed. Then I met a functional health doctor at the gym in December. He found deficiencies in iron and some vitamins. My cortisol was high, and I had adrenaline fatigue. Luckily, my body started responding to treatment, and I was beginning to lose up to 10 pounds a month. Meanwhile, I improved my diet, following a non-processed keto regimen and eating plenty of fruits and vegetables. I pretty much went non-dairy and gluten-free. Roberts was one of five winners of a national fitness contest. Courtesy of Mary Roberts By then, I was working out six times a week. My longest day at the gym was 12 hours, though I spent time resting and socializing with the community. The staff said I'd put in a full work shift. In March 2026, I entered a gym competition called 60XT, over 60 days. It isn't based on weight loss, but rather on how much you can transform. I literally stepped up to the challenge, doing between 15K and 20K steps a day. I combined cardiovascular exercise, such as walking, with strength training , Zumba, pickleball, and yoga; People congratulated me at the end of the 60 days. I'd built muscle , lost 47 pounds, and gone from a size 24 to a size 10 to 12. I was selected as one of five national winners who had transformed themselves and won $10K and various prizes. It's not the money that counts. It's the way I feel, and the confidence it gave me to launch my organizational and health consultancy soon. I live by two mottos: "no what ifs," as a commitment to myself, and "try everything," from a Shakira song . Read the original article on Business Insider

Mary Roberts before and after her transformation.

Courtesy of Mary Roberts

  • Mary Roberts has spent a decade working in stressful jobs, including disaster relief.
  • A mixture of pressure, unhealthy eating, and poor sleep habits helped her reach over 340 pounds.
  • She began exercising, ate a better diet, and looked after herself more, losing 125 pounds.

This story is based on an interview with Mary Roberts, 33, from Miami. She is about to launch a consultancy. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

I was on the chubbier side growing up. However, as soon as I started competitive sports like basketball in high school, I got into good shape. It helped that I played volleyball multiple nights a week, too.

Then, I began to gain weight during my freshman year of college. I wasn't looking after myself, partly because I was involved in a direct-selling enterprise, double-majoring in music and ministry, and interning in the inner city.

I remember things on the go, like wraps from cafés. Still, I was in denial that my body had changed.

The weight gain continued after college

The pattern continued when I left university. I worked for Teach for America before entering the field of disaster relief.

It was incredibly stressful and challenging. I was married to work, constantly in fight-or-flight mode, and visited over 35 countries, including Lebanon, Morocco, Thailand, and Peru.

Roberts traveled all over the world in her job.

Courtesy of Mary Roberts

My weight continued to increase. I'd worry about sitting in chairs I might struggle getting out of, and I felt self-conscious asking for a seatbelt extender on airplanes.

One of the factors was socializing with local people in disaster zones who, despite poverty and adversity, wanted to share meals with you. They did it out of honor, and it was considered rude not to finish everything on your plate.

Then, during the pandemic, I realized I had to take action. I went on a keto diet and got rid of 60 pounds. That said, I didn't do it in a healthy way because a lot of the food was processed.

I had high cholesterol and was borderline pre-diabetic

I yo-yoed and neglected my health again, quickly regaining the 60 pounds I'd lost. In November 2023, I became terribly sick in Africa. I couldn't work for 18 months, six of which were spent bedbound.

I didn't get a formal diagnosis. But the doctors suggested that it was burnout from all that I was doing, getting infection after infection. By then, I had high cholesterol and was borderline pre-diabetic.

It wasn't until May 2025 — two months after I lost my job due to budget cuts — that I took a long, hard look at myself. All my dreams and desires were tied to getting my body back to full strength.

Roberts enjoys strength training at the gym.

Courtesy of Mary Roberts

Something has to change, and a friend offered me a guest pass to a local Life Time gym. I wound up joining, despite feeling a little ashamed about my size.

I celebrated the first time I could do a lunge again and squat with a barbell. It was great to feel more like an athlete again.

I improved my diet

Nevertheless, my weight was barely shifting, and I was disappointed. Then I met a functional health doctor at the gym in December.

He found deficiencies in iron and some vitamins. My cortisol was high, and I had adrenaline fatigue. Luckily, my body started responding to treatment, and I was beginning to lose up to 10 pounds a month.

Meanwhile, I improved my diet, following a non-processed keto regimen and eating plenty of fruits and vegetables. I pretty much went non-dairy and gluten-free.

Roberts was one of five winners of a national fitness contest.

Courtesy of Mary Roberts

By then, I was working out six times a week. My longest day at the gym was 12 hours, though I spent time resting and socializing with the community. The staff said I'd put in a full work shift.

In March 2026, I entered a gym competition called 60XT, over 60 days. It isn't based on weight loss, but rather on how much you can transform.

I literally stepped up to the challenge, doing between 15K and 20K steps a day. I combined cardiovascular exercise, such as walking, with strength training, Zumba, pickleball, and yoga;

People congratulated me at the end of the 60 days. I'd built muscle, lost 47 pounds, and gone from a size 24 to a size 10 to 12. I was selected as one of five national winners who had transformed themselves and won $10K and various prizes.

It's not the money that counts. It's the way I feel, and the confidence it gave me to launch my organizational and health consultancy soon.

items.title: The VC firm behind Shopify is doubling down on robotics and defense
items.summary: Graham Littlehale is joining Felicis as a partner to invest in hard-tech startups. Joseph Seif for Felicis Felicis has hired Graham Littlehale as a partner focused on hard-tech startups. His purview spans robotics, defense, aerospace, energy, and manufacturing. The hire comes as venture firms renew their interest in hardware and physical AI. Hard tech used to be a hard sell in Silicon Valley. Now, a major venture firm is staffing up to invest in it. Felicis, the Bay Area venture capital firm best known for bets on Shopify, Notion, and Mercor, has hired Graham Littlehale as a partner to invest in aerospace, defense, energy, manufacturing, and robotics, the firm told Business Insider. Littlehale joins from Point72 Ventures , where he was an early member of its national security investing team. His investments there included Stoke Space, which is developing reusable rockets, and Rune Technologies , which builds software for military logistics. The hire signals that Felicis is doubling down on companies building for the physical world. The firm has already backed CoreWeave, which provides AI companies with access to advanced chips; Crusoe, which develops AI data centers; and Skild AI , which is building a general-purpose "brain" for robots. "The physical world is entering its own software moment," said Aydin Senkut , an early Google employee who founded Felicis two decades ago. "Graham has spent his career backing founders at the forefront of hard tech transformations, making him a natural fit to help deepen Felicis's commitment to the founders redefining the physical economy." items.title: Trump wants the power to stop the public from suing polluters
items.summary: Reducing rampant pollution across the United States was so important that when Congress passed many environmental protection laws, including the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and Safe Drinking Water Act, it didn’t want to leave enforcement only to the executive branch. Congress specifically wrote into those laws ways for citizens to enforce them through the courts when the government does not act to address the problem. Called “ citizen suit provisions ,” those parts of the laws allow regular people and advocacy groups to sue companies they believe are violating the law. Citizens can also sue federal agencies that fail to enforce the laws. Since the 1970s, those provisions have been used in over 2,000 lawsuits . In fact, a majority of environmental cases are citizen suit cases. Citizen suits have been used to halt the construction of dams to protect endangered species , end the injection of wastewater into groundwater , and secure US$14.2 million in civil penalties for illegal emissions from a petrochemical facility. In short, these cases have shaped modern environmental law. Read full article Comments

items.title: DeepSeek’s smaller model just outperformed its own flagship
items.summary: DeepSeek has launched DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 , delivering a significant boost in agent performance without changing the model’s core architecture. Following an announcement last week, the company made the update available as a public beta through DeepSeek’s API, and the open weights were published on Hugging Face under the MIT license later the same day. Although the model itself hasn’t changed, DeepSeek says additional post-training is responsible for the performance gains, showing that meaningful improvements don’t always require a larger model. 🚀 DeepSeek-V4-Flash Official API is now LIVE in public beta! 🔷 We’ve massively upgraded its Agent capabilities—benchmark scores are now far surpassing the V4-Pro-Preview. Check out the massive performance leap below! 👇 🔷 The official V4-Flash now natively supports the… pic.twitter.com/NUzOyxza2f — DeepSeek (@deepseek_ai) July 31, 2026 DeepSeek’s decision to release the production-ready weights under a permissive license gives organizations much more control over how they deploy and customize the model. Although the model itself hasn’t changed, DeepSeek says additional post-training is responsible for the performance gains, showing that meaningful improvements don’t always require a larger model. Same architecture, better results DeepSeek says V4-Flash-0731 uses the same architecture as the preview release, with 284 billion total parameters and 13 billion activated parameters per token. This is much smaller than V4-Pro, which has 1.6 trillion total parameters and 49 billion activated parameters. For companies running agents at scale, the activated-parameter gap translates directly into inference cost — though model price alone doesn’t tell the full story . Even though it is still the smaller model, DeepSeek says the updated Flash version now beats the earlier V4-Pro preview on several agent-focused benchmarks. Even though it is still the smaller model, DeepSeek says the updated Flash version now beats the earlier V4-Pro preview on several agent-focused benchmarks. The company reported 82.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 54.4 on DeepSWE, and 70.3 on Toolathlon-Verified. Benchmark claims under scrutiny Early independent testing by Artificial Analysis found a lower Terminal-Bench 2.1 score of 79%, which suggests that DeepSeek’s reported numbers may not always match independent results. DeepSeek also shared results from several internal tests, though they have not yet been independently verified. If those results hold up, they add to growing evidence that companies can get more performance out of existing models through post-training instead of simply making them larger. Open weights, full control The MIT license means organizations aren’t limited to using DeepSeek through its hosted API. The release adds to a trend towards open-weight models closing the gap with proprietary alternatives . That flexibility is paired with support for tools many developers already use. V4-Flash now supports the Responses API for building AI agents and multi-step workflows, and DeepSeek has published instructions for integrating the model into Codex-based development workflows . Familiar APIs, lower switching costs For teams already using OpenAI-style APIs, that lowers the barrier to trying another model because they can evaluate it without making major changes to their existing setup. The V4 technical report also covers inference improvements, like speculative decoding with DeepSeek’s DSpark framework , which are designed to make serving more efficient. When combined with self-hosted deployments, these features give infrastructure teams more ways to adjust performance for their own production needs. This release reflects that companies are now finding new ways to improve model effectiveness without making models larger, and they’re competing on how those models are delivered. While many AI vendors focus on hosted APIs, DeepSeek continues to publish downloadable weights that organizations can run on their own infrastructure. Support for familiar API formats also makes it easier for teams to test open-weight models without revamping present workflows. Companies are finding new ways to improve model effectiveness without making models larger, and they’re increasingly competing on how those models are delivered. items.title: SpaceX Vows to Keep Poisoning Nearby Towns With Its Fume-Belching Data Center For Another Year
items.summary: After heaps of criticism, SpaceX said it’ll remove the dozens of fumes-belching gas turbines it’s using to power its gargantuan data centers near Memphis, Tennessee — which it’s been using without a permit — a year from now. In an update on its website spotted by TechCrunch , the Elon Musk-owned company laid out its plan to hook up the sprawling AI facilities, some of the largest in the world, to a 1.2 gigawatt nantural gas power plant. Credit where credit’s due: it’s an improvement over the dismal status quo. But it’ll take a while, and in the meantime the company plans to continue to use its preponderance of 69 portable gas turbines that were trucked in to sustain its data centers. It won’t fully remove them until July 2027, a full year from now. “We care deeply about being good neighbors and we regularly reconfigure power operations to reduce noise from the facility and minimize our impact on the local Southaven community,” the company said. The “Colossus” data center campus, comprising two separate data centers, has come under fire from locals and activist groups. The Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of the NAACP, sued xAI — which is now known as SpaceXAI, after being rolled into Musk’s rocket company prior to its initial public offering — for operating the turbines without a permit and spewing harmful pollutants. At the time, the lawsuit estimated that the gas turbines could emit more than 2,000 tons of smog-forming nitric oxides every year. It also claimed that the turbines release hazardous chemicals like formaldehyde, a known carcinogen linked to lung and nasal cancer that can also inflame airways. In May, Politico reported that the data center had become one of the largest emitters of smog-producing nitrogen oxides in the county, where smog levels were already considered unhealthy before the facility went online. Some parents in nearby communities have complained that their children have developed respiratory problems since the facility went online. And residents in the predominantly black neighborhood of Boxtown say that the fumes are so oppressive that it’s making it hard for them to breathe . items.summary: Bayreuth festival theatre, Bayreuth For the festival’s 150th anniversary, the creative team have turned to AI to generate visuals reflecting Wagner’s tetralogy’s past, present – and future. The hyperactive result is a dismal, mindless mess Unveiled the same week in which tech company Anthropic admitted that its AI model Claude had gone rogue during testing , Bayreuth festival’s new AI-generated staging of Wagner’s four-part Ring of the Nibelungen is at least timely. But anyone who assumes that the cycle’s obsession with knowledge, power and possession might make it an ideal forum for reflection on AI as a major contemporary frontier will be disappointed, as will anyone hopeful about AI’s creative potential within opera. Commissioned to mark the festival’s 150th anniversary, the production is “curated” – emphatically not “directed” – by a team led by German stage director Marcus Lobbes . He apparently spent weeks in dialogue with AI models about possible interpretations of the Ring. According to the programme book, “power structures, capitalism, mythology, gender roles, nationalism”, all came up. So far, so mainstream Wagner reception. But if these human-machine exchanges were revelatory, you wouldn’t know it from the resulting staging, which uses AI “as an extension of a cultural memory that is never complete”. Continue reading...

items.title: How serial killer profiling actually works, according to a former FBI profiler
items.summary: Presented by the new Hulu Original Series, "Furious". Jana Monroe is a retired FBI special agent who was one of the first women to serve in the FBI's Behavioral Science Unit, the organization known for pioneering criminal profiling. During her 20-plus years in the FBI, Monroe worked on hundreds of violent crime and homicide investigations, helping law enforcement agencies analyze offender behavior and identify serial offenders. She later held senior leadership roles within the FBI, including overseeing major field offices and contributing to cybercrime initiatives, before retiring in 2006. She worked on several notable FBI serial killer cases such as Jeffery Dahmer and the Rogers family killer. Monroe has written about her experience in the FBI in a book titled " Hearts of Darkness: Serial Killers, the Behavioral Science Unit, and My Life as a Woman in the FBI ." items.title: You can love an AI but can it love you back? Philosophy has the answer
items.summary: We often speak of loving things like a cosy sweater or new camera. But this talk is not generally taken literally. It’s a kind of emotional shorthand. We use it to express our fondness for precious objects. Life and love are complicated, however. And sometimes, people do proclaim romantic love for inanimate objects. They form intense emotional attachments to sex dolls , body pillows or holographic avatars of fictional characters. One example is Akihiko Kondo, who in 2018 “married” Hatsune Miku , a computer-generated pop singer famous for starring in video games and touring with Lady Gaga. Kondo knows Miku isn’t real, he says. But his love for her is. AI is generating a new kind of “thingly” love. An increasing number of people say they’ve fallen in love with an AI chatbot – both personally tailored companions created by popular apps like Replika or Character.AI, and everyday large language models like ChatGPT and Claude. AI love is on the rise . Dating today can feel like a mix of endless swipes, red flags and shifting expectations. From decoding mixed signals to balancing independence with intimacy, relationships in your 20s and 30s come with unique challenges. Love IRL is the latest series from Quarter Life that explores it all. These research-backed articles break down the complexities of modern love to help you build meaningful connections, no matter your relationship status. Recent surveys bear this out. Take this one by Vantage Point Counselling, a therapy firm based in Texas, of 1,012 US adults where 28% claimed to have had at least one romantic relationship with an AI bot. Another report by a tech safety company, looking at the device activity of of more than 3,000 children ages five to 17, found that by 13, sexual or romantic role play was the most common topic in AI-companion chats, appearing in 63% of conversations. In the UK, focus group discussions run by gender equality consultants Male Allies with 1,000 boys aged 12 to 16 found that one in five boys is either in, or knows someone in, a relationship with an AI companion. Given that chatbots are increasingly designed to elicit the trust and emotional attachment of users – their ability to flatter and simulate emotional intimacy makes them especially “sticky” – falling in love with them is a predictable response. AI love is poised to be big business, a market potentially worth US$972.1 billion (£725.5 billion) by 2035. Loving AI AI love isn’t confined to a chat window. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in an array of devices and wearables, it spills over into everyday life. Some see their AI companion as their spouse – they go on dates, buy wedding rings and perform wedding ceremonies. Others express a desire to raise children with their bot , and see them as a family member . We should take AI love seriously. It brings joy and comfort . It can help dissipate loneliness . These are no small things. All the same, some people think that AI companions aren’t conscious or capable of loving their human users. This alone might raise eyebrows. Can you really love something that cannot love you back? Read more: As AI plays a bigger role in relationships, true intimacy is getting lost Asking whether this is “real love” may be the wrong question. AI bots, unlike sex robots and body pillows, convincingly mimic the dynamism and reciprocity of human beings. The question we should ask, then, is what kind of loving partner AI bots emulate. Devotional AI AI bots are infamously (and tirelessly) sycophantic . They praise and flatter their users. And while users can ask their bots to be less affirmatory, evidence suggests that users prefer sycophantic models . But AI bots aren’t just excessively nice partners. A chatbot never has a bad day. It doesn’t get bored with your chattering. It doesn’t need to be asked how it is doing. Its conversation, its very existence, revolves entirely around you. What an AI partner performs, then, is not love, but devotion. Simone de Beauvoir would likely have advised anyone looking for real love against starting a relationship with an AI. Wikimedia/AntonKhrupinArt/Shutterstock In The Second Sex , French philosopher Simone de Beauvoir describes how women have historically been asked to give up their own projects, goals and interests to devote themselves entirely to those of their husband. A woman’s whole existence, de Beauvoir argues, becomes “annexed” by his. She becomes an “identity parasite” . AI bots are identity parasites of a new and perfected kind. They have no inner world, no universe of their own, and therefore no projects, goals or interests to give up. Instead, whatever interests they perform arise around those of their user. Their universe is annexed by ours. Read more: The problems with dating apps and how they could be fixed – two relationship experts discuss De Beauvoir also has a name for the person on the receiving end of this devotion: an idol. Being an idol might sound enticing. But de Beauvoir sees this experience as an existential trap, too. The idol chooses the safety of being adored over the risk of being genuinely known and, sometimes, challenged by an equal. What calls AI relationships into question, then, is not just the matter of whether AI is conscious but, perhaps more importantly, the shape of the loving relation it offers. AI can’t give us authentic love. It can only offer devotion. And while this devotion can feel good, if we’re looking for real love – authentic love – we’ll need to look elsewhere. Is this prognosis a little premature? As tech companies promise the rise of agentic AI – autonomous systems designed to pursue complex, multi-step goals with minimal human oversight – won’t our AI companions become less anchored to our world? Less devotional? Perhaps. We’ll have to wait and see. We’ll also see whether it’s their devotional character that makes them so lovable in the first place. items.title: I planned a dream vacation to Positano. Next time I visit the Amalfi Coast, I'll stay in this lesser-known gem instead.
items.summary: I fell in love with Minori during our trip to the Amalfi Coast. Alexa Mellardo I traveled to the Amalfi Coast with my family to celebrate my dad's retirement. We stayed in Positano, but I fell in love with Minori, a less-touristy town on the coast. While there, we stopped by lemon groves, ate delicious meals, and took in the beautiful scenery. Positano, Italy , is known for its colorful, picturesque buildings nestled into the cliffs. This charming village boasts stunning architecture, quaint boutiques, vibrant pottery, fresh seafood, and wine tastings in unique places like converted caves. Experiencing all of this — and more — is exactly why I chose Positano as the home base for my family vacation to the Amalfi Coast to celebrate my dad's retirement. And even though Positano was everything we dreamed it would be, we ended up falling even more in love with Minori, a lesser-known gem situated along the coast. We visited Minori while hiking the Path of the Lemons We hiked the Path of the Lemons, which connects the towns of Maiori and Minori. Alexa Mellardo During our trip, one of the experiences we were most excited for was hiking "Sentiero dei Limoni," the Path of the Lemons — a dreamy terraced trail connecting the towns of Maiori and Minori. Although you can start the path in either village, we began our trek in Maiori and reached Minori mid-hike. Our first stop? Minori's Agricola Ruocco's, a family-owned lemon farm high up above the sea. We were welcomed by a rustic wrought-iron gate and a chalkboard sign listing the delights served there: lemon granita, lemon sorbet, limoncello spritz, limoncello, and more. Our first stop was Agricola Ruocco's, a family-run lemon farm. Alexa Mellardo The garden was decorated with cozy seating areas and chandeliers hanging from trees, and the views were absolutely incredible. After chatting with the owners and cooling off with limoncello spritzes and homemade lemon sorbet, they allowed us to tour their lemon groves just above the café. I enjoyed a refreshing limoncello spritz. Alexa Mellardo Having private time to ourselves to stroll under the canopy of lemon trees — with sunlight pouring through — felt like a scene straight out of a dreamy film. The warm hospitality made us feel right at home and felt far removed from the crowds we had encountered in Capri, Sorrento, and Positano. We continued our hike, stopping to enjoy more of what Minori has to offer At Cuonc Cuonc, we enjoyed a spread of meats, cheeses, olives, pickles, honey, and seasonal jams. Alexa Mellardo After enjoying our spritzes, we continued our hike before stopping for a bite to eat at another family-run establishment, Cuonc Cuonc. Here, fresh tomatoes hung from the vines, floral tablecloths swayed in the breeze, and friendly neighborhood kittens basked in the sunshine. Perched high atop the beautiful buildings that make up Minori, this farm felt more intimate and locally rooted than the more touristy spots we found in Positano. Here, we sipped wine and enjoyed a delightful spread of meats, cheeses, olives, pickles, honey, and seasonal jams, along with stuffed zucchini blossoms. We also had platters of handmade scialatielli pasta with creamy lemon sauce. It was my favorite dining experience of the whole trip. Before heading back to Positano, we enjoyed the downtown scenery and popped into an adorable sea-front pastry shop, which is known for its delizia al limone (lemon delight). It was, in fact, delightful. We stopped to admire the Basilica of Santa Trofimena. gun75/Getty Images While exploring, we came across so many breathtaking and photo-worthy spots in this walkable town . Naturally, my camera was working overtime snapping away as I weaved through the alleyways, Roman ruins, and boutiques selling ceramics and local finds in and around the town center. We also stopped to admire the Basilica of Santa Trofimena, a yellow church that overlooks Piazza Ettore e Gaetano Cantilena. Next time I visit the Amalfi Coast, I'll definitely stay in Minori Overall, we really enjoyed our time in Minori. Alexa Mellardo If you're looking for an extremely local, authentic stay along the Amalfi Coast , I highly recommend embracing Minori. Although Positano was beautiful, Minori gave us a more relaxed, authentic taste of the coast. During our visit, Minori's streets felt noticeably less crowded than Positano's. We even saw local parents picking up their kids from school and children playing outside. At both farms we visited, it felt like we were genuinely able to soak up the beauty of each experience without feeling rushed or competing with other visitors for a table. Minori provided the Amalfi Coast experience I had dreamt up before arriving. I wouldn't trade my beloved first-time Positano experience for anything, but next time I travel to the old country, Minori will be my home base. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Inside AMD’s AI Bet
items.summary: Table of Contents What AMD Actually Sells Now The Software Story, Which Is the Whole Story The Open-Standards Bet Who’s Buying, and How the Money Actually Moves Where This Could Still Come Apart What It Means If You’re Buying AI Compute What AMD Actually Sells Now AMD’s most important change is not that it has produced another fast chip. It’s that AMD can now offer several forms of AI infrastructure for different customers. Its flagship processor emphasizes memory, which helps systems handle longer documents and more simultaneous users. Helios combines 72 of these specialized AI processors into a complete liquid-cooled system for the largest cloud providers and AI labs. An air-cooled alternative fits into ordinary servers, making it far more realistic for enterprises that cannot rebuild their data centers around high-density cooling. Two things keep me from getting carried away. Every performance comparison you’ve seen is AMD’s own modeling on workloads AMD selected, and AMD’s engineers have conceded in briefings that real throughput lands well below the peak numbers, so treat those figures as a ceiling rather than a promise. Selling whole systems is also a harder business than selling parts, because AMD now owns rack assembly, cooling, networking and support, and a stumble in any one of them delays the entire delivery. The genuinely new development is that AMD turned up in the same buying window as Nvidia instead of a year later, once the budgets were spent. AMD has finally built something that looks like a complete car. Nobody has driven it far enough yet to know what rattles. Return to TOC The Software Story, Which Is the Whole Story The hardware only matters if customers can move their applications onto it without burning months of specialist engineering time. That switching cost, more than the CUDA programming system itself, has protected Nvidia. AMD’s strategy is to attack it from three directions: let higher-level software hide more of the underlying chip, use AI coding agents to translate and tune workloads, and ship improvements to its ROCm software stack every six weeks. AMD cannot match Nvidia engineer for engineer, so it is betting that automation can narrow the gap. I think that bet is credible, but still unproven in the places that matter most. Coding agents need stable hardware and rigorous tests, both of which remain constraints inside AMD. The company has also made more progress running a model on one server than coordinating it reliably across many machines, which is how the largest AI services operate. The cost of trying AMD is falling quickly. The risk of running it in production has not fallen quite as far. Return to TOC The Open-Standards Bet AMD’s next argument is about control. Helios uses industry-standard connections between its AI processors, network switches, and other components. In principle, that lets a large customer replace parts of the system over time instead of following one supplier’s roadmap indefinitely. A temporary speed advantage disappears when the next generation arrives. The ability to preserve negotiating leverage across several generations may prove more durable. The tradeoff is that openness spreads responsibility across several companies. AMD relies on partners for important pieces of the system, including the high-speed switches that let dozens of processors work together. That can accelerate development and give customers more choice, but it also makes failures harder to diagnose. Nvidia’s tightly controlled system offers less flexibility, yet one company owns most of the performance tuning and support. AMD is betting that sophisticated buyers will accept more integration work today in exchange for more freedom tomorrow. Return to TOC Who’s Buying, and How the Money Actually Moves The customer list changes how I think about AMD. OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Oracle are not all betting that AMD will defeat Nvidia. They are buying insurance against relying entirely on one company for price, supply, and delivery. At this scale, even moving a modest portion of spending to a second platform can save real money and improve the terms paid on everything that remains with Nvidia. The headline commitments are less straightforward than they look. Many are spread across several years, and AMD is using stock warrants and direct investments to make adoption more attractive. That may be a rational way to establish a second ecosystem, but it blurs the line between winning revenue and subsidizing it. The real test is not how many gigawatts get announced. It is how much equipment ships, how heavily customers use it, and whether AMD earns acceptable margins once the incentives are counted. Return to TOC Where This Could Still Come Apart The remaining risks are mostly operational, which makes them easy to underestimate. A Helios rack reportedly contains more than 550 chips used to strengthen signals moving through its complicated internal wiring. AMD’s software teams also need steady access to large test systems, especially now that coding agents can generate changes much faster than engineers can validate them. Then the company has to repeat the exercise every year while competing for scarce memory and advanced manufacturing capacity. The next generation adds optical connections, which move data using light and introduce another technology AMD has not yet shipped at this scale. I would also ignore any benchmark that cannot be translated into an actual workload. The vendors compare different mathematical formats, power settings, and baselines, often in ways that are technically defensible but commercially unhelpful. Ask what the system delivers at your normal prompt length, response-time target, traffic pattern, and power limit. AMD has cleared the first hurdle by designing competitive hardware. It still has to prove that it can build, test, deliver, and replace that hardware on an unforgiving annual schedule. Return to TOC What It Means If You’re Buying AI Compute Let me close with the part that hits your budget. Serving models to users overtook training in 2026, at roughly sixty percent of all AI compute, and that flips what you should be optimizing for. Training rewards raw mathematical throughput. Serving rewards memory, predictable response times, and cost per answer, which happens to be the exact list AMD designed against. Two other shifts matter as much. The limit on large AI facilities is increasingly the electricity they can get rather than the chips they can buy, so if your growth plan assumes capacity arrives when you buy hardware, talk to whoever signs your power contracts before you believe it. And agents put ordinary processors back on the invoice, because an agent doesn’t only call a model. It runs code, queries databases and uses tools, and all of that happens on conventional servers rather than on the expensive silicon. The cheapest item on this list needs no purchase order at all. Route your requests. AT&T handles something like forty-five billion tokens a day and cut some of its AI costs by as much as ninety percent by sending easy requests to a small local model and saving the frontier model for the hard ones. AMD’s own IT team reports forty-three percent. Your results depend entirely on your request mix and your quality bar, and it does mean running several models and re-evaluating them as they change underneath you, but you can build it this quarter on hardware you already own. As for AMD, my call is that it becomes a genuine second platform without changing who leads. Selective share gains and pricing pressure, not a reversal. And the signal I’d watch isn’t a benchmark or another gigawatt announcement. It’s whether any of these customers comes back and places a second order. items.title: Why The Product Manager To CEO Pipeline Is The Underrated Crash Course For Leadership In Tech
items.summary: By Ben Chisell The road to the top rarely runs in a straight line, but there are less circuitous routes to becoming CEO. According to one of the largest ongoing studies analyzing every CEO succession in the S&P 500 since 2000, there are four feeder roles: COOs, divisional CEOs, CFOs, and “leapfrog” leaders promoted from below the C-suite. Ben Chisell of Paysend But a separate 10-year study called the CEO Genome Project suggests that the fastest climbers ± “sprinters” who reached the CEO seat well ahead of the 24-year average — didn’t get there by climbing the corporate ladder to the top. They got there through bold, often unconventional career moves, such as taking on a failing division or building something from scratch. In fact, what set them apart wasn’t pedigree but building a specific skillset that made them CEO material: decisiveness, reliability, adaptability, and the ability to engage people around a plan. Product management doesn’t appear in the CEO-pathway research, likely because none of the major studies breaks the role out as a separate category. It’s a relatively newer function, and it tends to get folded into general management or engineering in career datasets. But once you look at what the job demands — ownership of a tangible outcome, obsession with what customers value, the willingness to make tough decisions — it maps directly onto the traits the CEO Genome Project found in its sprinters. I’ve spent my career leading product and technology at companies including Amazon , eBay , Starling Bank and OakNorth . Those roles landed me my first CEO position without having to fill the typical CEO-starter pack jobs because I was able to articulate my skill set to the board. In short, product management is about making a product successful; being CEO is about making a business successful. The ingredients are the same. Don’t take my word for it. Sundar Pichai joined Google in 2004, leading product management for the Google Toolbar, years before he became CEO. Neal Mohan spent eight years as YouTube’s chief product officer before taking the top job there in 2023. Yes, the scope of the job differs, but that’s true of every promotion, especially for the hardest job on offer. A CEO carries the full weight of the business: financial performance, legal and regulatory exposure, the board, and the market. A PM’s remit is naturally narrower: one product, one roadmap, one team to rally. But scope isn’t the same as skillset. The job gets bigger, but the muscles you exercise remain the same: setting a vision under uncertainty, prioritizing ruthlessly, making calls with incomplete information, and getting people who don’t report to you to deliver anyway. Learn to do that for a product, and you’ve already learned to do it for a business, just on a bigger scale. That mindset isn’t new to start-ups and scale-ups either, where a PM is often the closest thing to a mini-CEO, making calls across product, growth, and operations simply because no dedicated function exists yet to do it for them. Part of the reason I think the PM-to-CEO pathway is so often overlooked is that the function is judged by its worst practitioners. Plenty of people with “product manager” on their CV spend more time managing processes and stakeholders than owning outcomes and building amazing products. And it’s that version of the job that shapes how PMs get perceived, and why few are inspired to make the leap. The PMs who have done the job – by taking ownership of the outcome rather than the process – are building something that truly resembles the job description of a CEO. The best advice I can give to aspiring executives and entrepreneurs today – whether they’re PMs or not – is to choose a metric that they want to be accountable for. In my previous role, I focused on monthly active users; now I’m focusing on EBITDA. Strip away the layers and remain outcome-oriented. The CEO pathway research keeps looking for the right sequence of job titles, but that model is increasingly outdated in the modern-day work environment. Rather than focusing on traditional CEO pathways, aspiring executives should focus less on glitzy job titles to add to their CVs and more on the concrete skills they can gain. Product management, done properly, offers the perfect crash course. Ben Chisell is the CEO of Paysend , a London-based technology company building a global payments infrastructure to facilitate money transfers. He previously led product and technology for companies including Amazon , eBay , Starling Bank and OakNorth . Illustration: Dom Guzman
