items.title: The career advice PwC's US CEO says he gives to his college-aged kids
items.summary: Paul Griggs said he has three children, and he doesn't discourage them from choosing consulting as a profession. Mandel NGAN / AFP PwC's US CEO Paul Griggs predicts fewer accountants and consultants will be hired. Griggs said he still encourages his kids to go into consulting. He said he values continuous education and would also encourage his children to pursue MBAs. AI may mean fewer consultants and accountants — at least at PwC. Paul Griggs, the Big Four firm's US senior partner and CEO, said PwC hired fewer consultants and accountants this year than it did two years ago. He expects that trend to continue as the firm hires more data scientists , engineers, and machine learning experts. That doesn't mean Griggs feels pessimistic about the future of consultants in the AI era. The Big Four executive said he has three kids , one who has been in the workforce for about a year and two who are still in college. Two of them may go into accounting, he said, and he's supportive of this plan. This is part of a series of stories from Business Insider's conversation with PwC US CEO Paul Griggs. He's also shared his advice on getting ahead in your career and the biggest mistakes companies are making with AI. To be alerted when the next piece publishes, follow reporter Ana Altchek here. Griggs said that anyone who has worked inside a professional services firm can see that the core work in accounting, consulting, and finance hasn't fundamentally changed. He pointed to PwC's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer report , which analyzed more than a billion job postings worldwide to examine how AI is reshaping skills and occupations. The report found that professional services roles are among the fastest-evolving. It also found that jobs where AI requires more human expertise are growing twice as fast as roles where AI is making it easier for non-experts to perform, with wages in those occupations rising 42% faster since 2021. In general, Griggs said AI creates value, which drives growth, and in turn creates demand for people, technology, and other solutions. The CEO said that PwC has the strongest pipeline of new business it's seen in the firm's history. "I think this is the biggest opportunity we've ever had," Griggs said. What to study While consultants and accountants aren't disappearing, AI is reshaping the skills those jobs require. Griggs said PwC is hiring more people from nontraditional backgrounds and expects to see more liberal arts majors in consulting and other business roles because AI can amplify the need for "broad knowledge." With that in mind, the CEO said he's a "big believer" in master's degrees and would support his kids going to MBA programs . "I would feel very comfortable encouraging any of my three kids to pursue further education if it's something that they were interested in," Griggs said. He said both MBA programs and liberal arts degrees cultivate continuous learners who are curious, which is a quality he prioritizes. "Those MBA programs, in so many ways, create the space for the student to go figure out how to research and discover, and not just get through the core coursework," Griggs said. Griggs said PwC plans to continue recruiting from MBA and other master's programs and maintains partnerships with several universities. Last year, for example, the firm designed a leadership program with Harvard Business School called RevUp, and about 4,000 partners took a course on leading in the AI era. The Big Four firm also developed an AI training program at Wharton with professor Ethan Mollick , which focuses on how partners can use tools commercially and understand how AI is affecting clients, Griggs said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I was laid off at 50. Instead of looking for another corporate job, I decided to pursue what scared me most.
items.summary: Edgar Tang was laid off from Netflix at 50. Courtesy of Edgar Tang Edgar Tang says surviving cancer helped prepare him for a layoff at 50. Years of rebuilding gave him the confidence to start over again — this time as a content creator. Tang says his lived experience is something an algorithm can't replace. Edgar Tang , 50, lives in Singapore and was laid off from his job as a video editor at Netflix in March. Rather than immediately looking for another corporate role, he began creating content about rebuilding life after 50. The following has been edited for brevity and clarity. When I was laid off at 50, I realized I had been preparing for that moment for nearly two decades. The thing that helped me respond to the situation started years earlier, when I was diagnosed with cancer. At 32, I was working abroad, and suddenly I was diagnosed with stage three Hodgkin's lymphoma. That reset what I thought were life's guarantees. There was trauma from getting cancer at such a young age, and also survivor's guilt that came from seeing my peers not survive. I returned home to Singapore to get treatment. After that, I was soul-searching, and ironically, I actually got depressed when my oncologist told me, "I think you are in the clear after three years of testing." Usually, people would get excited, but until that point, I thought, "I could get cancer again, so I'm going to live my life to the fullest." And now the doctor tells you you have a lot of time. So when I realized I had such a long runway, I felt even more lost. After that, I had a friend who struggled after moving to a new city and ended his life. That really scared me. I decided two things: One was that if I am directionless, I'm going to learn something. Two, if I'm scared about something, I should take incremental steps toward it. Edgar Tang was laid off from Netflix at 50.

Courtesy of Edgar Tang

  • Edgar Tang says surviving cancer helped prepare him for a layoff at 50.
  • Years of rebuilding gave him the confidence to start over again — this time as a content creator.
  • Tang says his lived experience is something an algorithm can't replace.

Edgar Tang, 50, lives in Singapore and was laid off from his job as a video editor at Netflix in March. Rather than immediately looking for another corporate role, he began creating content about rebuilding life after 50. The following has been edited for brevity and clarity.

When I was laid off at 50, I realized I had been preparing for that moment for nearly two decades.

The thing that helped me respond to the situation started years earlier, when I was diagnosed with cancer.

At 32, I was working abroad, and suddenly I was diagnosed with stage three Hodgkin's lymphoma. That reset what I thought were life's guarantees. There was trauma from getting cancer at such a young age, and also survivor's guilt that came from seeing my peers not survive.

I returned home to Singapore to get treatment. After that, I was soul-searching, and ironically, I actually got depressed when my oncologist told me, "I think you are in the clear after three years of testing."

Usually, people would get excited, but until that point, I thought, "I could get cancer again, so I'm going to live my life to the fullest." And now the doctor tells you you have a lot of time. So when I realized I had such a long runway, I felt even more lost.

After that, I had a friend who struggled after moving to a new city and ended his life. That really scared me. I decided two things: One was that if I am directionless, I'm going to learn something. Two, if I'm scared about something, I should take incremental steps toward it.

I also feared loneliness, but then I moved to New York, and it was the most amazing thing I've ever done for myself — just learning and immersing myself, getting to know so many new people. That gave me the confidence to then move to LA. There are incremental increases in your confidence level when you put yourself closer to your fears.

Later, I realized I had to return to Singapore to care for my elderly parents. That meant I had to rebuild again.

The best job I ever had

The layoff wasn't a huge surprise because leaders had given us a heads-up that restructuring was coming. On the day it happened, it was still rather emotional because I could mentally prepare for losing a job, but I wasn't prepared to lose the opportunity to work with people I really enjoyed working with.

That was the best job I ever had. It was the best culture fit, people fit, and product fit. I learned that when you have all these things lined up, you don't second-guess yourself. You don't try to dance around egos. You want to do your best, and the people around you will help you elevate.

I had the opportunity to say goodbye to people because I had a runway after the layoff news to close the loop on projects. After the tears had run dry, I decided to try content creation.

A leap of faith

Content creation came to mind because friends had been telling me over the years that I had a very interesting lived experience. It needed two ingredients for it to work: One was a nudge, which came as a layoff. The second was the leap of faith, because this kind of communication is about putting yourself in a public space. You can lose your privacy. You can crash and burn. You can face vitriol. You can embarrass yourself.

There was a time when I thought I could do faceless content, creating things that are anonymous but still insightful. Then I realized that being the face of it would be the most authentic and vulnerable way of sharing with people.

Now, I tell my own story

About a month later, I signed up for a content-creator course. By making videos, I'm actually seeking support as much as I am trying to give support to people in the same situation.

What I did before was tell stories for a corporation's products. Now, I tell my own story.

When you look at how disruption has been happening in almost every industry, you realize that no real corporate job is safe. So I started thinking about what I could actually own, and what I could own was my lived experience, which no algorithm can take over — at least for now.

When you go through something like a layoff, as much as the company can explain that it was not based on performance — that it was based on changes in business strategy — you internalize it, as if to say, "If I were valuable or relevant enough, I would have shifted with the changing business needs."

Your voice is something you own. I'm going to own it by sharing it and seeing how it can be both valuable and viable, versus jumping to the next corporate job.

Recovering from cancer, moving to new cities, and being a caregiver were disparate experiences that led me to where I am today. Now, with the layoff, it was the universe once again telling me not to overstay.

items.title: AI translators are getting more fluent – but communication is never just a matter of words
items.summary: raker/Shutterstock Speak into a phone and an app can render your words in another language in seconds. AI-powered speech translation can be fast, convenient and fluent. But fluency does not guarantee that people will understand one another. In the most recent census , 880,000 people in England and Wales (excluding tourists and other short-term visitors) said they could not speak English well, and 161,000 not at all. That’s more than a million residents who may need language support in their daily lives, including when trying to access essential public services . The linguistic range is vast. London alone is home to more than 250 languages . Tight budgets and a shortage of interpreters for some languages can make it difficult to secure an interpreter with the right dialect and expertise for a pressing legal, health or social care matter. Notice we say “interpreter”, not translator. In professional language services, translation typically deals with written texts, while interpreting facilitates spontaneous communication between users of different spoken or sign languages , whether face-to-face, by telephone or via video. In a conversation, each person responds to what has come before and shapes what will follow. Added meaning emerges as they hesitate, restart or refer back to earlier points. Words are only part of this exchange – tone, pace, pauses and non-verbal cues can all shape how an utterance is understood. Imagine a doctor asking a patient if they have missed any of their treatment sessions. The patient gives a hesitant “no” – perhaps because they are embarrassed, unsure or genuinely cannot remember. On the surface, this reply sounds simple enough, whether the patient says nie in Polish, hayır in Turkish or hapana in Swahili. But would an AI-powered translation device spot the subtle inference in the hesitation? AI systems work best when conditions are relatively stable: speech is clear, speakers take turns, and people say exactly what they mean. But human interaction is rarely so tidy. In contrast, a professional interpreter would almost certainly understand the full meaning and context of this answer. They would preserve the hesitation, flag any ambiguities, and allow doctor and patient to repair a possible misunderstanding before it has any serious consequences. As researchers in the field of public service interpreting, we are therefore concerned that any increase in adoption of AI translation services is done with due consideration for the skills and sensitivities that could be lost in the process. Complexities of human interaction Automated speech translation can offer some practical advantages, including on speed and availability. A 2024 survey of more than 2,500 workers across UK health and social care, legal and emergency services and the police found that a third of them had used machine translation at work. Such systems use a process in which speech recognition converts verbal communication to text, machine translation renders it in another language, then text-to-speech software produces spoken output in the listener’s tongue. Yet the appeal of instant solutions can obscure the complexities of human interaction, and the potentially serious consequences for those involved if communication goes wrong. In an asylum interview or a Mental Health Act assessment , for example, a language-related error could significantly affect a person’s health, legal status or liberty. One approach is to reserve automated speech translation for apparently straightforward interactions. However, even a routine exchange is rarely low risk in some public services: an appointment booking may reveal alarming symptoms; a housing enquiry may uncover domestic abuse; a casual conversation with a social worker may raise a safeguarding concern. We therefore believe technology should be introduced according to the risks of the specific interaction, with human oversight and a plan for escalation if the level of risk changes. At the same time, human involvement does not automatically guarantee quality. Good interpreting depends on qualified professionals, effective procurement and public-service staff who know how to work with interpreters. So any responsible approach to language access means investing in both professional expertise and the systems that support it. Video: Wired. A hybrid future? AI speech translation is likely to become ever-more accurate, fluent and useful. It could support qualified interpreters and, when none is immediately available, provide a temporary fallback. Ruling out its use altogether is both unrealistic and undesirable. The more constructive questions concern when and where it is appropriate; who should supervise its use; when a human interpreter is essential; and who should be held accountable when an AI system causes harm. It is also important to be realistic about how these systems may perform amid growing linguistic diversity. Some languages, dialects and accents are much better represented in training and test data than others. Research has documented systematic inequalities in language-technology performance worldwide as well as disparities in speech-recognition error rates within a single language. The risks in public services are therefore uneven. Output for under-represented languages and varieties may be less accurate – and these are often the same languages for which expert interpreters may be unavailable . As society learns to live with AI, it is important to cultivate communicative environments where technology supports and operates under human oversight, rather than replacing human expertise. However fluent technology becomes, communication is never simply the transfer of words. Meaning emerges as an interaction unfolds: through what people say, how they say it, what they leave unsaid – and, crucially, their ability to repair misunderstandings. These are distinctly human capabilities. Any responsible use of AI should strengthen rather than displace them. AI has long been discussed as a threat to jobs and livelihoods. But what’s the reality? In this series , we explore the impact it is already having on different occupations – and how people really feel about their AI assistants. Lucas N Vieira receives funding from UK Research and Innovation. He is the author of Translate: Multilingual Access to Critical Services in the Age of AI (Cambridge University Press, May 2026). items.title: Niche brands are finding online reach through Sam's Club
items.summary: Sam's Club is using its scale to bring local businesses to members across the US. Dominick Reuter Sam's Club is using its regular curation to include upscale regional brands Now Sam's Club is using its scale to connect local favorites with members across the US. Onyx Coffee launched a line in three locations, then doubled sales within four weeks of going online. Sam's Club wants to become the place where premium local brands go national. The wholesale clubs are primarily a place to load up on big-brand stuff at bargain prices, but they also pepper a few local surprises throughout the aisles. Now, the Walmart-owned chain is taking those smaller offerings online for everyone to buy. "We don't want to be the everything store to everyone. We want to be the curated store that you trust, and that's what keeps you coming back ," Sam's Club's head of e-commerce Greg Pulsifer told Business Insider in an interview on July 30. Now the Walmart owned warehouse chain is aiming to crack the code on how to make local gems discoverable to members across the US. Sam's Club merchant teams are already very skilled at finding high quality local products, but traditionally those items have only been available in a particular region. As the company's delivery and fulfillment operation speeding up, Pulsifer's team is stitching together that local discovery with a national reach. Case in point: Arkansas' own Onyx Coffee. Co-founder Andrea Allen told Business Insider that when her coffee bar launched a new brand of beans, Doyenne, that features women-led coffee producers, she wanted a channel that grow volume quickly without compromising quality. Most of the coffee Sam's Club sells is what's known as commercial-grade, but Onyx and Doyenne only source beans rated as excellent or outstanding by the Specialty Coffee Association, Allen said. Starting with a test run last year at three Sam's warehouses in northwest Arkansas, she said Doyenne was able to reach a different cohort of coffee lovers than at her shops in town. "My vet here locally is buying Doyenne at Sam's Club, and I know for sure he would never step foot into our cafe, not because he doesn't like it, but because that's not his space," she said. The demand signal at the club-level was strong enough that Sam's and Doyenne decided to expand to more than 50 US clubs and open up sales on samsclub.com, with fast local fulfillment and national shipping options . Things really took off from there, Allen said. Sam's Club says Doyenne sales nearly doubled within the first four weeks of online availability, and nearly a quarter of online orders are now shipped to locations where the product is not carried in-warehouse. Shoppers are also refilling on Doyenne at a higher rate than Sam's Club's typical whole bean customer, Pulsifer said. Sam's Club says it has sold nearly 15 tons of Doyenne beans this year as of the end of July. The company also said this growth path is similar to one that Oklahoma City-based Kize nutrition bars saw after a Sam's Club buyer spotted them at a local expo, brought the brand into the club, and scaled to national reach online. Other emerging brands are following as well, the company said. "Historically, premier brands relied on location and physical environments," Pulsifer said. "In a digital world, those barriers are gone." In the e-commerce era, Pulsifer said the sense of trust Sam's Club has cultivated over the years gives customers the confidence to try out new premium products online. "Innovative brands can grow without compromising their identity, and it supports their mission. I think it's a really it's a really cool thing," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The Ford Maverick Hybrid makes a strong case against buying more truck
items.summary: Ford's Maverick Hybrid packs a powerful punch in a reasonably sized package. So why are Americans still obsessed with ultra-big F-150s? Ben Shimkus/Business Insider The Ford Maverick Hybrid is a gas-sipping antidote to America's giant-truck obsession. It's easy to get carried away with options — and prices on the truck can soar. The Maverick is easy to drive and has a great interior (especially if you have a tall water bottle). Americans love a big ole, gas-hungry truck . The full-size Ford F-150 has been America's bestselling vehicle for more than 40 years. Its closest rivals, the Chevrolet Silverado and Ram 1500, are also top-sellers in the US — and equally gargantuan. Those trucks are running headfirst into the core issue facing American consumers: gas prices are super high . Ford has an internal solution. Nestled on their lots between those best-selling F-150s is a smaller, hybrid option, called the Maverick. The Maverick has a decent-sized bed and an upright truck shape, but occupies about as much mental space behind the wheel as a compact car. It's pricing starts at $28,145 , returns decent fuel economy, and fits inside parking spots without becoming its own geometry problem. I spent a week with one. I'm convinced it is a practical option for tons of American families. At least, if they don't get carried away with options. My 2026 Maverick Lariat AWD Hybrid cost $46,770 after options, including a moonroof, tonneau cover, tow package, and Ruby Red paint. That is nearly $19,000 more than the base hybrid — and enough to complicate the Maverick's argument as the affordable antidote to today's bloated pickups. The Maverick is upright — in good and bad ways The Maverick Lariat is plenty truck-like — and maybe a little pricey. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider I drove the Maverick about 150 miles around New York City and on a beach trip to the Jersey Shore with three friends. It was smooth and nimble at low speeds, with a turning radius that reminds me of a Volkswagen Jetta . Parallel parking was a breeze, and the large, blocky windows provided excellent visibility. The Maverick's upright construction shapes nearly everything about it, for better and worse. Its seating position is easy to climb into, and passengers get plenty of headroom. The vertical door panels also leave an unusual amount of storage above the cupholders — you'd be hard-pressed to find a water bottle that was too tall for the Maverick. The door gives enough space for the world's largest water bottle, I swear. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider The rear seatbacks, however, were so upright that my passengers' backs hurt after the beach trip. The speakers also sit next to their heads, making it difficult for front- and back-seat occupants to hear each other whenever music is playing. Hard gray-blue plastic covers much of the cabin. A Redditor who said they owned a Maverick once wrote that those surfaces will scratch if you look at them the wrong way. Still, the Maverick felt solidly assembled. I noticed no rattles, even through New York City's harsh roads. The hybrid returned 33.5 mpg, versus its 36-mpg combined rating. It was smooth around town but slightly whiny on the highway. Ford also supplied a "braking coach" that graded how much regenerative energy I captured whenever I stopped — an amusing feature until it began to feel like an overeager student who loved showing off their homework. The bed easily swallowed our bags, beach gear, groceries, and sandy shoes. It had more than enough space to haul all the family gear needed for a weekend getaway. The Maverick's placement inside Ford The interior is very upright and plastic-forward. It still works as a family hauler. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider The Maverick could feasibly replace some American SUVs — and that may be exactly what Ford wants. When I previously asked the automaker about its decision to discontinue the Escape, a representative pointed shoppers toward the Bronco Sport and Maverick. The Maverick hybrid, they pointed out, was Ford's cheapest hybrid. Ford also has a pickup that slots in between the Maverick and the F-150 called the Ranger. There's another pickup coming to Ford dealerships that could also challenge the Maverick. The automaker plans to launch a midsize electric truck in 2027 with a target starting price of about $30,000 . Ford says it will have more passenger room than a Toyota RAV4, plus a conventional bed and front trunk. Should Ford hit its target, the EV will offer a proposition remarkably similar to the Maverick's: manageable dimensions, everyday practicality, and a starting price around $30,000. That highlights a tension Detroit has yet to resolve during its transition to EVs — its fully electric vehicles are still in direct competition with their gas-powered counterparts. The Maverick nevertheless makes a convincing case for itself today. It gives buyers the useful parts of a pickup without the bulk or fuel bill of an F-150. It is best, however, when buyers show restraint. My loaded Lariat was a good truck. A Maverick Hybrid closer to $30,000 may be a great one. Read the original article on Business Insider

  • The Ford Maverick Hybrid is a gas-sipping antidote to America's giant-truck obsession.
  • It's easy to get carried away with options — and prices on the truck can soar.
  • The Maverick is easy to drive and has a great interior (especially if you have a tall water bottle).

Americans love a big ole, gas-hungry truck.

The full-size Ford F-150 has been America's bestselling vehicle for more than 40 years. Its closest rivals, the Chevrolet Silverado and Ram 1500, are also top-sellers in the US — and equally gargantuan.

Those trucks are running headfirst into the core issue facing American consumers: gas prices are super high.

Ford has an internal solution. Nestled on their lots between those best-selling F-150s is a smaller, hybrid option, called the Maverick.

The Maverick has a decent-sized bed and an upright truck shape, but occupies about as much mental space behind the wheel as a compact car. It's pricing starts at $28,145, returns decent fuel economy, and fits inside parking spots without becoming its own geometry problem.

I spent a week with one. I'm convinced it is a practical option for tons of American families.

At least, if they don't get carried away with options.

My 2026 Maverick Lariat AWD Hybrid cost $46,770 after options, including a moonroof, tonneau cover, tow package, and Ruby Red paint. That is nearly $19,000 more than the base hybrid — and enough to complicate the Maverick's argument as the affordable antidote to today's bloated pickups.

The Maverick is upright — in good and bad waysThe Maverick Lariat is plenty truck-like — and maybe a little pricey.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

I drove the Maverick about 150 miles around New York City and on a beach trip to the Jersey Shore with three friends.

It was smooth and nimble at low speeds, with a turning radius that reminds me of a Volkswagen Jetta. Parallel parking was a breeze, and the large, blocky windows provided excellent visibility.

The Maverick's upright construction shapes nearly everything about it, for better and worse. Its seating position is easy to climb into, and passengers get plenty of headroom. The vertical door panels also leave an unusual amount of storage above the cupholders — you'd be hard-pressed to find a water bottle that was too tall for the Maverick.

The door gives enough space for the world's largest water bottle, I swear.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

The rear seatbacks, however, were so upright that my passengers' backs hurt after the beach trip. The speakers also sit next to their heads, making it difficult for front- and back-seat occupants to hear each other whenever music is playing.

Hard gray-blue plastic covers much of the cabin. A Redditor who said they owned a Maverick once wrote that those surfaces will scratch if you look at them the wrong way.

Still, the Maverick felt solidly assembled. I noticed no rattles, even through New York City's harsh roads.

The hybrid returned 33.5 mpg, versus its 36-mpg combined rating. It was smooth around town but slightly whiny on the highway. Ford also supplied a "braking coach" that graded how much regenerative energy I captured whenever I stopped — an amusing feature until it began to feel like an overeager student who loved showing off their homework.

The bed easily swallowed our bags, beach gear, groceries, and sandy shoes. It had more than enough space to haul all the family gear needed for a weekend getaway.

The Maverick's placement inside FordThe interior is very upright and plastic-forward. It still works as a family hauler.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

The Maverick could feasibly replace some American SUVs — and that may be exactly what Ford wants.

When I previously asked the automaker about its decision to discontinue the Escape, a representative pointed shoppers toward the Bronco Sport and Maverick.

The Maverick hybrid, they pointed out, was Ford's cheapest hybrid. Ford also has a pickup that slots in between the Maverick and the F-150 called the Ranger.

There's another pickup coming to Ford dealerships that could also challenge the Maverick.

The automaker plans to launch a midsize electric truck in 2027 with a target starting price of about $30,000. Ford says it will have more passenger room than a Toyota RAV4, plus a conventional bed and front trunk.

Should Ford hit its target, the EV will offer a proposition remarkably similar to the Maverick's: manageable dimensions, everyday practicality, and a starting price around $30,000.

That highlights a tension Detroit has yet to resolve during its transition to EVs — its fully electric vehicles are still in direct competition with their gas-powered counterparts.

The Maverick nevertheless makes a convincing case for itself today. It gives buyers the useful parts of a pickup without the bulk or fuel bill of an F-150.

It is best, however, when buyers show restraint. My loaded Lariat was a good truck. A Maverick Hybrid closer to $30,000 may be a great one.

items.title: I'm a therapist for tech workers in Silicon Valley. There's a specific type of person who burns out — here's how I treat them.
items.summary: Nick Sanchez says exposure therapy helps his clients manage burnout while still working. Courtesy of Nick Sanchez Nick Sanchez is a licensed marriage and family therapist for high-performers in Silicon Valley. He says his clients are experiencing AI burnout and attention fragmentation. Sanchez uses exposure therapy to help clients manage burnout and build self-care routines. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Nick Sanchez, a licensed marriage and family therapist based in the San Francisco Bay Area. It's been edited for length and clarity. I would say 99% of my clients cite burnout as one of their biggest problems. As a licensed marriage and family therapist, I see a caseload of about 18 to 20 clients a week, most of whom are very high-performing individuals in Silicon Valley , such as business owners, executives, founders, and people in management within tech. AI burnout is a newer phenomenon I've seen. AI enables us to do deep work on multiple projects at once and learn new skills, but it never stops working. You have to be the one to decide when it's time to pause, and that's where AI burnout can come in. I think the type of person who burns out is the type of person who would work more if they could, so it hasn't been effective for me to simply tell them to work less. They're not looking to work less; they're looking to work smarter. I have to get their buy-in that, if they take breaks, they'll actually be able to push harder and more effectively. That's why I use exposure therapy techniques to help my clients heal from burnout and learn tools to manage it when it returns. Burnout has varying levels of intensity I've seen burnout play out in numerous ways as far as intensity, but I would describe it as similar to dysthymia, which is a low-grade depression. Burnout can make the things that used to bring us joy no longer bring us joy. Meanwhile, motivation and our desire to get through our to-do list can go out the window. Clients often come to me saying they're no longer performing at the level they used to be. I had one client who drove to their office for work and couldn't even get out of their car. They told me they physically couldn't get themselves to go in and give any more of themself. AI burnout is real — I've even felt it In addition to being a therapist, I'm the founder and clinical director of Silicon Valley Therapy, where I manage and train associates on their paths to licensure. I've personally experienced AI burnout while growing my business, and I see it in my clients. AI has increased my capacity to produce higher-quality work and take on roles that I'd previously have to outsource, but it takes a lot of time and is easy to fall down a rabbit hole. I see similar types of things with clients where they're taking too much on their plates. They also mention how AI fractures their attention . They're trying to focus way too granularly on too many different projects. With so many different types of LLMs and agents available, it's possible to be working deeply on four or five projects at a time, as opposed to being focused on one area at a time. That level of work requires a different muscle to develop in our brain. I don't even know if we should be working like that. It's important to manage burnout, not just avoid it If someone was terrified of dogs, I wouldn't take them to a dog park on day one of therapy. The first rung on the exposure ladder would be something like looking at pictures of dogs. The same thing goes for burnout. I wouldn't tell a burnt-out founder to take two weeks off from working and not look at their phone. They'd find another therapist. Instead, I might ask what they think about taking an hour out of the day to go on a walk, and or eat lunch outside. Ideally, they'll be off their phone, but it could even be something like watching a fun video. If they're not open to it, I'll go even shorter, like 30 minutes or 15 minutes. Usually, we'll get to a point where they feel as though it's doable. Once they start to notice the benefits, like their day going more smoothly when they take time to eat a proper, nourishing meal outside, their buy-in starts to work. Then we build a customized self-care routine or protocol over time. They're learning the skills to manage burnout, not avoiding the cause. My advice for managing attention fragmentation is the same as managing burnout. If you're running six different projects at once, what if you try working on only two and seeing how that goes, or chunking your day so it's not all spent working on your projects? AI has become a tool in therapy From a therapy point of view, I have a lot of clients who use AI to ask for journal prompts or breathing exercises. It's really awesome that there's a place where people can get that information and work through more surface-level versions of therapy. When they come to the session, we're able to have much deeper human-level conversations. Do you have a story to share about experiencing AI burnout? If so, please reach out to the reporter at tmartinelli@businessinsider.com. Read the original article on Business Insider

Nick Sanchez says exposure therapy helps his clients manage burnout while still working.

Courtesy of Nick Sanchez

  • Nick Sanchez is a licensed marriage and family therapist for high-performers in Silicon Valley.
  • He says his clients are experiencing AI burnout and attention fragmentation.
  • Sanchez uses exposure therapy to help clients manage burnout and build self-care routines.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Nick Sanchez, a licensed marriage and family therapist based in the San Francisco Bay Area. It's been edited for length and clarity.

I would say 99% of my clients cite burnout as one of their biggest problems.

As a licensed marriage and family therapist, I see a caseload of about 18 to 20 clients a week, most of whom are very high-performing individuals in Silicon Valley, such as business owners, executives, founders, and people in management within tech.

AI burnout is a newer phenomenon I've seen. AI enables us to do deep work on multiple projects at once and learn new skills, but it never stops working. You have to be the one to decide when it's time to pause, and that's where AI burnout can come in.

I think the type of person who burns out is the type of person who would work more if they could, so it hasn't been effective for me to simply tell them to work less. They're not looking to work less; they're looking to work smarter. I have to get their buy-in that, if they take breaks, they'll actually be able to push harder and more effectively.

That's why I use exposure therapy techniques to help my clients heal from burnout and learn tools to manage it when it returns.

Burnout has varying levels of intensity

I've seen burnout play out in numerous ways as far as intensity, but I would describe it as similar to dysthymia, which is a low-grade depression. Burnout can make the things that used to bring us joy no longer bring us joy. Meanwhile, motivation and our desire to get through our to-do list can go out the window.

Clients often come to me saying they're no longer performing at the level they used to be. I had one client who drove to their office for work and couldn't even get out of their car. They told me they physically couldn't get themselves to go in and give any more of themself.

AI burnout is real — I've even felt it

In addition to being a therapist, I'm the founder and clinical director of Silicon Valley Therapy, where I manage and train associates on their paths to licensure. I've personally experienced AI burnout while growing my business, and I see it in my clients.

AI has increased my capacity to produce higher-quality work and take on roles that I'd previously have to outsource, but it takes a lot of time and is easy to fall down a rabbit hole. I see similar types of things with clients where they're taking too much on their plates.

They also mention how AI fractures their attention. They're trying to focus way too granularly on too many different projects. With so many different types of LLMs and agents available, it's possible to be working deeply on four or five projects at a time, as opposed to being focused on one area at a time. That level of work requires a different muscle to develop in our brain.

I don't even know if we should be working like that.

It's important to manage burnout, not just avoid it

If someone was terrified of dogs, I wouldn't take them to a dog park on day one of therapy. The first rung on the exposure ladder would be something like looking at pictures of dogs.

The same thing goes for burnout. I wouldn't tell a burnt-out founder to take two weeks off from working and not look at their phone. They'd find another therapist.

Instead, I might ask what they think about taking an hour out of the day to go on a walk, and or eat lunch outside. Ideally, they'll be off their phone, but it could even be something like watching a fun video.

If they're not open to it, I'll go even shorter, like 30 minutes or 15 minutes. Usually, we'll get to a point where they feel as though it's doable. Once they start to notice the benefits, like their day going more smoothly when they take time to eat a proper, nourishing meal outside, their buy-in starts to work. Then we build a customized self-care routine or protocol over time. They're learning the skills to manage burnout, not avoiding the cause.

My advice for managing attention fragmentation is the same as managing burnout. If you're running six different projects at once, what if you try working on only two and seeing how that goes, or chunking your day so it's not all spent working on your projects?

AI has become a tool in therapy

From a therapy point of view, I have a lot of clients who use AI to ask for journal prompts or breathing exercises.

It's really awesome that there's a place where people can get that information and work through more surface-level versions of therapy. When they come to the session, we're able to have much deeper human-level conversations.

items.title: A former Oracle engineer on an H-1B visa says AI and tech layoffs pushed him into constant career-prep mode
items.summary: Ayush Raj Jha moved from India to the US in 2018 to pursue a master's degree in computer science. Ayush Raj Jha Ayush Raj Jha said he worries about AI's impact on software engineering. Jha said tech layoffs have created "constant fear and uncertainty" for H-1B visa holders. He shared how he's adapting to an evolving software engineering industry. When Ayush Raj Jha moved from India to Illinois in 2018 to pursue a master's degree in computer science, he was optimistic about the future of software engineering . Now, after years of layoffs and the rapid rise of AI , he's worried about the future of his industry — and his long-term future in the US. Jha is one of hundreds of thousands of workers in the US on an H-1B visa , for whom losing a job can mean more than losing a paycheck. They generally have 60 days to find a new employer or risk losing their legal status in the US. Major employers in tech rely heavily on H-1B workers. Federal data shows that the "Magnificent 7" companies, including the likes of Amazon and Apple, have had more than 200,000 H-1B applications approved since October 2020. "It's really started impacting the lives of people who are on visas," Jha said. "There's constant fear and uncertainty." He's among the tech workers who are looking for ways to stay competitive in an evolving industry. Some are responding by working harder and learning AI skills , while others are preparing for job searches or actively seeking more secure roles. AI's impact on software engineering After earning a master's degree from the Illinois Institute of Technology in 2020, Jha joined Motorola Solutions as a software engineer, where he worked on software for public safety agencies. In 2022, he joined Oracle as a senior software engineer, where he helped build cloud infrastructure used to deploy healthcare software to hospitals. ChatGPT was released late that year. Since then, Jha said two things have reinforced his concerns about AI's impact on software engineering. The first is his experience using AI tools. Ayush Raj Jha said learning AI has become essential to staying competitive as a software engineer. Ayush Raj Jha To stay competitive, Jha said he spends an estimated eight to 10 hours a week outside of work taking online courses on platforms like LinkedIn Learning and Coursera, experimenting with coding tools, and contributing to open-source projects. Seeing what the technology can do firsthand has both impressed and worried him, he said. "If we don't adapt to these new technologies, it just becomes impossible to stay relevant or even be employable at this point," he said. The second is LinkedIn. He said posts about tech layoffs have become a regular sight on his feed, serving as a constant reminder of how quickly the industry is changing. Business Insider is speaking with workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations. Share your story by filling out this form . Moving on from Oracle Earlier this year, Jha started looking for a more senior, higher-paying role where he could make a bigger impact. Layoffs at Oracle , most recently in March, had heightened his concerns about job security. While his primary focus was career advancement, he also hoped to find an employer that could offer greater stability, in part because of his visa status. Jha said his job search was fairly challenging, which he expected given the hiring slowdown across parts of the tech sector. Eventually, he found a staff software engineer opening at a customer service software company that came with a higher title and pay than his position at Oracle. The company's reputation for a strong engineering culture and ability to attract skilled professionals from diverse backgrounds was also a draw, Jha said. And it was privately owned, so Jha believed it might face less short-term pressure from market expectations, quarterly earnings, and shareholders — dynamics he hoped would make the role more secure than one at a public company. Jha accepted an offer in July. Before starting with his new employer in September, Jha said he plans to take a roughly two-month career break while his H-1B transfer is finalized. Advice for other engineers Jha believes his more than a decade of experience as a software engineer helped him land his new role, but he also believes his online coursework and open-source contributions were important. "I always try to stay up to date with market trends and emerging technologies rather than only focusing on day-to-day company work or simply building my resume," he said. Jha said his advice to tech workers, regardless of their visa status, is to always be prepared to interview for their next job. "At this point with AI adoption, it does not matter how well you perform even at your current company — you could be replaceable," he said. Do you have a story to share? items.title: AI is starting to rewrite the software that made Nvidia untouchable
items.summary: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang. Bloomberg/Getty Images AI is starting to write the software behind AI, challenging Nvidia's moat: its CUDA software. The shift to AI inference could also weaken CUDA's long-standing dominance. One founder said AI coding won't kill Nvidia's CUDA — it will create a new moat instead. Nvidia's biggest competitive advantage is no longer as untouchable as it once seemed. For two decades, Nvidia's crown jewel wasn't just chips; it was the software that turned them into the building blocks of AI, known as CUDA. Short for Compute Unified Device Architecture, CUDA is the brainchild of longtime Nvidia executive Ian Buck , who heads high-performance computing . It took years to build, with ready-made code for common AI tasks, tools to find bugs, and software that lets thousands of chips work together to train models. Now, some believe AI could eventually automate one of the industry's hardest jobs: building the software that powers AI itself. The industry is at an important threshold, says Jeremy Nixon , a former Google Brain researcher and the founder of AI software startup Infinity. He told Business Insider his startup used AI coding agents to recreate CUDA-like software for the chip startup D-Matrix in 10 hours — evidence, he said, that one of Nvidia's biggest moats is being crossed. Infinity founder and CEO Jeremy Nixon. Infinity.inc The pressure doesn't only come from startups. Cloud giants like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft have spent years building software around their own AI chips, while OpenAI and Anthropic have recently demonstrated AI models capable of generating system software. DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng recently said that coding agents , along with his startup's own programming language TileLang, have made AI software substantially easier to build. Coding agents aren't just helping challengers. Nvidia said developers increasingly use CUDA's code libraries to build AI applications, and that it also "uses AI coding agents to develop CUDA faster and validate at greater scale," said Ankit Patel, Nvidia's vice president of developer ecosystem. Inference could change the CUDA equation If CUDA's first advantage was software, the second is everything built on top of it. Millions of lines of code and internal workflows have been developed by companies, creating a powerful lock-in effect that makes switching to alternatives costly and cumbersome. Internal documents at Amazon identified CUDA as a major roadblock to adoption of its Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, Business Insider previously reported. CUDA's age is both an advantage and a constraint, said Chris Lattner , cofounder and CEO of Qualcomm-owned AI software startup Modular . Originally built for gaming long before the AI boom, CUDA carries layers of legacy technology, "like Microsoft Windows trying to fit onto a phone," he said. Modular cofounder and CEO Chris Lattner. Modular Others say AI's shift from training toward inference — where models answer requests and draw conclusions — creates another threat. With this evolution, companies care less about maximizing performance with the most powerful chips and more about running AI profitably, said Marshall Choy, chief business officer of Korean AI chip startup Rebellions. This could result in greater demand not only for specialized hardware but for software that can run across different chips. If companies can switch between chips without rewriting software, that reduces one of CUDA's biggest lock-ins. "That's where the CUDA moat from Nvidia gets broken because CUDA is no longer a factor in the inference side," Choy said. "It's an open source play." Nvidia said that its tightly integrated hardware and software offerings have become more valuable as AI models get put to work. "As AI shifts toward inference and agentic workloads, the need for deep, full-stack optimization only grows," Patel said. A shift toward specialized chips and software has Wall Street increasingly questioning Nvidia's CUDA advantage, said Luke Lango, chief technology analyst at InvestorPlace. He said Nvidia's stagnant stock price over the past year reflects some of these concerns. Nvidia's moat isn't disappearing — it's shifting Not everyone agrees that coding agents are eroding CUDA's edge. Some believe they could ultimately strengthen it instead. Though agents make it easier to generate software, AI-generated code still has to be verified and optimized, said Bing Xu, founder of AI software startup INT21. He believes CUDA has the deepest ecosystem of verification tools and other features that help coding agents work more efficiently. As agents become more common, he said, that ecosystem will become CUDA's next moat. "Agents can generate a lot of code in a short time, but verification is the biggest bottleneck," said Xu, whose last AI chip software startup, HippoML, was acquired by Nvidia. He left the chipmaker in April to build INT21. INT21 founder and CEO Bing Xu. INT21 While coding agents do make it easier to build chip software, the improvement is incremental, Lattner said. "The hype is not complete nonsense, but it is very overblown," he said, adding that writing code is only a small part of building software compared to more complex tasks like optimizing it for production — a critical task because software that maximizes a chip's performance reduces the cost of running AI at scale. Chip software is also something of a niche field, often worked on by elite engineers, Lattner said, giving coding agents far fewer examples to learn from than, for instance, app development, where AI has been trained on vast amounts of public code. And while AI may help rivals catch up, Nvidia benefits from the same technological shifts, Xu said. Whether coding agents weaken CUDA depends on whether competitors catch Nvidia faster than it can gain new ground. The world's dominant chipmaker is "not sleeping or keeping still," Xu said. This could result in greater demand not only for specialized hardware but for software that can run across different chips. If companies can switch between chips without rewriting software, that reduces one of CUDA's biggest lock-ins.

"That's where the CUDA moat from Nvidia gets broken because CUDA is no longer a factor in the inference side," Choy said. "It's an open source play."

Nvidia said that its tightly integrated hardware and software offerings have become more valuable as AI models get put to work.

"As AI shifts toward inference and agentic workloads, the need for deep, full-stack optimization only grows," Patel said.

A shift toward specialized chips and software has Wall Street increasingly questioning Nvidia's CUDA advantage, said Luke Lango, chief technology analyst at InvestorPlace. He said Nvidia's stagnant stock price over the past year reflects some of these concerns.

Nvidia's moat isn't disappearing — it's shifting

Not everyone agrees that coding agents are eroding CUDA's edge. Some believe they could ultimately strengthen it instead.

Though agents make it easier to generate software, AI-generated code still has to be verified and optimized, said Bing Xu, founder of AI software startup INT21. He believes CUDA has the deepest ecosystem of verification tools and other features that help coding agents work more efficiently.

As agents become more common, he said, that ecosystem will become CUDA's next moat.

"Agents can generate a lot of code in a short time, but verification is the biggest bottleneck," said Xu, whose last AI chip software startup, HippoML, was acquired by Nvidia. He left the chipmaker in April to build INT21.

INT21 founder and CEO Bing Xu.

INT21

While coding agents do make it easier to build chip software, the improvement is incremental, Lattner said.

"The hype is not complete nonsense, but it is very overblown," he said, adding that writing code is only a small part of building software compared to more complex tasks like optimizing it for production — a critical task because software that maximizes a chip's performance reduces the cost of running AI at scale.

Chip software is also something of a niche field, often worked on by elite engineers, Lattner said, giving coding agents far fewer examples to learn from than, for instance, app development, where AI has been trained on vast amounts of public code.

And while AI may help rivals catch up, Nvidia benefits from the same technological shifts, Xu said. Whether coding agents weaken CUDA depends on whether competitors catch Nvidia faster than it can gain new ground.

The world's dominant chipmaker is "not sleeping or keeping still," Xu said.

Deckoff, the CEO of asset management firm Black Diamond Capital Management, has sued nine social-media influencers, content creators, and conspiracy theorists, accusing them of trespassing on the property to capitalize on the islands' notoriety. Epstein used one of the islands, Little St. James, to build a sprawling compound, a site where accusers say he made them feel trapped and raped them. On one end of the island is a temple-like building that has been the subject of numerous conspiracy theories. Epstein painted it with blue and white stripes and topped it with a golden dome. Through his lawsuits, filed in US Virgin Islands court through a limited liability company, Deckoff is seeking damages from YouTubers who have undertaken what they describe as quests to unravel the islands' mysteries. Over the past year, influencers have taken videos of themselves renting jet skis, climbing onto shore, and unfurling banners demanding that the Trump administration release the Epstein files. Deckoff's staff has, at times, responded to the camera-wielding interlopers with violence, law-enforcement agencies have said in court filings. Ann Rodriquez, whom Epstein employed to manage the property — and who continued to manage it for Deckoff — was arrested on false imprisonment and assault charges in April after law enforcement officials found one content creator "hog-tied and totally naked" on a boat, according to a sworn statement filed to court. Another interloper said in a podcast interview that employees detained him and put him in what he said Rodriquez called the island's "dungeon." Deckoff's employees also destroyed two rental jet skis while they apprehended content creators, a US Virgin Islands-based rental company alleged. On one end of the island is a temple-like building that has been the subject of conspiracy theories. REUTERS/Marco Bello A spokesperson for Deckoff told Business Insider that the presence of "intruders" on Little St. James has been "dangerous for the people who live and work on the island." "We are concerned when those criminally trespassing on private property and endangering our staff are given a platform for their misconduct," the spokesperson said. In their videos, the influencers have cast themselves as truth-seeking warriors. Andrew Petersen, one of the YouTubers whom Deckoff accused of trespassing, said it was absurd that he's facing legal consequences while the Justice Department continues to take no law enforcement action against friends of Epstein who may also have abused girls or women . "Trespassing is illegal, and we definitely trespassed," Petersen told Business Insider. "It's like, what's the bigger story here?" Petersen and other interlopers haven't responded to the lawsuits in court. Petersen told Business Insider he and the friends and influencers he traveled with never meant to "mess up" Deckoff's property or damage his reputation — only to seek the truth about what was going on at "one of the most horrific islands in human existence, in our opinion." "For me, that's like buying a concentration camp from the Holocaust and like, 'Yeah, we're going to turn this into a resort.' What are you talking about?" he said. At the time Epstein purchased Little St. James in 1998, Ghislaine Maxwell was both his girlfriend and estate manager. Epstein built a sprawling compound on Little St. James. REUTERS/Marco Bello Epstein tasked Maxwell with making the island habitable. It was an enormous undertaking, one of her former assistants testified in Maxwell's 2021 Manhattan criminal trial in which she was convicted of trafficking girls to Epstein for sex. Maxwell arranged to ship not only home furnishings, but also sand and palm trees. ("He wanted more sand on the beach," the assistant testified.) Maxwell, along with Epstein's private jet pilots, took helicopter lessons so they could ferry passengers between Little St. James and nearby St. Thomas, where Epstein's planes landed at the airport. Over the years, Epstein used the island to draw powerful friends, nicknaming it "Little St. Jeff's." One accuser, Virginia Giuffre, wrote in her memoir that then-Prince Andrew had sex with her there. (He settled a lawsuit with Giuffre without admitting wrongdoing.) Records from the Epstein files show he hosted Google co-founder Sergey Brin , LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman , and now-Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick . Elon Musk emailed Epstein about visiting the island to "party," though he later said he never went there. Emails show Epstein used his connections with local politicians to cut red tape and make it easier to obtain visas for young women he wanted to fly in. Brin, Hoffman, Lutnick, and Musk haven't been accused of wrongdoing related to Epstein. Brin hasn't publicly commented on visiting the island . Hoffman has said his visit was part of a fundraising trip for MIT. Lutnick told members of Congress he and his family had lunch on Little St. James while sailing by on a vacation. After Epstein killed himself in 2019, while in jail awaiting trial on sex-trafficking charges, the executors of his estate hired Randall Bell to evaluate Little St. James and Great St. James, the neighboring island Epstein purchased in 2016. Bell specializes in appraising real estate locations where atrocities have occurred , such as the 9/11 terrorist attacks and the Sandy Hook school shooting. Over the years, Epstein used the island to draw powerful friends, nicknaming it "Little St. Jeff's." THE US JUSTICE DEPARTMENT / Getty Images Epstein's estate put the two islands on the market in 2022 for $125 million. Deckoff, a resident of the US Virgin Islands, bought them about a year later for $60 million. The estate used some of the funds to pay creditors, including victims and their attorneys who brought lawsuits against the estate . Deckoff and Epstein never met, and the two had no preexisting relationship, a spokesperson for Deckoff told Business Insider. Since Deckoff bought the islands in 2023, his plans to build a resort seem to have gone nowhere. The only construction permit Deckoff has requested is for a warehouse, a spokesperson for the US Virgin Islands Department of Planning and Natural Resources told Business Insider. One visible change is that the temple-like building — where Epstein played music, according to a piano tuner — was repainted and lost its distinctive blue stripes. On August 17, 2025, Petersen and five other influencers and friends climbed into kayaks and pushed off from St. Thomas , headed to Little St. James. A Category 5 hurricane was pummeling the US Virgin Islands. The high waves and wind gusts of up to 30 miles per hour had foiled their previous plan to use air mattresses as rafts with pool noodles tied around their waists in case they capsized. Petersen and his crew believed the worst of Hurricane Erin was over and decided to make another attempt, this time with kayaks and life vests. Andrew Petersen, one of the YouTubers whom Deckoff accused of trespassing, kayaked to the island in a hurricane. Courtesy of SideQuest Drew Petersen told Business Insider he was dead-set on landing on Little St. James because he wanted to seek the truth about the island once owned by a famous pedophile who kept company with royalty, heads of state, and billionaires. Conspiracy theories about underground tunnels and child sacrifices proliferated online. Deckoff's announcement that he wanted to build a resort didn't make sense to him. The Trump administration, at the time, was refusing to release the Epstein files . The Justice Department has since released millions of Epstein-related records. "The main thing we were really kind of after is, let's just make noise with this," Petersen said. "Let's put up this 'Release the Files' flag on the island since the government's trying to hold back all the Epstein files and they're still holding it back to this day." Petersen said that the group anticipated potential legal consequences, including possibly jail time for misdemeanor trespassing. He viewed it as necessary for his work as a self-described independent journalist. "If we end up going to jail for 30 days, that would be pretty insane," Petersen said. "But we just thought this is something that we don't think anyone else would want to do." They landed on the island's beach, walked over to Epstein's so-called "temple," then made their way to the main house. Have a tip? Contact this reporter at jshamsian@businessinsider.com or on the secure messaging app Signal at JacobShamsian.07. Here's our guide to sharing information securely . Petersen and his group then realized they made a "huge miscalculation," he told Business Insider. The storm was getting worse again. They decided to stay the night. Videos the group posted to YouTube and Patreon show them poking through rooms, staring aghast at a statue of a suffering woman, and lamenting the lack of snacks in the kitchen cabinets. Petersen said he found no underground tunnel system on Little St. James. "We checked out all these little structures that people claimed were the entrance, and they definitely were not that," he told Business Insider. "So our conclusion on that end is: I don't think there's any crazy underground tunnels." When morning came, they took videos of themselves tying a "Release the Files" banner to a palm tree outside the temple. As they paddled away from the island, members of the island's security team yelled at them from the shore. Other influencers followed. In February, YouTuber Ashton Hall, who goes by "Ash Alk," rented a jet ski and swam ashore with a camera. "This is exactly how I managed to sneak onto Epstein's island, step by step," Hall said in a video he later posted to YouTube . Influencers called for the Justice Department to release its Epstein files. The DOJ has since released millions of Epstein-related records. Courtesy of SideQuest Drew On Little St. James, Hall staged what he called a "protest" to ask "whoever to unredact the files." Much of the video was spent complaining that he didn't have the proper footwear for the rocky beach. He urged Deckoff not to sue him. "I'm not anyone special or important," Hall said in the video. "I'm just a YouTuber, bro. Please don't sue me. I'm not that important." This year, Little St. James's caretakers began taking more aggressive tactics against unwelcome visitors. On March 1, two YouTuber brothers, Eloi and Marcel Gil Sancho, approached the island on rented jet skis. Marcel Gil Sancho has nearly a million subscribers to his YouTube channel , which has titles like "I spent 24 hours with the MOST DANGEROUS TRIBE in AFRICA" and "2 HEADS and 1 BODY! How do they live? Who's in charge?" The brothers flew a drone over the island to take footage for a documentary, Eloi Gil Sancho later told law enforcement officials . It landed on the island's beach, and Marcel swam ashore to retrieve it, then returned to his jet ski, Eloi Gil Sancho told US Virgin Islands police, according to a sworn statement filed to court. According to Eloi Gil Sancho's account, they were then intercepted by a boat piloted by Rodriquez, the island's caretaker. She pulled out what looked like a Glock handgun, pointed it at Marcel, and ordered him to swim to her boat, according to Eloi. "E. Gil Sancho stated that Ann Rodriquez was operating the boat and repeatedly yelled 'I will kill you' at them," a US Virgin Islands detective wrote in a sworn statement . A coast guard member who responded to the scene found Eloi "hog-tied and totally naked" in the back of the boat, according to the sworn statement. Marcel was taken back to one of the islands, Eloi told him. The weapon turned out to be a BB gun "designed to resemble a Glock 19-style handgun," according to another sworn statement . Rodriquez said she threw the Gils' memory cards with the drone footage into the ocean, according to the affidavit. In May, the US Virgin Islands Attorney General's office brought false imprisonment, assault, and destruction of property charges against Rodriquez. She hasn't entered a plea. Reached by phone, Rodriquez declined to comment. Deckoff's staff has, at times, responded to interlopers with violence, law-enforcement agencies have said in court filings. Bloomberg/Getty Images "Hell no, have a good day," she told Business Insider. On April 25 — weeks after the Sancho brothers' expedition to the island — a similar scene played out with two other men, Benjamin Owen and Ryan Dalton. Dalton is the founder of Closed Horizon, a sort of GoFundMe for solving conspiracy theories. Its website says 160 users have contributed $54,112.90 toward a $100,000 goal for an investigation to prove that Epstein is still alive . He told Business Insider he took the trip to bring attention to the campaign. "It's ground zero for the Epstein Criminal Network, and it's iconic," Dalton said. "And it's a place where we felt that it'd be really powerful to announce the reward program for proof of life." The two rented a boat, and Owen and Dalton swam ashore. Owen planned to plant a flag bearing the logo of his organization, We Fight Monsters, which assists victims of human trafficking and opioid addiction, he said in a June podcast interview . When they saw the temple-like building on the island, they "got a little excited" and "kind of forgot that you're not allowed to go beyond the beach," Owen said in the interview. A group approached on all-terrain vehicles. Owen and Dalton ran back to the water to swim to their boat, Dalton told Business Insider. Dalton made it, but when he turned around in the water to look, Owen was surrounded, Dalton said. One of the people on the island, Emery Poleon, called her mother, Rodriquez, Owen said on the podcast. "Mom tells her to duct tape me and put me in the dungeon," Owen said. "And I'm thinking in my head, 'What an awful choice of words for somebody who works for a billionaire trying to rebrand this island from what it used to be. Why would you call it the dungeon? That is a strange thing to say." Owen said that his wrists were zip-tied together. Law enforcement officials found him "restrained with duct tape," a police detective said in a sworn statement . Poleon later told a law enforcement officer that she had conducted a "citizen's arrest." US Virgin Islands prosecutors brought a trespassing charge against Owen and an assault charge against Poleon's boyfriend, Paul J. Arnold III, who prosecutors allege struck Owen. Arnold hasn't entered a plea. His attorney, David Cattie, declined to comment. Poleon declined to comment. Deckoff's holding company, LSJVI, LLC, has filed lawsuits against Owen and Dalton, Eloi and Marcel Gil Sancho, Hall, and Petersen and the passel of influencers he traveled with. In their videos, the influencers have cast themselves as truth-seeking warriors. Courtesy of SideQuest Drew Deckoff's lawsuits seek to disgorge the influencers and content creators of any money they made from their videos. Petersen told Business Insider his group had already donated $30,000 of revenue from the videos to Polaris, an organization that fights human trafficking. Hall and Eloi and Marcel Gil Sancho haven't publicly responded to the lawsuits and didn't respond to Business Insider's requests for comment. The suit against Owen and Dalton, filed in May, accused them of trespassing and called them delusional fame-seekers. "Defendants believe that they are entitled to trespass and burglarize property in their search for evidence that a man who died seven (7) years ago is alive and (maybe) living on Little St. James," the lawsuit says. The LLC is represented by Cattie, the attorney who represents Rodriquez and Arnold in their criminal cases. Cattie referred questions about the lawsuits to a spokesperson for Deckoff. Deckoff "will continue to pursue every legal remedy, particularly for people who film themselves trespassing and make money off subsequent videos," his spokesperson said. Deckoff's lawsuits seek to disgorge any money influencers have made from their videos. THE US JUSTICE DEPARTMENT/ Getty Images The office of US Virgin Islands Attorney General Gordon Rhea declined to comment on the prosecutions. Owen told CBS News he found it "scary" that there's "a billionaire coming after me." He declined to comment for this story. "My attorney got pretty upset with me for talking to media while my criminal case is still pending," Owen told Business Insider. Owen's attorney declined to comment. Dalton declined to comment on the lawsuit. Dalton said Little St. James will remain "a lightning rod for truth-seekers." "Our federal government has abdicated their duty to show the American people what happened there and prosecute the people involved," he said. "And so in absence of that, I think that there are a lot of people who are willing to go there and try to understand it." Read the original article on Business Insider

"Mom tells her to duct tape me and put me in the dungeon," Owen said. "And I'm thinking in my head, 'What an awful choice of words for somebody who works for a billionaire trying to rebrand this island from what it used to be. Why would you call it the dungeon? That is a strange thing to say."

Owen said that his wrists were zip-tied together. Law enforcement officials found him "restrained with duct tape," a police detective said in a sworn statement. Poleon later told a law enforcement officer that she had conducted a "citizen's arrest."

US Virgin Islands prosecutors brought a trespassing charge against Owen and an assault charge against Poleon's boyfriend, Paul J. Arnold III, who prosecutors allege struck Owen. Arnold hasn't entered a plea. His attorney, David Cattie, declined to comment. Poleon declined to comment.

Deckoff's holding company, LSJVI, LLC, has filed lawsuits against Owen and Dalton, Eloi and Marcel Gil Sancho, Hall, and Petersen and the passel of influencers he traveled with.

In their videos, the influencers have cast themselves as truth-seeking warriors.

Courtesy of SideQuest Drew

Deckoff's lawsuits seek to disgorge the influencers and content creators of any money they made from their videos. Petersen told Business Insider his group had already donated $30,000 of revenue from the videos to Polaris, an organization that fights human trafficking. Hall and Eloi and Marcel Gil Sancho haven't publicly responded to the lawsuits and didn't respond to Business Insider's requests for comment.

The suit against Owen and Dalton, filed in May, accused them of trespassing and called them delusional fame-seekers.

"Defendants believe that they are entitled to trespass and burglarize property in their search for evidence that a man who died seven (7) years ago is alive and (maybe) living on Little St. James," the lawsuit says.

The LLC is represented by Cattie, the attorney who represents Rodriquez and Arnold in their criminal cases. Cattie referred questions about the lawsuits to a spokesperson for Deckoff.

Deckoff "will continue to pursue every legal remedy, particularly for people who film themselves trespassing and make money off subsequent videos," his spokesperson said.

Deckoff's lawsuits seek to disgorge any money influencers have made from their videos.

THE US JUSTICE DEPARTMENT/ Getty Images

The office of US Virgin Islands Attorney General Gordon Rhea declined to comment on the prosecutions.

Owen told CBS News he found it "scary" that there's "a billionaire coming after me." He declined to comment for this story.

"My attorney got pretty upset with me for talking to media while my criminal case is still pending," Owen told Business Insider.

Owen's attorney declined to comment. Dalton declined to comment on the lawsuit.

Dalton said Little St. James will remain "a lightning rod for truth-seekers."

"Our federal government has abdicated their duty to show the American people what happened there and prosecute the people involved," he said. "And so in absence of that, I think that there are a lot of people who are willing to go there and try to understand it."
